# E P I S T L E

...to bring some work into the public light, they take pains to inscribe and consecrate it to some Great Person <term>Magnati: a person of high rank, wealth, or influence</term>, or a friend, or another patron, and they do this for four reasons in particular: namely, that by this very act they might devote not only their own names, but also the memory of the patron himself to a kind of immortality; next, that they might prepare for themselves a defense <term>patrocinium: the protection, support, or advocacy given by a patron</term> against the envious and biting <note>The Latin "caninosque dentes" literally means "dog-like teeth," a common metaphor for vicious or snarling critics.</note> critics who are always accustomed to gnaw at the works of others while failing to see their own, and who think nothing is right except what they do themselves; furthermore, so that some illustrious name prefixed to that work might be like an ivy-bush <note>In the early modern period, an ivy branch or wreath was the traditional sign hung outside a tavern to indicate that wine was sold within. The author is suggesting the Prince's name acts as a "brand" of quality.</note>, under whose sign—as if it were some noble wine—the work may be recognized, praised, and sold; and finally, so that there might be a public monument to testify to the respect and gratitude for favors received, and that the patron's kindness and generosity <term>munificentia: the quality of being lavishly generous, particularly a virtue expected of high-ranking nobility</term> may shine forth.

These very reasons, I say, also impelled me to lead my mind to inscribe and consecrate to Your Highness this inscrutable <term>Chymico-Philosophical: relating to the intersection of alchemy and natural philosophy</term> harmony. For if I wished to recount such great and varied favors of Your Highness toward me, this dedication would grow almost into a volume. Wherefore, in order that in some part...

Since alchemy is the true follower of nature, as Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and polymath whose works on nature and science were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> states, and is entirely produced and founded upon the operation of nature—especially since it is based on certain preparations of natural beings <note>original: "entium naturalium." In this context, "beings" refers to physical substances or entities found in the natural world.</note>—it will therefore be most fitting to know the properties of natural beings. Indeed, for those who do not wish to wander into error in this science, it is necessary to understand the origin and cause of these things, and first of all, to have a knowledge of the "naturalness" <note>original: "naturalitatis." This refers to the essential nature or the inherent qualities that make a thing what it is.</note> and the forms of beings. Since all natural things exist from these two principles <note>This likely refers to the Aristotelian concept of "matter" and "form" as the two primary principles of all physical things.</note>, it follows that one must know the operation of nature, so that through this science one may know how to rule and direct the work. Generally, and first, one must learn about the naturalness of natural things: how the wisdom of God divided the circles and spheres of the entire world into two separate parts, namely the natural world in one and the celestial in the other. The first part is the sphere <note>original: "orbis."</note> of the four elements <term>four elements|The traditional building blocks of the physical world: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</term>, beginning from the earth and reaching up to

sphere of the Moon, in which the second part of the world begins by ascending, even to the starry heaven, the first world was created in common matter <note>original: "materia communis." This refers to "prime matter" (materia prima), the formless "stuff" from which all things in the universe were thought to be made.</note>. Thus it is that the wisdom of God created matter endowed with form, about which the Philosophers and the Teachers of Holy Scripture <note>original: "Doctores scripturæ sacræ." The author is harmonizing Greek philosophy (like Aristotle) with Christian theology.</note> write many things. He further divided this matter into four parts, and He endowed each one specifically with coldness, heat, dryness, and humidity. These properties and forms—such as heat and cold—are contrary by nature and cannot stand together in the same place. Therefore, within the aforementioned matter, these properties were divided separately into four parts, which are called the four elements. This was done so that, through an intermediary <note>The author is referring to the Aristotelian idea that you cannot combine two opposites (like fire and water) without a middle ground that shares a quality with both.</note>, coldness could be joined to heat and humidity to dryness. Consequently, it was brought about that all natural things could exist in their "naturalness" through the joining together of these four elements.

And for this reason, the four elements were created for the sake of the inherent nature of all things: because every thing has its natural existence from the mixing and joining together of the four elements. This is not to be understood as if each element were joined to another on its own—for naturally one element resists the place of another—but rather that one is compressed, drawn, and <term>sublimated</term> <note>In this context, sublimation refers to the process of a substance being refined or "raised up" into a higher state through the action of heat.</note> into another. Thus, we will never find a simple and pure element without the mixture of another. Hence, in truth, we will not find earth so dried out that it does not contain moisture within itself; nor will we find water that does not contain "earthiness" <note>original: "terrestreitas." This refers to the solid, mineral-like residue or sediment often found in water or left behind after distillation.</note>, as is observed when distilling water. Indeed, it is very rare to find earth without its own internal heat,

<header>And the Alchemical Art.</header>

<sig>A 5</sig>

<meta>catchword: men.</meta>

And it should be noted <note>The Latin transcription reads "potandum" (to drink), but the context and typical manuscript shorthand strongly suggest "notandum" (to be noted).</note> how in every visible thing—that is, visible to the eyes—heat (which is fire) is enclosed within earth, and air within water. Exactly how these things come to be is not very important to know here. Rather, we must simply understand that from the beginning, by joining the four elements, nature prepares the **common matter** <term>common matter: also known as "prime matter," the basic, formless substance from which all things are made</term> of all things. The more nature makes this matter subtle, active, and fit—digesting and preparing it for a specific form—the closer it is to its eventual shape, and the more quickly the **form of the thing** <term>form: in medieval philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or identity of a thing that gives the raw matter its specific characteristics</term> appears. 

This is just as a craftsman at the beginning of his work takes a rough material and works a likeness out of it: the more finely he shapes, removes, and moves the material, the more the image appears. Once the material is prepared and the excess parts are removed, the completed form of the object is revealed. In this way, the form is led out and extracted by stripping away the excesses of the material; nature acts in exactly the same way. 

First, nature creates a suitable matter from the four elements and applies its operation to this matter until it removes and separates the impurity and the excess parts. It refines the matter until it is so subtle and active that the form of the thing perfectly appears and exists. But if the matter still retains some stain or impurity, then the form of the thing does not appear perfectly or in its entirety, but is instead defiled by that impurity. Thus, all forms of natural things are drawn out from the pre-existing matter, and every natural thing—whether it be **animal**, **vegetable**, or **mineral**—takes its primary matter from the four ele- <note>The word continues on the next page as "elementorum" (elements).</note>

# On the Principles of Nature

<meta>The text begins by completing the word "elements" from the previous page.</meta>

...elements, Nature receives them, and from them the **form** <term>form: in medieval philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature or identity that makes a substance a specific thing, like a "lion" or "gold," rather than just raw matter</term> is subsequently drawn out. Thus, all things are included in these three categories: they are either things that must sprout—such as all plants, trees, and herbs—or they are things that neither sprout nor grow <note>The author is distinguishing between biological growth and the "growth" or formation of minerals in the earth</note>, such as all stones and minerals, and these are called **metallics**. Each of these three categories is further divided into many various parts. 

So it is that among animal things there are humans, lions, bears, sheep, cattle, and so on. Likewise, the vegetable nature is divided into many parts: for some are either the vine <note>original: "vinum", literally "wine", but here referring to the source plant</note>, or wheat, or an apple or a pear, the pear tree or the apple tree, and so forth. In the same way, metallic things are multiplied: for some are stones, and others are minerals, and so on. 

And just as things are multiplied or divided, so they have many various materials. Such a complex natural character comes from the many ways the elements <note>original: "metallorum". While the Latin word usually means "metals," the author immediately lists the four elements (earth, water, air, fire), suggesting he views these as the "metallic" or fundamental building blocks of matter</note> are joined together. For example, perhaps five parts of earth, three parts of water, two parts of air, and one part of fire are joined; or in another compound, six parts of water, four parts of earth, one part of fire, and three parts of air are joined; and this is true for every individual thing. 

In other things it is done differently, and the ways these elements can be joined in unequal proportions are beyond counting. So too, the parts and the materials of all things are innumerable. Such a joining of elements according to the **right proportion** <term>proportion: the specific "recipe" or ratio of the four elements that defines a specific substance</term> of any given thing is known only to Nature. She alone knows the certain measure of how much to take from each element as it suits the matter of things. And when she has reached the right proportion through her mediating actions, and has adapted it to the **common matter** <term>common matter: the basic, underlying substance shared by all physical things before they take on a specific identity</term>, then the form and essence of the thing...

# And the Alchemical Art
<meta>catchword: such</meta>

...appears. But for such an operation, purpose, and final goal, and for the preparation <note>original: "habilitationem," meaning the process of making the elements fit or capable of taking on a specific form</note> of the elements, the influences and powers of the stars and planets serve greatly. These powers help Nature to work, to join, and to unite the elements, much like the skill within a craftsman. This is the means by which he draws out the figure and shape of an image, just as the image held in the craftsman's heart shapes and formats that same image into the physical material.

It is the same in matter if the celestial influences serve the matter toward the form of fish; they then help to join, prepare, and ready the elements so that from such a conjunction and union, the form and essence of fish may appear. But if the influences and heavenly powers serve the form of **gold**, Nature also works through these intermediaries upon such a compound of elements until the elements are united in such a way that gold arises from that substance and essence. 

Just as every specific proportion of elements brings forth a particular appearance, state of form, and essence—much like an accumulation of many different things creates many different species and forms in their gathering—it is united and joined in the elements so that perfect forms exist. These are the forms which the influences or virtues of the stars, descending from the higher realms into matter, were intended to serve. Then the work of Nature ceases, because it has brought its intention to its final end, just as a craftsman stops once he has drawn out the form of the thing which he had held in his heart to bring forth in the material. Thus, Nature always works through stellar influences and powers, which are the **seeds of forms** <term>seeds of forms: original "semina formarum." A philosophical concept suggesting that the "blueprints" or spiritual potentials of all physical things are planted into matter by the stars or the divine</term>, because through...

# On the Principles of Nature
<meta>catchword: accumu-</meta>

...such <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of celestial influences.</note> virtues, matter is inclined toward a form similar to those virtues. When the form is prepared and drawn out from the matter through these mediating virtues, Nature then ceases its work; it no longer operates to produce that specific form, as it has been fully prepared and perfected. 

However, from that point on, such a thing receives either growth or decay according to how Nature continues to work within it—at least, provided the thing is of a kind that can increase or decrease. These influences of the stars are called the **generative virtues** <note>original: "virtutes feminalitatis," literally "virtues of feminality." In this philosophical context, it refers to the receptive, nurturing power—likened to a womb—that allows a form to take root and grow in matter.</note> of the form. Because there are generally three types of natural existence—namely, **animal** (or things that sprout), **vegetable**, and **metallic**—there are likewise three influences of generative power and of the virtue of forms: the animal, the vegetable, and the metallic.

Regarding these virtues, a few things must be understood. The formal virtue and the **generative force** <note>original: "vis feminalis"</note> descend from the higher realms first to the elements. From the elements, they proceed into the general nature of things, where they are included and preserved. They remain there to help "draw out" the natural form from the matter, as stated above. 

These virtues descend via the rays of the stars, as if traveling down their own dedicated paths into the lower world—that is, to the four elements. They are gathered in great abundance especially in the **earth**, because the earth is the **center** <note>original: "medium," referring to the Aristotelian view of Earth as the heavy center of the universe toward which all things fall.</note> of the elements. It is in the earth that all the rays of the stars are accumulated. The earth, drawing to itself the generative forces of the forms of all things, allows them to be collected and gathered together, just as all the lines of a circle are united at a single center point. And if the rays of the stars accumu- <note>The text breaks here; the catchword "accumu-" suggests the next page continues with the "accumulation" of these stellar rays.</note>

...the influences of celestial virtues descending from the higher realms. To capture these virtues, and especially those of metals, the Philosopher **Ramon Llull** <note>Raymundus Lullius (c. 1232–1315). While Llull was a famous Majorcan philosopher and logician, many alchemical texts were later attributed to him by followers seeking to lend authority to their work; these are now called "Pseudo-Lullian" works.</note> devised certain waters to be prepared and placed beneath the earth. Into these waters, these virtues ought to be captured and stored, since it is the nature of celestial virtues and the "seeds" of things that when they descend into the earth, they are moved—and in turn, they move—to procure and increase certain **agile spirits**. <note>original: *spiritus agiles*. In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances or refined energies that can bridge the gap between the physical and the celestial.</note> They do this by condensing and preparing these spirits for themselves as a seat and a support, as Llull says again. 

And if by our art we can prepare a suitable and agile spirit—that is, a **subtle matter** <note>original: *materia subtilis*. This occurs because the aforementioned virtues draw or seize from the prepared spirits; for as Llull says, such spirits and subtle matter placed in the earth attract virtues coming from above from a distance greater than two bolts from a crossbow. 

Just as a **magnet** <note>original: *magnes*. Alchemists often used the magnet as a primary example of "action at a distance" to explain how invisible celestial forces could affect physical objects on earth.</note> attracts iron, so by these instruments are the mineral virtues coming from above captured. Literally "the mercury of the common people," referring to ordinary quicksilver as found in nature, rather than the "Philosophical Mercury" sought by adepts.</note> into good silver without any need for fire. They possess great and even supreme power if they are captured in high and subtle matter. But as for how this water is prepared, Llull himself explains...

Therefore, we must know only the natural properties of gold and the virtues of the form of gold, and even their disadvantages, since from these two gold is procreated. ### ON PRECIOUS STONES.

Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on the natural sciences and minerals.</note> says in the third chapter on stones: although nature is the beginning and origin of art <note>In this context, "art" refers to alchemy, viewed as a method of assisting or accelerating natural processes.</note>, it will therefore be most fitting to first know the natural beginning and procreation of metals. In a similar way, Geber, King of Spain <note>original: *Geber Rex Hispaniæ*. This refers to the author of the *Summa perfectionis*, a foundational alchemical text traditionally attributed to the 8th-century Arabic polymath Jabir ibn Hayyan, though likely written by a 13th-century European author.</note>, says in the first chapter or of his *Summa*: if anyone does not know the beginning or origin of nature, and likewise does not know the naturalness and **formal virtue** <note>original: *formalem virtutem*. The internal "blueprint" or spiritual power that gives a substance its specific properties.</note> of gold, he is far removed from our art; for he has no root upon which to found his intention. And again in the same work he says: he who does not know the origin of the way metals are generated according to the intention of nature—even if he knows the starting point—cannot reach the end of this science; because this art, as the Master of Ferrara <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a 14th-century alchemist.</note> says in chapter 27, consists in the recognition of the **matter of gold** and the operation of nature.

Thus, the art imitates nature’s operation as much as it can. For Albertus says in the first chapter of his book on metals <note>original: *libro metallorum*, referring to his treatise *De Mineralibus*.</note>: the matter of stones, from which stones are formed, is not far removed from the elements. That is to say, no full transmutation of the elements—namely water and earth, which are the matter of stones—has yet taken place. As this same Albertus posits in chapter 20 of the first book, the matter of stones is, in its first degree, a **viscosity** <note>original: *viscositas*. A sticky, glue-like quality believed to bind elemental earth together into solid rock.</note> and an earthy humidity. Thus, coarse stones are generated from earth mixed with a viscous humidity. But the **transparency** <note>original: *perspicuitas*. Referring to the clarity and light-reflecting quality of gems.</note> of precious stones comes from their matter being water mixed in some way with a subtle and agile earth, so that a perfect transformation of water and earth has not yet occurred, as happens in the matter of metals.

<summary>This page argues that alchemical success requires a deep understanding of how nature naturally forms minerals. It defines the physical composition of stones as a mixture of earth and water, distinguished by their degree of viscosity and clarity.</summary>

Nature has digested, boiled, and prepared this quicksilver by using sulfur as a middle agent.

This most pure **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> alone, being free from all coarse sulfurousness, is fixed into **gold**. In this way, the first method of the natural generation of gold is made clear.

And if the quicksilver receives any impurities, or if some obstacle or harm should befall it through excessive heat, or through the weakness of the fire, or through an unclean location or matter—that is, if the quicksilver has been mixed with coarse and unclean **sulfurousness** <note>original: "sulphuritate"</note>, or if some other disadvantage or obstacle occurs which nature cannot consume, separate, and boil down—then gold is not made from it. # On the Alchemical Art

<header>And the Alchemical Art.</header>

Certain things follow from which sound doctrine and the greatest subtlety can be drawn to perfect the final result. Now let us approach the art; and it must be noted that although art imitates nature, it cannot imitate it in every way and in all parts. Specifically, in the generation of gold, art does not imitate nature exactly, because nature generates gold from **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"</note> or from **imperfect metals** <note>base metals like lead or copper that were considered "unripe" forms of gold</note> by removing their unclean **sulfurity** <term>sulfurity; the combustible or "oily" principle within metals believed to cause corruption, rust, and foul odors</term>. 

First, the art is unable to do this because it does not have, and cannot have, such a specific **digestion** <term>digestion; the process of slow, consistent heating intended to "ripen" a substance</term> and temperate heat for the quicksilver. Second, it is unable because it would be impractical for a human to wait as long as nature does to remove the impure sulfurity from imperfect metals. 

And even if art can imitate nature most closely and in many ways, it still only imitates it in certain parts, as far as it is able. Therefore, there are some who have been unable to remove the sulfurity from the imperfect metals themselves when preparing a **tincture** <term>tincture; a highly concentrated substance or "medicine" used to transform base metals into gold or silver</term> or **medicine**. For those who do not remove the unclean sulfurity of the quicksilver and imperfect metals, but only hide and cover such filth—creating the appearance of gold or silver—are doing what is false and forbidden by all the **Philosophers** <note>in this context, "philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval authorities on alchemy and natural science</note>. 

Therefore, those who "tint" the entire substance of imperfect metals so that no impurity is removed from them are **falsifiers** <note>original: "falsarii"; counterfeiters or fraudulent alchemists</note>, because the "evil sulfur" remains within them. True gold, however, must not contain such sulfur within itself. Still, others intend to purge imperfect metals entirely of their sulfurity or sulfur using certain waters, salivas, and with 
alu <meta>catchword: alu (likely "alumen" or alum)</meta>

# And the Alchemical Art

<page-num>31</page-num>

...powers in the vegetable nature; but it is required that through multiple purification and distillation they arrive at a metallic nature, and finally serve it. Therefore, there is only one stone and one foundation necessary for the art, namely the **metallic virtue** <note>the inherent power or essential property that allows a substance to act upon metals</note>. Although sometimes vegetable or animal things are taken up <note>alchemists often experimented with organic matter like hair, blood, or plants</note>, they nonetheless do not remain in the vegetable or animal nature, but are transmuted into a metallic and sulfurous nature which contains the metallic power. 

For this reason, **Ferrariensis** <note>Likely referring to the 14th-century alchemist Guilelmus Tecenensis or perhaps Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*</note> said in the twentieth chapter of his *Questions*: it is impossible to **coagulate** <term>coagulate; to turn a liquid substance, like mercury, into a solid or semi-solid state</term> **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> without sulfur or some other thing that possesses a sulfurous nature; for sulfur is the coagulant of quicksilver. And if sulfurous qualities are present in wine—since it is flammable <note>original: "urens," literally "burning"</note>—then a metallic nature is present within it. 

Because of this, there are some who labor with wine and gold or silver, so that they may draw from the wine its most agile **spirit** <term>spirit of wine; a historical term for ethanol or concentrated alcohol, prized for its ability to dissolve substances</term>. They use this to strengthen the virtue of gold, so that the spirits may be **fixed** <term>fixed; rendered stable and non-volatile so they do not evaporate when heated</term> with it. By these means, the **tincture of gold** <note>the concentrated essence or "color" of gold used to transmute other metals</note> is subsequently expanded and multiplied. Certainly, between the spirit of wine and the spirit of gold, there is the greatest agreement or participation, since both possess a hot nature. Therefore, the spirit of wine is inseparably fixed with gold. 

But it should be noted that the spirits of the **middle metals**—namely **vitriol** <term>vitriol; sulfate minerals used to create powerful acidic "spirits"</term> and the like—possess a coarse frictional quality <note>original: "grossi oris frixionis"; likely referring to the sharp or corrosive "bite" of mineral acids</note> and have a greater agreement with gold, since they arise as if from the same source: that is, from the ores of metals. This is more so than the spirits of wine, which come from the vegetable nature, even though the spirits of wine are more agile and subtle.

<page-num>40</page-num>

...maining. Therefore, it will be nothing else than this: first, if at least a correct and certain **tincture** <term>tincture; a transformative essence or "dye" used by alchemists to change the properties of metals</term> is to be produced, one must have an **active substance of mercury** <note>original: "substantia agilis mercurii"; this refers to a purified, "living" state of mercury, different from common quicksilver</note> that is optimally prepared in terms of its degree and essence, just as nature forms it within the earth. In the same way, when nature has most actively perfected mercury, she then infuses into it the **form of gold** <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the internal principle that gives a substance its specific identity—in this case, making it gold rather than just matter.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that we obtain this active mercury, and into this we must infuse and restore the tincture. Whether we receive this mercury from **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, or from gold, or from whatever source such active matter might come, it is required that it be **subtle** <term>subtle; refined, vaporous, or purified of all heavy, "gross" material</term>, clear, clean, and pure, just as it was in the beginning when nature first led it into the form of gold.

And for this reason, the first book of the **Stoics** <note>The author attributes this alchemical principle to Stoic philosophers, who viewed the world as permeated by a rational, active spirit.</note> says: "In the subtlety of our art, let us prepare the matter so that we may bring forth a thing similar to how it was at the very beginning, freed from every adverse transmutation." That is to say, it must be a **simple thing** <note>A "simple" substance in alchemy is one that has been purified down to its basic essence, separated from the "gross" or "earthy" impurities of the four elements.</note> separated from the earthy substance of the elements—not that it is a thing entirely without elements, but rather a thing most subtly prepared. 

And therefore **Plato** <note>The author uses Plato to highlight the difference between natural growth and alchemical artifice.</note> says: "Our operation is not entirely like the operation of nature; because nature makes **composite** <term>composite; a physical object made of mixed elements, as opposed to a pure, simple essence</term> and natural things out of simple elements." But we do the opposite. For when we make simple things out of composite ones—such as from gold—we separate the active nature and the essence, from which we then create a composite thing, which is the tincture. And this simple and extracted thing is called **matter** in this context; therefore, active mercury is a thing which nature did not "perfect," because she did not make a tincture from it, but only gave it a form, further...

The method here is similar: if indeed gold is reduced into this active mercury and its form is given back to it, then it is most greatly activated and refined for **penetration** <term>penetration; the ability of an alchemical substance to soak into and transform another metal</term>. 

And let this be said concerning one part, namely the matter of gold, which is rightly called the **mercury of the Philosophers** <note>A specialized, purified form of mercury believed to be the "seed" of all metals, distinct from common quicksilver.</note>, which is the medium for joining the tincture. **Geber** <note>An influential alchemist, typically identified with Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note> writes many things about this in his *Summa*, and through this, the whole work is most easily completed. And therefore it is called the **manifest stone** <note>original: "lapis patens"; the aspect of the Philosopher's Stone that is visible or external.</note>. Now we must speak of the **hidden stone**, which is called its form and soul.

### On the Principles of Nature

...[is] dead and robbed of its soul: for it is itself matter. Therefore, let us return its form and soul to it, so that it may be made alive and stabilized. Therefore, the proper form must be applied to this matter; and it should be known that such a form is nothing other than **gold**. 

Although the aforementioned matter <note>referring to the refined mercury discussed on the previous page</note> could appropriately be called "form" or "soul" in relation to gold—and gold itself could be called "matter" and "body" because this matter is more active than gold—nevertheless, in this context, this active matter is called "body" or "matter." And the body of gold is called "form" and "soul"; because, as **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; referring to the Persian scholar Al-Razi. He suggests here a reversal of roles: the solid "body" provides the structure or "form" for the volatile "spirit."</note> says, the body is the form, while the spirit is the matter. And he speaks well, because matter does not have its existence without form, just as that active matter does not have its being and permanence except from the body of gold. 

For this reason, the body and gold serve as a kind of bond and form for the aforementioned **mercury** <term>mercury; here referring to the philosophical or "sophic" mercury, a purified essence rather than common quicksilver</term>. And therefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of the Hermetic arts.</note> says: "Without the **red stone** <note>original: "lapide rubeo"; the Philosopher's Stone in its final state, capable of transmuting metals into gold.</note>, a true tincture is not made." 

Likewise, **Geber** <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy.</note> says: "No metal is submerged in mercury, except gold." But he ought to say: gold is liquefied and submerged in the aforementioned mercury if a **tincture** <term>tincture; a transformative liquid or powder used to change the properties of a substance</term> is to be made from it. And again, he says in his *Summa*: "With gold, spirits are mixed and are fixed by the subtlety of art." 

Also, **Morienus** <note>original: "Morigines"; a legendary hermit-alchemist known for his dialogues with King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: "The work is not brought to completion until gold and silver are joined"; and by "silver," he signifies the mercury mentioned before. And this is what **Rhazes** intends when he says: "The red servant," as mentioned above, etc. Also, this means...

### And of the Alchemical Art

**Virgil** intends this in the sixth book of the *Aeneid* <note>original: "6. Æneid."; referring to the famous passage where Aeneas must find the Golden Bough to enter the underworld.</note> in a certain story where he describes how **Aeneas** and the **Sibyl** approached a thicket: and when the middle part of the branch was plucked, it always grew back. And this is the "golden river" which **Ovid** and many poets have hidden within the wit of their speeches. Such gold and such an art is called **ferment** <term>ferment; a substance (like yeast in bread) that transforms and "leavens" a larger mass of matter into a higher state</term>, which perfects the **tincture** <term>tincture; the color-changing essence that allows for transmutation</term>. Certainly, the entire art lies hidden within it, since it is the body that retains the soul. For just as the soul cannot demonstrate its powers except within a body, so the tincture is not perfected without the introduction of the body.

Therefore, as soon as this matter has been extracted, arisen, and prepared, let it be brought back to the body and the ferment; for by this it is stabilized, so that it does not flee, and is fixed. And this is what **Plato** means when he says in the fourth book of the Stoics <note>A likely reference to a pseudo-Platonic alchemical text common in the Middle Ages; the "Stoics" here refers to a specific section or school of thought within that tradition.</note>: "Let the soul be joined to this body from which it came, and no other: because it has no life except through its own body." Just as dough does not want to be leavened with something foreign, but with its own nature, so the aforementioned **mercury** is not fermented by anything other than its own body. 

And for this reason **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says that the ferment of gold is nothing other than gold. Although the **first matter** <term>materia prima; the base, chaotic substance before it is refined</term> may be white, it is nevertheless of a golden nature, because it comes from gold, and in the end it is transmuted into a saffron redness when the ferment is applied to it. And these are those two elements which are joined into one, namely the **moist** and the **dry**. The "moist" is that agile mercury extracted from gold, which has been made volatile and fluid; and this is accomplished through the first operation.

### On the Principles of Nature

...fermentation. This body is called the **hidden stone**, because none of the **Philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophorum"; a term alchemists used to refer to themselves and their predecessors</note> could wonder enough at how it was that the aforementioned fugitive mercury would attract the body placed near it and make that body fugitive as well; and conversely, how the fixed body would pull back the fugitive mercury and preserve it forever so that it would not flee. For they are of one nature; therefore they are united.

Consequently, that body is called the **hidden stone** because it alone carries the agilities and virtues that are not perceived by the senses, except when they are captured solely through the aforementioned pure and extracted mercury, which is placed before these virtues.

Thus **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 13th-century authority in alchemy.</note> speaks, saying: "Mercury cannot have a saffron <note>original: "croceum"; a deep yellow color signaling the approach of the final gold-making stage</note> color except by the mixing of a tinging substance which is known to Nature alone." Note: he believes this is **gold**, because it secretly contains the entire **tincture** <term>tincture; the essential "soul" or color-changing power of the stone</term>. And for this reason, he says elsewhere: "For gold is the perfect tincture."

And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of the Hermetic and alchemical tradition.</note> says this: "This is the **blessed stone**; without its mixing, the manifest stones—that is, the entire tincture of the aforementioned mercury—perish." And this blessed stone is the heart, the form, and the tincture of gold, which all the Philosophers seek. Concerning this, Hermes writes, saying: "Even at the end of this age, **heaven and earth are joined together**," <note>original: "cælum & terra conjunguntur"</note> understanding by "heaven" and "earth" the two entities mentioned before.

And this work is bipartite, meaning it has two parts. The first part concerns the **preparation of mercury**; the second concerns the **fixation** and **fermentation** of that same mercury; because then...

# And the Alchemical Art.

...the true union of the elements takes place; because the active principle <note>original: "res agens"</note> and the passive virtue <note>original: "virtus patiens"</note> are rightly joined, uniting together. And thus when such things are composed and rightly prepared, as is appropriate, and placed in a glass vessel <note>original: "in vitro"</note> at a tempered heat, then nature acts of its own accord. Just as nature works the form within natural matter beneath the earth; so it does also in the glass vessel within the proposed and prepared matter. 

For since matter is the foundation of birth <note>original: "ortus"; meaning the origin or rising of a new substance</note>: if it is rightly disposed in all ways, it then receives the operations and conceives the form of the thing for which the matter was intended, just as the influences and operations of the stars <term>influences of the stars; the alchemical belief that celestial bodies directed the growth and "ripening" of metals underground</term> are always present. 

And therefore, art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Great Art" or *Ars Magna*</note> is solely the preparation, the preparer, and the enabler of matter. But nature, for its part, works the form within such matter as is fitting; thus from the two aforementioned things, only one substance is produced which tinges metals into gold. Such a substance is called the true and right **soul** and **form** of gold, and this is a necessary result. 

For this reason **Plato** <note>Alchemists frequently cited Plato’s theory of "Forms" to explain how a material could be transformed by changing its internal essence.</note> posited certain separate forms, where men thought this form could only be joined to its matter through alchemy—that is, to the most subtle matters existing within imperfect metals. Yet this form does not accept the metals in their entirety, but only the most subtle and purest matter which leads to gold, leaving behind the other hidden matter. 

And so the intention of the alchemists is not the making of gold, but they only intend to create a thing higher than gold: namely, the **tincture** <term>tincture; a potent liquid or powder, often called the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "staining" or transforming base metals into gold</term>, which acts as the very form of gold. And this form is also called the **ferment**.

# On the Principles of Nature

...[fermen]t, both in respect to imperfect metals, although gold may be the ferment in respect to the aforementioned extracted mercury. And this mercury and its ferment are of one and the same nature: because the body penetrates the mercury and is united with it, so that the ferment is made spiritual, subtle, and agile, just like mercury; and they are united just as water mixed with water. Thus, that which was hidden in the body is made manifest, and the manifest is hidden, in the same way that melted wax is of one nature with hard wax, and conversely, hard wax with liquid. 

And from these two, a single **coagulum** <term>coagulum; a thickening or curdling agent, often compared to rennet in cheesemaking</term> is made; in a similar way as rennet curdles only those parts of the milk that are of the nature of cheese, and does not curdle the whole of the milk into cheese, but only certain parts. The **tincture** <term>tinctura; the "medicine" or elixir used to "dye" and transform base metals into gold</term> does not curdle all parts of the imperfect metals, but only those which agree with gold, and those alone it tints into gold. These parts are nothing other than pure **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>; however, it does not tint the remaining parts. 

Likewise, it should be known that in a similar way, when clean and pure quicksilver is curdled, that is gold and a perfect metal. But if sulfur alone is congealed, it remains totally dead; however, when sulfur and quicksilver are congealed together, that is an imperfect metal, and such sulfur is stripped away and separated from those imperfect metals, if indeed the work is to be completed. And just as nature removes such sulfur in its ores <note>original: "mineris"</note> from those imperfect metals over a long period of time; so Art...

### And the Alchemical Art.

...through the mediation of the **tincture** <term>tinctura; the alchemical "medicine" or elixir used to transform base metals into gold</term>, it accomplishes this in a short time.

And if the **imperfect metals** <note>original: "metalla imperfecta"; base metals such as lead, tin, or copper, which alchemists believed were "growing" toward the perfection of gold</note> share in the nature of gold, it is specifically through those properties in which they agree: for just as gold is malleable and fluid when melted, so too are the other imperfect metals. This is a sign of their proximity; and the more closely things agree in nature, the more willingly they are mixed, united, and received by one another. For it is manifest that the other metals flow together with gold into a single compound, which other things—such as stones, wood, and herbs—do not do. And this is a certain sign of the kinship of nature between gold and the other metals.

Therefore, the **art** <note>original: "ars"; specifically the Art of Alchemy</note> teaches us to **transmute** <term>transmutare; the process of changing one substance into another</term> imperfect metals into gold, but not other things such as stones and so on. This is because of the great difference between the nature of gold and those objects; indeed, it would be a most great and miraculous thing to transmute such objects, if they had to be reduced to a **matter** <term>materia; the underlying substance or "stuff" of a thing</term> that could receive the tincture and form of gold. If this matter were not already found prepared within the imperfect metals themselves, the art of alchemy would be entirely invalid. However, since nature has already prepared such matter within the imperfect metals, the art is therefore possible. Through this art, and with the mediation of nature, we are able to prepare the form and matter of those metals from certain **spirits** <note>original: "spiritibus"; in alchemy, volatile substances like sulfur or mercury that were thought to give metals their properties</note> in which metallic virtues reside, in the manner written above.

<summary>This page explains that alchemy is possible because metals share a common "kinship" and physical properties like malleability. It argues that while you cannot turn stones or wood into gold, you can transmute base metals because nature has already provided the necessary underlying "matter" within them.</summary>

# On the Principles of Nature

And let this be said as a **general instruction** <note>original: "documentum generale"</note> for ingenious and true **Alchemists** <term>Alchymista; practitioners of the art of transmutation and chemical medicine</term>, who—through the refinements and experiments regarding the **principles of the art** <note>original: "principiorum artis"; the fundamental laws or starting points of alchemical work</note> in their operations—will without a doubt find the **truth** <note>original: "veritas"; here meaning the successful discovery of the Philosopher's Stone or the realization of the Great Work</note>, provided they understand the aforementioned points well and take them to heart.

[The na]ture <note>original: "tura"; likely "natura"</note> of all metals can be preserved, destroyed, and converted into another nature, according to the "more and the less" <note>This refers to the intensity or "degree" of a quality</note>. They also have the power to provide, preserve, and remove whiteness; indeed, every other color is known to be compatible with metals through them. They also possess the power and virtue of granting, maintaining, and removing porosity, and consequently of bestowing fixity <term>fixity: the state of being "fixed" or stable when exposed to fire, preventing evaporation</term> and removing impurity. They can also grant, preserve, and drive away coldness, moisture, dryness, and heat, according to the more and the less.

Take it, therefore, according to the power it possesses in the degrees of its own nature.

**Compound medicine** <term>compound medicine: a complex alchemical preparation, often a precursor to the Philosopher's Stone, designed to "heal" base metals into noble ones</term> was invented for this purpose: to address various "sicknesses" and temperaments <note>imbalances in the metal's qualities</note>. In this way, the circulation of all elements is achieved.

Thus, Fire recovers its heat, which had been weakened by the qualities of the other elements. Air similarly recovers its moisture, Water its coldness, Earth its dryness, and so on. Through this mixture occurs the mingling of the elements. Once the Elements have been separated and reduced to their simple states <note>stripped of their combined forms to reach their pure, primal nature</note> as much as possible, one must proceed to the mixing in this way. It might seem that a middle state arises from fire and water, or from air and earth, but it is not so; this is because the secondary qualities are not in the same degree as the primary ones. Therefore, in the balancing of the Elements, there is a double path. One way is to preserve the primary qualities and reduce the secondary ones to the same degree as the primaries—for example, with fire, which is dry at the end of the third degree, you would reduce it <note>or "bring it up"</note> to the end of the fourth.

The other path is more apparent, yet it is the same: you preserve the primary qualities and entirely destroy the secondaries. For instance, you might destroy the dryness in fire so that only the heat remains. Thus, since one degree contains sixty minutes, four degrees contain two hundred and forty minutes.

I speak, therefore, of balancing fire in this manner: Fire is hot in the fourth degree and dry at the end of the third. And this is one reason for the <term>multiplication of the medicine: the alchemical process of increasing the quantity or potency of the "Philosopher's Stone"</term>. And thus from the equalized mixture of the elements arises a single incorruptible **quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence," a celestial substance superior to the four earthly elements and immune to decay.</note>, since there is no action nor passion <note>In Aristotelian physics, "action and passion" refers to the way elements react to and change one another; a substance without them is eternal and unchanging.</note> between them, and it is so enduring that it is one [and the same], which was my principal intention.

**Vocabulary:** elements, fire, earth, water, air, quintessence, medicine, proportion, balanced state.

# THE BOOK OF
# LIGHTS
## BY RHAZES OF CHESTER,
### THE MOST CELEBRATED PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN.
->Most Celebrated.<- <note>original: "Celeberrimi"</note>

---

> If you, an athlete, desire to undergo alchemical labors,
> Then undergo these four nimble pyres:
> So that they do not flee away, thinned out into smoke,
> Those aerial birds, their flight put to rout by the mass; <note>In alchemy, "birds" or "volatile spirits" refer to substances that easily evaporate or sublimate when heated.</note>
> First mortify the living spirits and restrain their rages,
> Gathering them together with their fluid cold,
> Until they come forth at last, compelled by such chains,
> And become like an exceedingly white gem.
> Let the water, which penetrates, cook and cement them together
> Until the desired work is reached.
> Let arsenic, sulfur, and salt be joined with Mercury,
> To which the title of Ammoniac <note>original: "Armonis." Likely referring to Sal Ammoniac (ammonium chloride), a vital reagent in medieval alchemy.</note> gave praise,
> So that just as Uzifur <note>original: "Uzifur." An archaic term for cinnabar or vermilion (mercury sulfide).</note> is a fixed connection once put to flight,
> So may there be a stony mass of the three mercuries:
> Mixed in equal weight under the same volume of liquid,
> Let them be dried first, and afterwards let the heating wave cook them.
> Once cooked, let them become a stone; once dissolved, a stone again;
> Let the appearance of shining crystal be within it.
> The son of the bird, generated in a single night,
> Let him gather into a mass, so that it becomes the stone itself. <note>The "Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note>

<summary>This is the title page for the "Book of Lights," attributed to the medieval authority Rhazes of Chester. It features an allegorical poem describing the stabilization of volatile spirits into a "stony mass" or "white gem," representing the early stages of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It is brought about as if by a falling force.
An uncertain spirit, moving forward and returning,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Joins these parts together after they have been divided and cut back.
Once it has seized a part, it does not know how to let go;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Separated by its own strength, yet a strong associating force.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as a flame seeks the lowest depths through the middle of the smoke.
The fat of the milk <note>original: "adeps." The cream or butter.</note> becomes moist and hot like air,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Providing fuel for the fire, slippery and light.
What remains is thus proven to be hot and dry to you:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Drying and dissolving with a light moisture.
This is the hidden cause which gives precious things from vile ones,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And transfers to the interior what it takes from the exterior.

--- The <term>Lunar Pill</term> <note>original: "Pillula lunaris" — the tincture for making silver.</note>, let it become the thinnest silver <note>original: "Lunae"</note>
->As if it were a spider's web held for a long time.<-
*Mixed for a long time with well-purified <term>Mercury</term>,*
->Until, being mixed, it disappears into it entirely.<-

->When the Sun <note>Gold</note> is joined thoroughly with Mercury.<-

# Rhazes of Chester.
<meta>catchword: Sa-</meta>

For things closed in shadowy darkness cannot
Become known to you by a very tiny light.

### The Purest Alchemy of Jupiter.
<note>original: "Iovialis alchimia" — Jupiter is the alchemical name for the metal tin.</note>

Excellent Jupiter, varied and in need of a better state,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Must be healed from here with more diligent care.
He is excessively cold, but is proven to be drier,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which is most clearly evident from his **shriek** <note>original: "stridore" — Alchemists referred to the crackling sound made when bending pure tin as the "cry of tin" (*stridor stagni*).</note>.
This is why, when joined to Venus <note>original: "Veneri" — the alchemical name for copper.</note>, he dissipates her
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Entirely by his dryness and annihilates her.
Indeed, he turns her to ash as she enters the flames with him;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The moisture within them perishes in even a modest fire.
For this reason, he must be moistened before the violent pyre,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Lest he quickly perish and vanish into nothingness.
Let liquid **alum** be joined with thin **arsenic**
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For three days first, and then let it be joined to him.
Let the same be done with **lye** for a second three days,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And let pig’s fat do that very same thing.
Let the moist things meet with the hot things in that same vessel,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In an equal proportion that tempers them in every way.
Finally, let alum joined with **white lead** <note>original: "cerusa" — a white pigment produced from lead, often used in alchemical preparations.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Feed him, until he becomes as clear as water.
If all these things are not enough for him to shine,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Let both types of **bone ash** <note>original: "osseus pulvis" — powder made from calcined bones, often used in the purification process called cupellation.</note> be there to feed him.
When he has become snowy white, shining without darkness,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And lacking any stain, let him thus be **silvered** <note>original: "lunificetur" — literally "made into the Moon," meaning transformed into silver.</note>.
Thus his food is the **Lunar Pill** already mentioned,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as the glory of Saturn <note>original: "Saturni" — lead.</note> is now more powerful.
Then let him be **goldened** <note>original: "solificetur" — literally "made into the Sun," meaning transformed into gold.</note> with vitrified sulfur,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Until he reaches the desired radiance.

<summary>This page provides poetic instructions for the transmutation of Jupiter (tin), describing how to overcome its inherent "dryness" and brittleness through various moistening agents before applying the Lunar and Solar tinctures.</summary>

### Rhazes of Chester.

Whose cause may be more powerful for it, and itself
->Rather this than that, rather here and him.<- <note>original: "sitis" — likely meaning "condition" or "thirst." The verse is obscure, suggesting a choice between opposing forces within the metal.</note>
While these opposites come together in the same thing,
->So that they do not destroy each other, but rather support each other.<-
Mars, laboring without end by nature from dropsy,
->Is incurable, and therefore a plague unto himself.<- <note>original: "Hydrope Mars" — In alchemical theory, Mars (iron) was often described as being "sick" with "dropsy" (edema), a metaphor for an excess of watery impurity or "rust" that consumes the metal from within.</note>
Contrary things against nature are within the same;
->They do not flee from one another, just as in other things.<-
They are helpful to each other and do not overpower themselves,
->Yet they are always warring within their opposites.<-
Here, a place cannot be formed from opposites, and the rule
->Of equals implies that they accompany one another.<-
Bind the times with the capable purity of an equal pair,
->For the equal of one is like the equal of the other.<-
Thus, while those things not fleeing from themselves are joined,
->A perpetual weakness of Mars thrives in both.<-
Dryness and cold are within and without,
->Yet both reign together more on the outside.<-
Moisture, cold, and a small amount of heat
->Possess the interior; from these, they are made shining.<-
It is earthy, enduring fire and rejoicing in the same,
->By which its own rust flees, destroying itself.<- <note>original: "rubigo" — rust or iron oxide. The text describes the purification of iron through fire, which removes the "rusting" quality.</note>
Thus the very first beginnings of the elements hold this one
->Besieged, nor can it exist among its native elements.<-
It must be cured in stages: first the moistures,
->Then heat, so that dryness may flee from here.<-
And afterwards cold, so that a moist vapor may be within it;
->Let it become like sand, and let it also be sanguine,<- <note>original: "sanguineus" — meaning blood-colored or relating to the humor of blood. This refers to the color changes in the alchemical work.</note>
And let it be watery, thickened, and phlegmatic;
->Remaining both within, let it cease to be black.<- <note>original: "phlegmaticus" — the phlegmatic humor, here describing a cold, moist alchemical state that replaces the "blackness" (nigredo) of the raw metal.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the alchemical nature of Mars (iron), describing it as a "sick" metal suffering from internal elemental conflicts (dropsy) and rust. It outlines a process of curing the metal by balancing its moisture, heat, and cold to transition it from a black, "rusty" state to a refined, shining one.</summary>

*Soft dishes and sweet drinks must always*
*Be given to the same, so that it may cast off its darkness.*

*Nor should it flee from wine, beer, or strong cider.*

*In the morning and at noon.*

*In such a way for three or four more days.*

Book of Lights

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which is fine and powdery, joining them together.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;on the outside cannot damage it with its powerful force.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;which should be white, then lemon-yellow, then red.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;so that you may assign each distinct thing to its own place.

All labor in this world tends toward this single goal:
->To gather the wandering riches of the Moon and the Sun.<- <note>original: "Lunæ, Solis." In alchemy, the Moon represents Silver and the Sun represents Gold.</note>
From this, they render the hearts of men wandering, since these riches are themselves wandering,

->And desire them, even though we are situated in the middle way.<- <note>The author refers to the "Golden Mean" or a life of moderation between poverty and excess.</note>

->For a passing life, for which a little is enough.<-

->So that, content with its own measures, it may reign everywhere.<-
Therefore, it pleased me, after studying many teachings of the ancients,
->To grasp the highest masteries <term>magisteria</term> in summary.<- <note>A "magisterium" or "mastery" refers to the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work" itself.</note>

->Seeking hidden gains for a long time:<-

->To the seeker—granted me what I desired.<-

->The prayers of a pious heart, so that he may lead it toward better things.<-

->Grace will piously lead these gains to the harvest.<-
Let no one seize for himself the riches of the Deity <note>original: "Deitatis."</note>
->Which were conferred freely, and let him always rejoice in Him for that reason.<-

### Concerning the seven bodies. <note>In alchemy, the "seven bodies" are the seven metals known to the ancient world: Gold, Silver, Iron, Mercury, Copper, Tin, and Lead.</note>

There are seven bodies to be varied in various shapes

The earthy and the watery parts must exist in abundance,
*Carrying the fires, yet restraining their excess,*

A short discussion must also be held regarding the spirits,

The transformation of things cannot happen in any other way,
*Unless a "healing treatment" removes their defects.*

Otherwise, the seeds of "good grain"—sown and cultivated with such labor—
*Cannot bear their alchemical fruits.*
For a long time, these fields have been choked by such great

Only the surface is grazed by the oxen;
*The deep root remains, constantly sprouting anew.*

### On the Seven Bodies <note>In alchemy, the "Seven Bodies" are the seven metals known to the ancient world, each associated with a celestial body.</note>

->While a moist and warm drink is good for it.<- <note>Alchemists often used medical metaphors—food, drink, and medicine—to describe the chemical reagents added to a metal to change its elemental balance.</note>
*Dryness drives away its softness, while heat increases it;*
->Moisture expels the blackness and brings forth the shine.<-

*Let the body be cleansed, and let its spirit be cleansed,*
*Which is to be infused into it, amassing great riches.*
*The fleeting Moon is both spirit and body, and from her* <note>original: "Luna fugax." In alchemy, "Luna" refers to silver, but when called "fleeting" or "fugitive," it often refers to quicksilver (mercury) or a volatile state of silver that has not yet been "fixed" into a solid, stable metal.</note>

*Below, but broad and hollow from above.*

*Made bright by fires placed beneath at a gentle heat.*
*The middle of another vessel is filled with water to receive this,*
*So that it may boil and the secluded, fleeting Moon may emerge:*
*Until the failing oil makes that fugitive substance*
*Fixed, so that the hammer may strike it into a plate,*
*And it may endure the flames like other hard metals;*
*If it has any filth remaining, let the fire purge it away.*

### E P I L O G U E.

*Before the salt stops crackling, it must first*
*Be given to the burning rays of a glowing fire,* <note>original: "Ut sal non crepitet." This was a standard step to prepare salt for alchemical use.</note>

*Until the murmurs and crackling cease.*
*Afterwards, if it endures being exposed to the glowing coals,*
*It is called a "fixed alchemical substance."* <note>original: "fixum dicitur alchimicum." In alchemy, to "fix" a substance means to make a volatile material stable and resistant to heat.</note>
*If it flees or crackles, the cooking is not complete;*
*Let it be done again until it stands and is silent on the pyres.*
*Either the ash must be burned until it becomes like charcoal,*
*Or it flows down like a star under heavy fire.*
*This shall be the root of the entire alchemical struggle,* <note>original: "radix alchimici totius agonis." Salt was considered one of the three "prime" substances in later alchemy, but here it is presented as the essential foundation for the chemical work.</note>

*Giving an open path for the remaining spirits,*
*So they may enter, and expel what lies hidden within;*
*Let the dark things bestow starry rays.*
*For unless every dark thing hiding within is put to flight,*
*The interior cannot be made bright.*
*Thus whatever lies hidden inside and out cannot leave;*
*That which remains within will not take the throne.* <note>original: "non capiet solium." This implies that the perfected metal (the "King") cannot be established if impurities remain.</note>

*Thus, the appropriate transformation of things will not occur*
*For the sake of which so many laborious wars are waged.*
*For the whole of alchemical labor toils toward this end: that what*
*Lies hidden within may come forth, and what is visible may flee.* <note>original: "ut intus quod latet exeat, & quod patet aufugiat." This is a foundational axiom of alchemy: to make the internal, "spiritual" essence of a metal manifest, while making its external, "accidental" properties disappear or volatilize.</note>
*For base bodies are precious on the inside,*
*Which, when given to the lights, pile up riches.* <note>The "lights" or "luminaries" (luminibus) refer to the celestial bodies—the Sun and Moon—which correspond to Gold and Silver.</note>
*The common people despise base things because they abound in them;*
*Those things become dear to them which they are unable to possess.*
*The needy and the greedy are not refreshed even by those things*
*Which others desire, though they may have them in plenty.*
*For every lot in life is blessed for a man according to his will,*
*Unequal even when equal, and equal even when unequal.*
*There are those for whom gold is like base iron; for some,*
*Iron is dearer than the remaining bodies.* <note>The term "bodies" (corporibus) is the standard alchemical term for metals.</note>
*There are peoples for whom silver becomes dearer than gold;*
*Whiteness pleases them more than the saffron-yellow ray.* <note>original: "candor quàm croceus radius." A reference to the "white" work (creating silver) versus the "yellow/red" work (creating gold).</note>
*What is dear to some is thus base to others; what*
*Pleases one displeases another in every way.*
*Therefore, not undeservedly, the human race under an unfair*
*Will flees what is right, seeking empty detours.*
*O, would that it come—that which the Prophet asks for*
*Every morning: that the perpetual day may come,* <note>This likely refers to biblical passages in the Psalms or the Prophets (such as Isaiah) longing for the "Day of the Lord" or an eternal light that never fades.</note>
*For which night does not substitute darkness, nor the accustomed*
*Labors of the past, and the allurements of the flesh,*
*Nor may the wild beast tear, nor the hidden thief snatch away*
*What every man now possesses under a groan.*

->The End.<-

*And making the clay of the burden dissolved by the heat,* <note>The "clay of the burden" likely refers to the "lute" or sealant used to close the vessels, or the physical dross of the material itself.</note>
*Let it burn the fleeces and also scorch the feathers with the milk.* <note>In alchemical poetry, "feathers" and "fleeces" often symbolize volatile components or surface impurities that are "scoured" away by the chemical "milk."</note>
*Then let it be dried, and thus the salt will also be found lacking,*
*Full of mysteries by which the needy man is unburdened.*
*If you know how to mix shining butter with the salt,* <note>original: "butyrum." In alchemy, "butter" refers to a substance with an oily, soft consistency, such as "Butter of Antimony."</note>
*So that the most celebrated sacred supper may be full of feasts.*
*Let him not be ignorant, but rather let him labor to know,*
*While the reins of the Sun have passed for three times seven cycles,* <note>original: "ter septenis... Solis habenis." This refers to a period of 21 days.</note>
*That which lies hidden in the tomb by means of the round drops,* <note>The "tomb" is the sealed vessel or the furnace; the "round drops" refer to the process of distillation and condensation (refluxing) within a circular glass vessel.</note>
*And so, it stays upon the green lion—but the white one does not swim—* <note>The "Green Lion" is a famous alchemical symbol, usually representing vitriol or a powerful acidic solvent capable of dissolving gold.</note>
*All things are thrown into confusion as if they were cast out by the sea,*
*Neither will they be dissolved again, nor conceived.*

*Everyone will rejoice: for the sailor will reach the harbor.* <note>The "harbor" is a common metaphor for the successful completion of a stage of the Great Work.</note>
*Therefore, while the winter is watering, let the white foam be removed,*
*And let the whole be treated just as was taught before.*

# GUIDO DE MONTANOR
## *ON THE CHE- mical Art.*

---

GUIDO de Montanor, a true and authentic philosopher, and one abundantly steeped in chemical experience, whom many falsely assert to have been Greek, was without a doubt a native of French soil. This philosopher not only wrote the present treatise on the Philosopher’s Stone—which in every respect most perfectly demonstrates his excellent doctrine and the possession of the blessed stone to true philosophers—but he also left to posterity another book on the chemical art, which we published a year ago in the German tongue for the benefit of our fellow countrymen (may it be happy and auspicious). In that book, it can be clear even to the one-eyed <note>original: "lusco"; a Latin idiom meaning something is so obvious that even someone with impaired vision could see it.</note> with how much industry and with how much labor he toiled in this art, and with what spirit he intended it for others who love God and keep watch over this craft. For he describes not only the practice of the "first work," but also teaches the method of the entire operation under a veil of words <term>verborum involucro: a "wrapping" or "shroud" of words. Alchemists used allegories and metaphors to hide their secrets from those they deemed unworthy or unprepared.</term>. ### C H A P T E R I.

->The Method of Purifying Mercury.<-

The method, therefore, of removing its superfluous earthy substance is to sublimate <term>sublimare: the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify it.</term> it once or twice with glass and saltpeter until its substance is taken as the whitest. Therefore, do not mix the water of one stone with another stone, because you would err greatly if you did so. ### CHAPTER III.
### On the Matter of the Elixir.

Now, however, let us return to choosing the matter of the **Elixir**, since it has been sufficiently known that from **Mercury** and **sulfur** all meltable things <term>liquibilia: a technical term for metals or substances that can be liquefied by heat</term> are generated. Their purity and impurity either perfect or corrupt these things, and no impure thing can adhere to these meltable things, nor exert pressure upon them, because it is composed or created from them. For from the two aforementioned—namely, sulfur and mercury—all meltable things are generated, and nothing adheres to them, nor is joined to them, nor transforms them, unless it took its origin from them. And so, by right, we must take mercury and sulfur as the matter for our stone; for nothing meltable is generated from mercury by itself, nor from sulfur alone by itself, but from the mixture of both. Therefore, our matter must be chosen from the mixture of both. But

Our final secret is most excellent; and because it must be made from a mineral thing, we are bound to choose that which is nearest and most closely related to it. Suppose we were to choose mercury and sulfur themselves in their own nature as they are: we would have to mix them proportionally (of which proper proportion human intellect is ignorant) and afterwards cook them until they coagulate into a solid mass. 

For this reason, we are excused from taking both of these in their own proper nature—namely, mercury and sulfur—because we do not know their proper proportion, and yet we find bodies <note>In alchemical terminology, "bodies" (corpora) refers to the metals, such as gold, silver, or lead, which were believed to be already "perfected" or "coagulated" combinations of mercury and sulfur.</note> in which we find the aforementioned proportion already coagulated in the proper way. 

Hold this secret, then, and note that all meltable things <term>liquibilia: metals or minerals that can be liquefied by heat</term> are naturally worked from the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and its sulfur, because it is the property of quicksilver to be coagulated by the heat or vapor of sulfur; for every dry thing naturally drinks up its own moisture. 

Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that coagulates the quicksilver comes from its earthy, subtle, and airy substance, digested by the action of heat, then raised up, cooked, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power to coagulate quicksilver. 

But quicksilver, in its first root, is composed of a very subtle white sulfurous earth, strongly mixed with clear water, until it becomes a single substance that does not rest on a flat surface <note>This describes the high surface tension of mercury, which causes it to form spherical beads rather than wetting a surface like water.</note>. And it is homogeneous in nature; for either it remains entirely fixed in the fire, or it flies away from it in smoke, since it is incombustible and airy. And this is a sign of perfection. And therefore when afterwards with the earth...

### C H A P T E R V.

### On the First Matter.

I say that there are two kinds of first matter <term>materia prima: the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are created</term>: one, namely, the primordial matter, which was water before heaven or earth existed, as is said in the Book of Genesis: "The earth was formless and empty, and the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters." <note>original Latin: "Terra erat inanis & vacua, & spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas."</note> And it is said in the same place: "God made the firmament in the midst of the waters, and divided the waters from the waters." That water existed before heaven and earth. And thus, water was the primordial matter of all things.

The other primeval matter, however, is called in this art the "first matter of mineral bodies." This is a viscous water in the bowels of the earth—that is, running through and united within the veins—in such a union that the moist is held by the dry and the dry by the moist in an equal arrangement. This viscous water was created from that primordial water by the power of God. And from this viscous water, all mineral bodies have their beginning, matter, and form.

### CHAPTER V.
### On the Operation of the Elements.

What is the operation of the elements? I say that the operation of the elements is simple generation and natural transformation. For this reason, Aristotle says that every corruptible body <note>In medieval science, "corruptible" refers to anything in the physical world that is subject to change, decay, and death, unlike the "incorruptible" stars and heavens.</note> is either an element itself or is composed of elements. But the generation of every compound consists of the four simple elements <term>four simple elements: the classical building blocks of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</term>.

For this reason, it is necessary that our stone, having been reduced to the first origin of its sulfur and mercury, be divided into elements; because otherwise it cannot be purified, nor can it be joined, since its smallest parts cannot enter into one another unless the body is divided into its own smallest parts. However, once divided, the body is well purified, and is joined together once again, and the Elixir <term>Elixir: the sought-after substance of the alchemists, also known as the Philosopher's Stone, capable of perfecting base metals and healing the body</term> which we seek is produced.

For the experiment <note>original: "experimentum"; here meaning the practical laboratory process or the "great work" itself</note> destroys its specific form, introducing a new species. Hence, after the division of the elements, nothing is seen or touched of them except for earth and water, whose work is visibly recognized; but the others, air and fire, are neither seen nor touched, nor is their place or their work or their power seen, except within the primary elements—that is, within earth and water. This is because fire always changes colors during the cooking <note>original: "decoquendo"; the process of heating a substance over a long period to mature it</note>.

For when the elements are diligently cooked, they rotate into one another and are converted into foreign natures—that is, into colors—because that which was melted becomes solid, the moist becomes dry, the thick body becomes a thin, fleeing spirit <note>original: "spiritus tenuis fugiens"; "fleeing" refers to volatility, or a substance's tendency to evaporate or escape when heated</note>, and the fleeing spirit...

<summary>Guido de Montanor explains that to create the Elixir, the "stone" must be broken down into the four fundamental elements (Earth, Water, Air, and Fire) through heating. This process of "cooking" allows the elements to transform into one another, changing their physical properties and colors until a new, purified substance is formed.</summary>

Indeed, once this nature is liquefied with its bodies (that is, its complexions), it performs the most exalted operation. And note that God created all things in the beginning. First, He created man from the mud of the earth, so that man was created out of the earth through the power of God, and from that mass, Adam was the first man. And from Adam, the Highest Creator created and extracted Eve; and from Adam and Eve, sons and daughters are procreated.
