### CHAPTER VI.

#### On the leaven of the stone.

What is the **leaven** <term>leaven: (Latin: fermentum) a substance, like yeast in bread-making, that possesses the power to transform and "rise" a larger mass into a new state</term> of our stone? Know for certain that the body is the leaven of the spirit, and the spirit is the leaven of the body, without which neither the blackness, nor the whiteness, nor the redness can be achieved. And this spirit is called the **sun of the Philosophers** <note>original: sol Philosophorum</note>, solar water, arsenic, and the moon. And when the body is whitened, it is likewise called the sun of the Philosophers and **incombustible sulfur** <note>a substance that can withstand the highest heat of the furnace without being consumed</note>.

Hence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> testifies that no one ever could, nor henceforth will be able to dye the sun (that is, the earth) except with the sun (that is, solar water); nor will he be able to make the sun (that is, the **venom** <term>venom: in alchemical terms, this refers to a potent, transformative elixir or "poison" that kills the base metal to revive it as gold</term>) except from the sun (that is, from the elements). And this is their dyeing sun, which we have mentioned, which came forth generated from the stone of the Philosophers. 

We truly honor the sun because our spirit is not perfected without it. For without the sun and its shadow, no dyeing venom is generated: because body does not act upon body, and spirit does not act upon spirit, for the reason that **form** does not receive an impression from **form**, nor **matter** from **matter**. <note>The author uses Aristotelian logic: for change to occur, there must be an active "form" working upon a passive "matter." Two identical things cannot change each other.</note> For like does not act upon its like, nor is it acted upon by it, nor is either of them made more worthy than the other. Therefore, neither of them acts upon the other, because an equal shall have no dominion over its equal. 

Nevertheless, the body receives an impression from the spirit, just as matter does from form. Whence they are naturally suited to act and be acted upon by one another. The body truly dyes, while the spirit penetrates. Yet the body does not dye unless it is dyed, because the thick earthy substance does not

An example of this is the power of women: when they have conceived, the womb is immediately closed, and the fetus is generated by the heat and moisture of the blood. It never receives external breaths <note>original: *flatus*; literally "blows" or "breaths," here referring to outside air or disturbances</note>, as it were, except when it has been born. However, it is not extracted all at once, but emerges little by little every day, until it is completed over a long time. That which is dissolved always seeks the higher part <note>referring to the process of sublimation or evaporation within the vessel</note>, until the remainder is more settled. For this reason, always beware of a large fire, lest you reach the **solution** <note>the liquid state</note> before the necessary time; for this leads to a distant removal, robbing the work of its proper operation and motion. # Book of the Chemical Art.

What is the **Philosophic nest**? I say that it is deservedly called the Philosophic nest. Now let us see what kind of place the generation of liquefiable things <note>original: *liquibiliū*; a term used for metals or substances that can be melted</note> occurs in. It is clearly perceived that the place of minerals is such because at the base of the mountain there is a steady, lasting heat of equal measure, whose nature is always to ascend. In ascending, it dries and coagulates everywhere the viscous water hidden in the belly and veins of the earth into **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury; original: *argentum vivum*</term>. From the heated earth, a "fatness" flows and runs everywhere, and **sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur*; in alchemy, sulfur and mercury are the two primary components of all metals</note> is generated from it.

And wherever in the veins of the earth the vapor of that sulfur—generated from the fatness of the earth as was said—meets the vapor of quicksilver—created from the thickness of the mineral water as was said—there, through the heat in the mountain (which is not perfectly lasting), various liquefiable things are generated over a long time according to their diversity. And it is especially to be noted that the mineral mountain is stony everywhere on the outside and is firmly closed; for if the heat were able to escape entirely, the liquefiable things would never be procreated. 

Therefore <note>original: *E.*; an abbreviation for *Ergo*</note>, it follows that if we wish to imitate nature, the **furnace** <term>furnace: original: *furnus*; often specifically the 'athanor' or 'slow-heat' furnace</term> must be made in such a way that the fire placed within it, when it rises, finds no exit, and the heat reflects back upon our **egg** <note>original: *ovum*; the sealed glass vessel containing the alchemical matter</note>, which is itself firmly closed. 

We have already declared the construction of our furnace and its proper proportion. Know also that the **Philosophers' Egg** <note>original: *ovum Philosophorum*</note> is our perfected **stone** <term>stone: the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work</term>, having a mineral, vegetable, and animal nature. It is called a **mineral stone** because it is collected from the earth like an ore, and it is the mother of all liquefiable things. However, it is called **herbal or vegetable**, because it is made from the juices of three herbs joined together in equal measure (whose names I will tell below), after they had stood...

...[if they were kept] in warm horse dung for ten days, I saw **Mercury** <term>Mercury: quicksilver; original: *Mercurium*</term> flow out of the same color and power as mineral mercury. This toad is nourished and grows to the size of a real toad, and its form will be terrible to behold.

And this "animal" by itself is an **Elixir** <note>original: *Elixir*; a preparation capable of transforming metals</note> over **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter: tin; original: *Iovem*</term> and **Saturn** <term>Saturn: lead; original: *Saturnum*</term>. Therefore, this stone is an animal. And note that according to the mineral, its **projection** <note>original: *proiectio*; the act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten base metal to transform it</note> is made, and it is converted into a liquefiable substance <note>meaning it becomes a metal</note>. Therefore, let no one doubt that this mercury is the stone which, killing itself, rises again and gives life, and transforms itself into **Sun** <term>Sun: gold; original: *solem*</term> and **Moon** <term>Moon: silver; original: *lunam*</term> with the addition of ferment.

*   The **glass vessel** stands for the shell.
*   The **white liquid** stands for the white of the egg.
*   The **lemon-colored body** <note>original: *corpus citrinum*; a yellowish-orange substance</note> stands for the yolk.

The second reason is that, just as a bird is made from the white and the yolk, and without those two...

So it is in all things concerning the **Philosopher’s Stone** <term>Philosopher’s Stone: the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting long life</term>. For from the white liquid and the lemon-colored body, by means of a tempered heat <note>The original Latin text reads *colore* (color), but the context of the mother bird's warmth suggests the author intended *calore* (heat).</note>, the **Bird of Hermes** <note>original: *avis Hermetis*; a famous alchemical symbol representing the volatile spirit rising during distillation, often associated with the transition from the black stage to the white stage of the work</note> is created, while the vessel remains closed and never opened until its perfect completion. 

The third reason [for the name] is that just as oil is made from eggs—which is the tincture of yellowness—so from the Philosopher’s Stone is made an oil, which is the tincture of yellowness and redness. And just as in mines, the heat does not touch the matter of **sulfur** <term>sulfur: the active, "combustible" principle of the Stone, representing the soul</term> and **mercury** <term>mercury: original: *argenti vivi* (quicksilver), the passive, fluid principle representing the spirit</term> directly—for the earth of the mountain stands between them everywhere—so too the fire or heat must not directly touch the vessel containing the aforementioned materials. 

Instead, it must be placed in another closed vessel, so that the heat surrounding the matter above, below, and on all sides is better, more expansive, and more tempered. Hence in the book called *The Light of Lights* <note>original: *Lumen luminum*; a classic alchemical treatise often attributed to the Persian physician Rasis or to Aristotle, focusing on salts and alums</note>, it is said that our mercury must be composed in a triple vessel. Nevertheless, the superfluous things joined to that **philosophic mercury** <term>philosophic mercury: a purified, "living" essence of matter, distinct from the common quicksilver sold in markets</term> are removed during the operation, and what is lacking is supplied by the help of this art. 

The fitting of our vessel is such that it is placed—with the matter contained within—upon our furnace by means of a **dish** <term>dish: original: *scutella*; here referring to a shallow pan used for an ash-bath or sand-bath to ensure even heat distribution</term>, in such a way that two parts of the vessel are exposed at the top, and a third part is buried in the ashes in the aforementioned dish. Underneath the vessel, there should be ashes to the thickness of two fingers, and the vessel should sit straight and level, and the ashes should be well-compressed around it. Once this is completed, let our **lamp** <term>lamp: original: *lichnium*; a wick-fed lamp used to provide a constant, low, "natural" heat</term> be lit with common fire and placed in the furnace beneath the dish,

### CHAPTER VIII.

#### On the Philosophical Clay.

What is Philosophical Clay? I say that Philosophical Clay is called our clay, the **bond of Solomon** <note>original: *vinculumque Salomonis*; a reference to the legendary seals used by King Solomon to bind spirits, here metaphorically applied to the airtight sealing of the alchemical vessel</note>, and the **seal of Hermes** <note>original: *sigillum Hermetis*; the origin of the term "hermetic seal," referring to a container made perfectly airtight</note>. Therefore Hermes says: seal the mouth of the vessel well with our seal, so that it cannot breathe. For the spirit is ready to flee when it is agitated <note>original: *verberatus*; literally "beaten" or "lashed," referring to the spirit being driven upward by the action of the fire</note>. Briefly, indeed, I tell you that our vessel can be sealed with nothing except glass alone, which is a subtle secret of the Philosophers.

Note for certain that the Philosophers called the first **tincture** <term>tincture: a specific stage or color-state in the alchemical process</term> **lead** <term>lead: original: *plumbum*; symbolizing the heavy, "dead," and chaotic starting material of the Great Work</term>; the second tincture—its blackness achieved through boiling—they called the **moon** <note>original: *lunam*; while "Luna" usually means silver, in this context it refers to the whitening stage following the initial blackness</note>. 

The third tincture, when it putrefies, they called **bronze** <note>original: *æs*; can refer to copper or bronze, representing a shift toward a metallic soul</note>. The fourth tincture—when the moisture of sublimated (that is, distilled) **living gold** <note>original: *auri vivi*; likely referring to a purified mercury or a specific "philosophical" solvent</note> is poured over it—they called **putrefaction**, and after the departure of the blackness, when the lemon-yellow color appears, they called it **gold**. 

The fifth tincture they named **burnt bronze**, **red lead**, the **flower of gold**, and the **ferment of gold** <note>ferment of gold: a substance added to the mixture to "leaven" it and direct the transformation toward gold, much like yeast in bread</note>. The sixth tincture they called the **purple sun**. And the seventh is the **fiery dyeing poison**; when the poison is made like white marble, the tinctures and colors now draw near, and he <note>the alchemist</note> does not allow them to flee from the fire. **Alabar** <note>original: *Alabar*; an obscure alchemical term, sometimes identifying a specific mineral or a state of lead</note> is bronze, and it is the first work.

I offer immeasurable thanks to Almighty God, who revealed to me the secret <term>arcanum: a deep secret or mystery, often used in alchemy to describe the "great secret" of transmutation</term> of alchemy <note>original: *Alchimiæ*</note> through experience, which I sought out by the goodness of His prompting and the diligence of my own labor, and I came to know the One. I have resolved, therefore, to compose this work by divine grace, in which I have added few of my own thoughts, and almost none; but extracting everything from the books of the ancient Philosophers, I have compiled it summarily into a brief compendium: just as the diligence of readers will be able to discover through the individual titles. But I know that this unpolished writing of mine will be rejected by many who are stripped of [true] knowledge,

# Book on the Philosopher’s Stone

<meta>catchword: aliud</meta>

[...from the divin]ity <note>The text begins mid-word with "-itate," likely "divinitate" (divinity).</note> of the elements, He created for Himself: and therefore **our heart is restless, until we come to Him** <note>A famous quote from St. Augustine's *Confessions*: "inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te."</note>. For every **rarefaction** <note>original: *raritas*; refers to the alchemical and physical state of being thin or porous, as opposed to dense.</note> of the elements ascends toward the fire which is above the stars. Therefore we, having been created from that, rightly strive upward toward God as our beginning. 

However, all sensitive beings, and likewise vegetables, being composed from the **density** <note>original: *spissitudine*; the "thickness" or material weight of the lower elements.</note> of the elements, He distinguishes into diverse species. Whence, when they are dissolved by death, they not undeservedly return to earth and water, as if to their own mother. For the density of the elements naturally tends downward toward its center, namely the earth. 

Yet, for all things consisting of nature, there is a fixed limit of size and growth, so that within its own species it may increase what is similar to itself. Some of these are made of **dissimilar parts** <note>In Aristotelian biology, "dissimilar" or "anhomeomerous" parts are complex organs like hands or leaves, as opposed to "similar" parts like flesh or wood.</note>, such as from flesh, blood, and bones, or from wood, bark, and leaves. Those things which consist of dissimilar parts possess their own seed within themselves, whereby, being fixed to the earth, they are multiplied and grow, like vines in groves. 

But those things which consist of **similar parts** <note>original: *consimilibus*; referring to minerals and metals which were thought to be uniform in substance throughout.</note> are not multiplied unless they are reduced to their **first matter** <note>term: *primam materiam*; the fundamental, undifferentiated substance that exists before it takes on a specific form.</note>. Wherefore the Philosopher says: *Let the practitioners of the art of alchemy know...* <note>original: *Sciant artis alchimiae*; this is a reference to a famous passage often attributed to Avicenna (Ibn Sina) which argues that alchemists cannot truly change species of metals, only imitate their appearance, unless they reduce them to their primary components.</note>

Therefore, the bodies of all things, both perfect and imperfect, were composed from the beginning of creation out of four principles; and these are the four elements of nature: **air, fire, earth, and water**, which Almighty God coagulated, mixed together, and planted together in peace. For in these four elements the **secret of the Philosophers** <note>original: *arcanum Philosophorum*; the hidden knowledge or substance required to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is hidden. Two of these, namely earth and water, alone have power and visibility; the other two, namely fire and air, are neither seen nor touched, except within the former elements. When, however, these four elements have been joined and perfectly mixed, and changed and extracted from their natures...

# Ioannis Saure

<meta>catchword: metal-</meta>

...become something else. From this it is established that all changeable things are similarly generated through the elements and are naturally transmuted. Whence the ***Rosary*** <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), one of the most famous medieval alchemical treatises.</note> says: "Simple generation and natural transmutation is the operation of the elements." But it is necessary that the elements be of one kind, not of different kinds, otherwise they would not have **action and passion** <note>original: *actionem, & passionem*; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to the capacity of one thing to act upon another and the other to be changed by it. For this to happen, the substances must share a common underlying nature.</note> toward one another: because, as ***Aristotle*** says, there is no true generation except from things that are compatible in nature. 

Therefore, do not seek in nature that which is not in her: since things are not made except according to their own nature. Never does the elderberry tree bring forth pears, nor the bramble pomegranates; we never gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 7:16, used here to argue that the "seed" of the Philosopher's Stone must be found within the metals themselves, not in unrelated substances.</note>. For things bring forth nothing except what is like themselves, and nothing bears fruit except its own fruit. It is necessary, therefore, that our **medicine** <note>original: *medicinam*; a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone or the elixir of transformation.</note> be taken especially from those same things in which it most consists, omitting salts and alums and other common things, from which many attempt to elicit the medicine fruitlessly. For neither salts nor alums enter into our **mastery** <note>original: *magisterio*; refers to the "Great Work" or the alchemical process itself.</note>, but the Philosophers, as ***Theophilus*** says, named salts and alums and the rest in place of the elements <note>Meaning these were "deck names" or allegories used to hide the true ingredients from the uninitiated.</note>. 

But you, who desire to make the **Elixir** wisely and usefully, recognize the mineral roots from which you should make your work, because, as ***Geber*** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic and Western alchemy, known for the "Sulfur-Mercury theory" described here.</note> says, you will find the limit of the thing in the veins of the earth. For **Sulfur** and **Mercury**, which are the natural roots and principles upon which nature founds her action in minerals and the caverns of the earth, are a **viscous water** and a **stinking spirit** <note>These are traditional descriptions of the alchemical principles: Mercury (the water/liquid principle) and Sulfur (the fire/spirit principle).</note>, flowing through the passages and bowels of the earth. From these arises a smoke, which is the matter of metals, ascending as one through a most tempered heat and **reverberating** <note>In alchemy, "reverberation" refers to heat reflecting back onto a substance, but here it describes the natural cycling of vapors within the earth's crust.</note> upon its own earth, as is more fully evident in the book of ***Geber***, until through a tempered **decoction** <note>A long process of "cooking" or heating by nature or art.</note> over the course of thousands of years, a certain natural **fixation** <note>The process by which a volatile substance becomes solid and resistant to fire.</note> takes place there, and it becomes...

# Book on the Stone of the Philosophers.

<meta>catchword: metal-</meta>

metal. Similarly from gold, which is our **sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur*; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter.</note>, reduced into **mercury** <note>original: *mercurium*; the passive, feminine, and fluid principle.</note> by mercury—which is called "thickened water"—and united with its own earth through a tempered **decoction** <note>original: *decoctionem*; a process of heating a substance in a fluid, similar to simmering or boiling, to extract its essence.</note>, a smoke arises from the veins of its own earth (that is, from itself). This smoke is afterwards turned into a most subtle water, which is called the **soul, spirit, and tincture** <note>original: *anima, spiritus & tinctura*; these terms describe the volatile essence that gives the Stone its power to transform other metals.</note>, as will appear in what follows. When that water has been reduced back into the earth from which it came, and is sprinkled everywhere through its own veins, it creates a certain **fixation** <note>original: *fixionem*; the process by which a volatile substance is rendered solid and resistant to fire.</note> there, and the **elixir** is made complete.

And thus, through the ingenuity of man, Art works in a short space of time more than Nature works in cycles of thousands of years. And yet, we do not perform the work, but Nature; nor do we change it, but Nature; we are merely the administrators. Whence **Medus** <note>A philosopher character in the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says in the *Assembly*: "Although our Stone naturally contains the **tincture** <note>The "stain" or "dye" capable of changing the color and nature of a base metal into gold.</note> within itself, having been perfectly created in the earth, it nonetheless has no motion of its own to become an element unless it be moved by Art."

Therefore, let us choose minerals that are natural and closely related, according to the words of **Aristotle** in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*: "Since Nature has procreated all metallic bodies from the smoke of sulfur and mercury," a point from which you will find none of the Philosophers disagreeing. It is expedient, therefore, that you know the principles of the Art and its primary roots; for he who does not know the principles will not find the correct end.

Whence **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary "Father of Chemistry," though these writings are often attributed to a 13th-century European "Pseudo-Geber."</note> says in the beginning of his book: "He who is ignorant of the natural principles within himself is already far removed from the Art, because he has no true root upon which to found his action." Likewise in another place: "It is necessary that our Art be discovered by an ingenuity that searches into Nature, subtly examining natural principles and the foundations of Nature." And yet, although one may know its principles, one cannot follow Nature in all things, as the same Geber says in the first chapter: "Dearest son, we reveal a secret to you;"

*...since craftsmen are mistaken in this, those who desire to imitate nature in all its properties and differences. Just as all gold is sulfur, but not all sulfur is gold, because in the latter there is the corruption of sulfur; indeed, the purest sulfur is proven true in the former. When it has been whitened in this work, it performs the operation of white sulfur, congealing the mercury and converting it into pure gold <note>original: *aurum obrisum*; a technical term for gold of the highest purity, often associated with biblical or refined gold.</note>. Therefore, use the more noble member—that is, gold—because it is the genus of genera and the form of forms. For it is the first and the last among metals, just as the Sun is among the stars.*

Therefore, the best stone of the mercurials <note>original: *mercurialium*; substances or spirits derived from or related to Mercury.</note>

# Book of the Philosophers' Stone. #

...weight and quantities, and we can know this by the fact that no one agrees with another on weights. Therefore, there is a great error, because although the medicine may be well prepared and well mixed, unless the quantities of things are just according to reason, you have lost everything regarding the truth and the final completion. We see this in the testing: when the body is transmuted, it is placed in the **cupel** <note>original: "cineritio," a vessel made of bone ash used to refine precious metals. Base metals are absorbed into the ash, while gold and silver remain.</note>, because there it is consumed and destroyed slowly or quickly depending on how much it approaches or lacks equality; and if the proportions were correctly set according to reason, it would never be corrupted. Therefore, no one but a wise person can pass through this stage—one who does everything according to reason, true subtlety, and natural ingenuity. 

**Curlides** <note>Likely a corruption of Euclid or an authority from the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note>, a most wise man, advises us to work on nothing except in **Sun** <note>original: "Sole," the alchemical term for Gold.</note> and **Mercury**, which joined together constitute the **Philosophers' Stone**. Hence **Rosinus** <note>A common Latinization for Zosimos of Panopolis, an early alchemist.</note> says: "The white and the red proceed from one root, and they sprout forth with no body of another kind intervening"—that is, from the Sun. However, the Sun itself, in the absence of Mercury, is deprived of its effect, because true generation occurs only from matter and form. 

It is proper for you to know that no stone, nor gem, nor any other thing, except this stone, is suitable for this work; but you must labor to repeat the solution of the **yellow body** <note>original: "citrini corporis," referring to the gold plates mentioned on the previous page.</note>, reducing it to its first nature. Hence Rosinus says: "We truly dissolve gold so that we may bring it back to its prior nature, that is, Mercury." When they are joined as one, they then possess within themselves every <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative essence or "dye" that changes the nature of a metal.</note> that can endure fire. For this reason, Rosinus says in *The Doors of Secrets*: "Perform a marriage between the **red husband** and the **white wife**, and you shall have the entire mastery." Likewise, **Merlin** <note>The legendary wizard, who was frequently cited as an alchemical authority in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says:

*And certainly our **solution** <note>original: "solutio," the alchemical process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state, often equated with the "death" of the metal before its resurrection.</note> is nothing else than that the body be converted into moisture, and be revealed in that matter of **mercury** <note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver."</note>, without which the sulfurous saltinesses are diminished. The Philosophers in their books have established a double fire: **dry** and **moist**. They called "dry fire" the common fire of any combustible thing. In this blackness, the whiteness is hidden; and when that moisture has returned upon its blackness, and through gentle roasting has been fixed with its earth, let it be white, in which whiteness the redness is hidden. And when it has been cooked with an increase of fire, its earth is turned into redness <term>rubedo: the final stage of the Great Work, signifying the completion of the Philosopher's Stone</term>, as will be taught later. 

Now let us proceed. Let us return to the black stone perpetually closed in its vessel. Therefore, let the vessel stand continually in a moist fire <note>original: "igne humido," likely referring to a water bath or *balneum mariae*</note>, until the white color appears.

The cause of the appearance of different colors in the Medicine <term>Medicine: the transformative substance, also called the Elixir or the Stone</term> is the gradual fading of that blackness. Since blackness and whiteness are the extreme colors, and all other colors are intermediate, therefore, whenever some degree of that blackness decreases, another color appears, and then another, until the other extreme—namely, whiteness—is reached. # Ioannis Saure

the philosopher says: *"It ascends from the earth to heaven, and again it descends from heaven to earth, and receives the power of the things above and the things below."* <note>This is a famous passage from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, describing the circulation of the "One Thing" between spiritual and material planes.</note> *And note, that if between the blackness <note>original: "nigredinem"</note> and whiteness <note>original: "albedinem"</note> a red or yellow color appears, do not worry about them: for they are not permanent, but fleeting, because permanent and perfect redness <note>original: "rubedo"</note> cannot be achieved unless whiteness has come first.* Whence **Rosinus** <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: "No one can reach the third stage from the first, except by way of the second." In this matter it is clear that whiteness must always be expected, since it is the completion of the whole work, nor will it change into any true color except red.

Now you have learned how to make the white matter; now it is necessary to make the red. *For the white matter and the red matter do not differ in any essential way, except in this: that the red <term>medicine</term> <note>In alchemy, "medicine" refers to the Elixir or the Stone in its curative and transformative state.</note> requires greater refinement, longer <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of maintained, gentle heat to mature the substance.</note>, and a stronger fire in its management.* And this is because what is the end of the operation for the white is the beginning of the operation for the red; what is completed in the one is only started in the other. Therefore, unless you first whiten this medicine, you will not be able to produce the true red. But now let us say briefly how it is done.

The medicine for the red must first be placed in our <term>moist fire</term> <note>original: "igne humido," likely referring to a water bath (balneum Mariae) or the heat of decomposing organic matter.</note> until the white color appears, as was said before. Afterward, the vessel is removed from the moist fire and placed in an earthen pot half-filled with sifted ashes and moistened water, so that the glass vessel containing the medicine is buried in the ashes up to its middle. Beneath the earthen pot, a slow, tempered, and continuous fire is kept; however, the heat of this <term>dry fire</term> <note>original: "ignis sicci," a sand or ash bath allowing for higher temperatures than a water bath.</note> should be at least double the heat of the moist fire. Through the benefit of this heat, the white medicine receives the <term>tincture</term> <note>The coloring principle or transformative power.</note> of redness. Indeed, you cannot err if you [maintain] the dry fire...

### Book of the Stone of the Philosophers

...you have continued. Whence **Rosinus** <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Greco-Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: *“Cook it with dry fire and dry <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or effect oxidation.</note> until it becomes like cinnabar <note>original: "cinabrium"; a bright red mineral form of mercury sulfide</note>, to which you should not add water, nor oil, nor vinegar, nor any other thing, until the red is cooked to completion.”* And certainly, the more red it becomes, the more it is worth; and that which is cooked more is more red. Therefore, the more red it is, the more precious it is. And for this reason, burn it with dry fire without fear. Whence **Eximenus the Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to a speaker in the "Turba Philosophorum," an influential early alchemical assembly text.</note> says: *“In the red furnace, cook the white until it is clothed in purple beauty; do not cease, even though the redness may be somewhat slow to appear.”* For by increasing the fire, as I have said, after the white of the first colors you will have the red; however, between those colors, yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note> will appear, but its color is not stable, because after it, the perfect red does not take long to appear. When that arrives, be certain that your work is completed. For **Hermes** says, *“Between the white and the red, only one color will appear, namely yellow, but it varies according to more or less.”* Likewise, **Maria** <note>Maria Prophetissima, or Mary the Jewess, a foundational figure in Western alchemy.</note> says: *“When you have the true white, and then the deceptive yellow, and finally the perfect red, then you will have the glory of the brightness of the whole world.”*

Our <term>medicine</term> <note>In this context, the "medicine" is the Philosopher's Stone or Elixir itself.</note>, that is the <term>elixir</term>, is multiplied in two ways: by solution and by fermentation. Solution occurs in two modes, namely through the solution of heat or the solution of rarity. Solution of heat is when you take the medicine placed in a glass vessel and bury it in our <term>humid fire</term> <note>original: "igne humido"; often referring to the gentle, moist heat of a water bath (balneum Mariae) or decomposing horse dung.</note> for seven days or more, until the medicine is dissolved into water without turbidity. Solution of rarity is when you suspend the glass vessel containing the medicine in a bronze pot with a narrow opening in which water is boiling; the mouth of the vessel must be closed so that the medicine is dissolved by the rising vapor of the boiling water.

...medicine. <note>The text begins with the end of the word "medicina" from the previous page.</note> *But note that the boiling water should not touch the glass vessel containing the medicine by a space of three fingers <note>A traditional measurement roughly equal to the width of three fingers, used here to ensure indirect heat.</note>. For **Merodus** says: *“Know for certain that the more our stone is dissolved and coagulated, the more the spirit and the soul are joined and retained by it, and from this, at every turn, the tincture is multiplied.”*

# Book of the Philosophers' Stone.

Likewise, in another way, the medicine is multiplied through <term>fermentation</term> <note>original: "fermentum"; in alchemy, a ferment is a substance (usually pure gold or silver) added to the medicine to "ripen" it and direct its power toward a specific metal.</note>. The ferment for the "white" work <note>The stage of the work producing silver.</note> is pure **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver.</note>, and the ferment for the "red" work <note>The final stage producing gold.</note> is the purest **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical name for gold.</note>. Therefore, let one part of the medicine be projected <note>Cast upon or added to.</note> over twenty or forty parts of the ferment, and the whole will become medicine. Let it then be placed over the fire in a glass vessel, and let it be sealed in such a way that air neither enters nor exits. Let it be dissolved and refined <note>original: "subtilietur"; the process of making a substance more spiritual or less dense through heat.</note> as many times as you wish, just as you did with the first medicine; and one part of this medicine will receive as much power as one part of the first medicine possessed. Whence **Rosinus** <note>The Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century Egyptian alchemist.</note> says: "Now we have completed our medicine in the hot and the moist, just as it had a tempered nature; whence whatever is added to it will be of the same <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature.</note> as that to which it is added."

Therefore, join it so that it may generate its like. However, do not join it with just any other thing so that it might be converted to itself, except with that from which it originated in the beginning of its solution. This is to "betroth" <note>original: "desponsare"; a common alchemical metaphor for the chemical union of two substances.</note> and join that revivified earth through its own revivified soul, by the mixing of its first body from which it arose. Likewise, in the book called *The Salutary Gem* <note>original: "gemma salutaris"; likely a reference to a specific alchemical treatise or a symbolic title for the Stone.</note>: "The white work requires a white ferment, and when it is whitened, the ferment is white; so too, when it is reddened, it is a ferment of redness." And just as that earth is the "ferment of ferments," because when it is joined to the **Moon** [silver], the whole will be a Medicine to be projected upon **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver.</note> and upon every imperfect metallic body to turn it into silver; and when the red is joined to the **Sun** [gold], it will be a medicine to be projected upon Mercury and upon the Moon [silver] to turn them into gold. For the soul, spirit, and <term>tincture</term> <note>The concentrated essence capable of coloring or transforming metals.</note> can then be extracted from them by a tempered fire. Whence **Rosinus** says: "Let the craftsmen of alchemy know that species cannot truly be transmuted unless they are reduced to their prior state."

A medicine of the **third order** is that which, when projected upon imperfect bodies, removes all their corruption, and reduces them from a corrupted mineral state into an incorruptible mineral state.

Therefore, the Philosophers performed their projection in various ways, but this way is better: Let one part be projected upon a hundred parts of prepared **mercury** <term>mercury: While it can mean common quicksilver, in this context it often refers to "Philosophic Mercury," a purified elemental principle of liquidity and transformation.</term>, and the whole will be medicine, and it is called the "second medicine." # Book on the Philosophical Stone.

Furthermore, sublimation is not a rising upward, or to ascend, but rather to make another nature from the low <note>The author is clarifying that alchemical sublimation is a change in "dignity" or quality, not just the physical movement of vapor.</note>. Just as that man is sublimated—that is, placed into a position of dignity—so also are bodies said to be sublimated, that is, converted into another nature. Thus, to sublimate means to refine and to make more worthy. 

All of this is accomplished by our blessed water <term>aqua benedicta: a symbolic name for the universal alchemical solvent, often associated with Mercury, used to dissolve and "purify" the matter</term>; and the same water kills and gives life. It causes black colors to appear during the mortification <note>original: "mortificatio"—the symbolic "death" or breakdown of the material, often called the *nigredo* or black stage.</note> as it converts the matter into earth. Afterwards, many and various colors will appear before the whitening, the final goal of which is the *albedo* <term>albedo: the "white stage" of the Great Work, representing the purification of the matter into a silver-like state.</term>

And the colors are infinite during the "sending forth" of the body prepared with the ferment; no true tincture <note>In alchemy, a tincture is a potent substance capable of staining or transforming other metals.</note> is made except from our copper <note>original: "ære nostro." While *aes* means copper or bronze, in this context it refers to the "Philosophical Copper," the base material of the work.</note>. And thus they bestow many names upon it, yet it is but one thing, which is our water. 

Morienus the Philosopher <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says that the perfection of our stone is likened to the order of a human being's creation. For first comes the union, second the conception, third the pregnancy, fourth the birth, and fifth follows the nourishment, or food. 

Let me help you understand this: Our seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> is the Mercury with which the earth is joined—the perfect body—which earth is called the Mother of all metals, and is named thus. When the earth truly begins to retain the body in some way, then it is called conception, and the male acts upon the female. And this is what the Philosophers have said: Our Mastery <term>magisterium: the entire process of the Great Work or the Stone itself.</term> is nothing but the male and the female and their union. While the water—that is, the quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi"—literally "living silver" or Mercury.</note>—dominates the earth, the water grows, multiplies, and increases. And when the earth is whitened, then it is called pregnancy...

### Chapter 65 ###

The **Matrix** <term>Matrix: Latin for "womb"; in alchemy, this refers to the vessel or environment where the "seed" of the Stone is nurtured</term> or earth is properly called the vessel of nature, which retains the formative power of the stone. Into this vessel, the natural heat of the stone is infused—this heat is the formative power that exits the vessel by means of the **fifth spirit** <note>original: "spiritum quintum"—likely a reference to the Quintessence, the purest or fifth element that transcends the four physical elements</note>. For this reason, it is called the matrix or the nurse, as if it were bestowing the natural power of sulfur and feeding it. 

### Chapter 66 ###

**VINCENT** <note>Likely referring to Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century encyclopedist whose works often included alchemical theories</note>: Nothing else is of use to you except what comes from vapor and sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a gas and then cooling it back into a solid, used here to purify the substance</term>. For when you see these natures become water, purified by the heat of the fire, and the entire body of **magnesia** <note>original: "magnesiæ"—in medieval alchemy, this was not the modern element magnesium, but a name for the "maternal" raw material used to create the Stone</note> liquefied into water, then all things have been turned into vapor. By right, the vapor then contains its equal. Therefore, they have called both the moisture and the vapor by the same name, because one has been converted into the other inwardly through decoction <term>decoction: the process of boiling a substance to extract its essence</term>. 

The spirit never dies, because there is nothing that can overcome or corrupt it; rather, it vivifies both body and soul, and therefore **nature rejoices in nature** <note>original: "natura naturâ lætatur"—a foundational alchemical maxim emphasizing that only substances of the same "nature" can work together to achieve transformation</note>, etc. For this spirit extracts life—which it does not have of itself, that is, the soul—from the process of generation. Thus, it sends what is inside to the outside, and what is outside to the inside; and so, flowers are extracted from its belly, and it causes itself to germinate. Therefore, it cleanses both inwardly and outwardly, until the red—that is, the natural red, or the red hidden in the body—is turned into white.

# Book on the Philosophical Stone #

...the marriage between body and spirit. Whence Paganus <note>Paganus is often a name used in medieval alchemical compendiums like the *Turba Philosophorum* to represent a "pagan" or ancient philosopher</note> says: He who understands quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury; "argentum vivum" in Latin</term> to be extracted from bodies in such a way, and knows how to mix it and make it friendly to those bodies, shall know one of the greatest secrets of nature and the principal path of perfection. However, when he says, "he who knows how to mix it with bodies," it is as if he says that no one succeeds without the conjunction of this mastery <term>mastery: the "magisterium" or the completed process of the Great Work</term>, etc.

From this it is clear that our quicksilver is not the quicksilver of the common people, nor is it prepared by common sublimation <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again; the author warns that common chemical methods are insufficient for alchemy</note>, but rather it is pre-created from a certain muddy and vile substance by a single path—namely, by our natural mastery. Nevertheless, do not think to elicit the stone from this quicksilver alone through any mastery, because by itself it will never arrive at ultimate perfection. 

Whence the same Paganus says: And we humbly testify clearly through our experiments that it is perfected with a mixture—that is, with the body or its sulfurous earth—and without that, the mastery is prolonged even unto despair; therefore, strive to conquer Mercury in the mixing. 

Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note>, as the principal inventor in this mastery, faithfully declared it to be commended by revealing the clear truth to his posterity and successors, when he said openly: "Its nurse is the earth" <note>original: "nutrix eius terra est"—a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes</note>. For since it is established that the entire power of the stone is realistically in that earth, it will not be made whole unless the quicksilver is led into it; and therefore he adds: "it ascends from the earth into heaven and again descends from heaven to earth, and receives the force and power of things above and things below" <note>original: "ascendit à terra in cælum & iterū descendit de cælo in terram..."—this refers to the circulatory distillation process where the spirit and body are unified</note>, namely, the whole power when it has been turned into its own earth.

# Book on the Philosophical Stone #

->N 4<-

...is unknown to them. Therefore, it is necessary to be ignorant of how to make those things. Likewise, metals differ in species, just as a human and a donkey do. Therefore, just as a donkey is not made from a human, so other metals are not made from [different] metals. Likewise, according to **Aristotle** <note>The author cites a famous passage from the "Meteorologica" (actually written by Avicenna but attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages) which was the primary weapon used by critics to argue that alchemy was impossible.</note>: let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of nature cannot be changed; they can, however, make things similar to them, such as dyeing a white substance with a red or yellow color so that it appears to be gold, or wiping away the impurity of lead so that it appears to be silver. Nevertheless, it will always remain lead, even though it possesses qualities of this kind, etc. 

However, in our own experiments in our times, **Moon** <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver, associated with the cooling, reflective properties of the night sky.</note> was perfected in such a way that it withstood all the examinations and tests of gold in the **cement** <term>cement</term> <note>original: "cemento"; a refining process where a metal is surrounded by a powdered mixture and heated to a high temperature to test its purity or "fix" its color.</note>, and it possessed the true weight and all the characteristics found in the truest gold. We have also seen in our times a very great **elixir** <note>The transformative agent or "Medicine" of the alchemists, believed to be capable of "healing" base metals into gold.</note> perfect mercury into true Silver. 

And this is also an argument against those who say that man cannot produce one genus from another genus. For if someone places horse dung where heat may touch it, from there proceed beasts which they call **albates** <note>original: "albates"; likely referring to the spontaneous generation of woodlice or small white insects often found in decaying organic matter.</note>. Furthermore, if someone places a fish bone beneath seaweed and wax and lets it remain there for a month, he will find it has become worms called **centipedes** <note>original: "centipes"; the author uses this as an example of "spontaneous generation," a common medieval belief that life could arise from non-living matter under the right conditions.</note>. And thus, from the non-living, he draws forth a living thing. 

Aristotle's reasoning can be understood in another way when he says that species cannot be changed. I say that it is true that species, when considered in a general or universal sense, can in no way be changed from one species into another. In this way, his reasoning holds true. However, regarding mineral species—that is, the specific types contained under that general category—I say that they indeed *can* be changed into other species. For if someone puts the crumb of wheat bread in a glass vessel...

### Anonymous Philosopher ###

<meta>catchword: unguen- (unguent/ointment)</meta>

**Sulphur** <term>sulphur</term> <note>original: "sulphur"; in alchemical theory, sulphur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of matter, complementary to the passive, fluid mercury.</note> is the fatness of the earth <note>original: "pinguedo terræ"</note>, and the mineral of the earth, thickened through temperate cooking. It possesses the strongest power of operation and is of uniform substance in its parts; for this reason, its oil cannot be removed from it by distillation, but by cooking it in "sharp waters" <note>original: "aquas acutas"; likely referring to corrosive acids or strong solvents like vinegar or mineral acids.</note>. It also congeals **mercury** <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; the fluid, metallic principle.</note> into either perfect or imperfect bodies <note>i.e., gold/silver or base metals like lead/tin.</note> according to its own perfection or imperfection, and according to whether the sulphur is clean or unclean. 

Place the matter in a large, long vessel and close its opening; however, let it have a small hole in the middle like the hollow of a small quill, so that it is able to breathe, and place it upon the furnace among the ashes. Let the matter of the stone be one pound, and it must be inspected once every day because of the colors that appear, and because of the heat and the reduction of the water; in this way, you can observe the appearing colors. And when the water is diminished, pour in other water with great care, lest the cold water touch the hot glass and cause it to break, or the cold glass touch the hot water; for this reason, it is better to use a well-glazed earthen vessel. 

The Sages have called this the **Vinegar of the Philosophers** <term>Vinegar of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "acetū Philosophorum"; a specialized alchemical solvent used to dissolve metals or "wash" the matter.</note>, the water of life, corrosive water, and **Virgin’s milk** <term>Virgin’s milk</term> <note>original: "lac virginis"; an alchemical term for various white precipitates or mercurial distillates that resemble milk.</note>. For it desires to be converted into a milky color with the mixture of its own nature, and afterwards to be reduced back into a crystalline color. Moreover, let this be distilled seven times, and then it will be clean and pure, and fully rectified with its own water. Note that the white color is completed through heat and moisture, and the red color <note>The "White" and "Red" stages (Albedo and Rubedo) are the final stages of the Great Work, signifying the completion of the Silver and Gold elixirs respectively.</note> through heat and dryness. 

**Aristotle** <note>While the historical Aristotle did not write on alchemy, many medieval texts were attributed to him (pseudo-Aristotle), lending the "Art" philosophical authority.</note> said: God placed three principal keys in this art: the first is water, the second is **unguent**—

Know therefore, Son of Chemistry, that he who does not possess a natural talent and a mind that investigates subtle things, as well as the individual natural foundations and techniques in the art—which we cannot attain without the properties of our art—does not find the true root of this precious science. ### Johann Wittich

...so that you, who are not sons of the Philosophers <note>original: "filij Philosophorum"; a term used to describe true initiates or students of the alchemical arts</note>, might not understand that it is a single thing, common, and composed of diverse things—namely, from the four elements. And this is entirely true: that our stone is composed of diverse things, namely from the four elements and four substances.

The first substance is hot and moist; the second is hot and dry; the third is cold and dry; the fourth is cold and moist. And all of this is within our stone, and from these things, or materials, all things in this world were created by **the power of God**. And because our stone has within itself and contains all these qualities, for this reason the Philosophers have named our stone by every name in this world; and according to their diverse intentions and diverse operations, they placed it in diverse things and spoke according to their own understanding.

And you should know that their intention was perfect and clear, though to those who do not understand, it seems truly the opposite. Whence Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential authority in medieval alchemy</note> says in the final chapter on perfection: *Since we have published for you the art investigated by us alone, most true and certain, etc.* Therefore, let the craftsman see to it that he has a complete purpose in his mind. Some Philosophers said that this art is found in "spirits," such as quicksilver <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; liquid mercury, considered one of the primary "spirits" because it vaporizes when heated</note>, and they spoke the truth. Some Philosophers said it is in sulfur; some in arsenic; some in sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sale armeniaco"; ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metals and aid in chemical reactions</note>; some in a variety of salts, such as in common salt, in salt alatron <note>likely a reference to soda or natron</note>, in salt aton, and in all salts. Similarly, some Philosophers place it in tutty <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "tutijs"; zinc oxide collected from furnace flues, often used in making brass</note>, such as in marcasite <term>marcasite</term> <note>a metallic-looking iron sulfide mineral</note>, in tutty, in magnesia <note>at this time, "magnesia" referred to various dark or shiny minerals like manganese or even magnetites, not modern magnesium</note> and in antimony, and lapis lazuli. ## THE FOURTH ARRANGEMENT.

Take Azoth <term>Azoth: A term for the "universal solvent" or the essential spirit of mercury, considered the beginning and end of the alchemical work.</term>, the Philosopher’s stone as it has been thinned out, and put it into the Lion <note>In alchemy, the "Lion" often refers to a strong corrosive solvent (like aqua regia) or a specific metallic state that consumes other metals.</note>, and fasten it so that it cannot breathe, and place it in our Sun to be cooked in the month of May—that is, at the furnace—until the whole thing is congealed into a stone or a red powder; or hold it in the Sun until it is congealed and the entire matter is fixed, and nothing rises. Orpiment is not understood here as the common kind, but the Philosophical, which is a perfect thing, leading to perfection.

## THE FIFTH ARRANGEMENT.

You should take ERNOCH or ZONOCH and put it with the green Lion <note>The "Green Lion" usually represents vitriol or a raw, acidic mineral state that has the power to dissolve gold.</note>. There are certain winds <note>original: "venti"; these refer to the volatile gases or vapors released during heating which must be captured or "fixed."</note> in it, but you must guard them, and allow the matter to stand in the sun so that the whole is fixed and nothing rises, but instead it is turned into a powder or a most red stone. Roast this whole thing gently, and then it is called KIBRIK in Arabic <note>original: "KIBRIK"; from the Arabic 'kibrit', meaning sulfur.</note>, and in Latin sulfur—not common sulfur, but the Philosophical kind.

*Note: when Jupiter <note>Jupiter is the alchemical name for Tin.</note> is joined with Luna <note>Luna is the alchemical name for Silver.</note>, it is not easily separated without arsenic; but when joined with Luna, it loses its screeching <note>Tin is known for the "tin cry," a crackling sound made when the metal is bent; alchemists believed "killing" this sound was a step toward transmutation.</note>. Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead.</note> also is hardened and made red, and is mixed with Sol <note>Sol is the alchemical name for Gold.</note>, and is not easily separated. Though it is made hard and infusible <note>Infusible: unable to be melted.</note>, it may yet become fusible <note>Fusible: capable of being melted.</note>. ## THE SIXTH ARRANGEMENT.

Take the Kibrik <term>Kibrik: An Arabic-derived term for philosophical sulfur, considered the active, "male" principle of the Stone.</term> of the Philosophers, ground most finely without any difficulty, and put it into the Green Lion <note>The "Green Lion" typically refers to a powerful acidic solvent, often vitriol or aqua regia, capable of "devouring" or dissolving metals.</note>, and close the mouth of the vessel. Then place it in the Sun during the days of July <note>The "days of July" refers to the highest heat of the alchemical furnace, mirroring the peak of summer.</note>, and let it remain until the whole is dissolved. And when it has been dissolved, leave it in the said Sun until the entire matter is fixed <note>Fixed: rendered solid and resistant to heat, so that it no longer evaporates.</note>, and nothing rises, and it is turned into a white stone. Then it is called Enbarich <term>Enbarich: An Arabic term for the purified "calx" or white stage of the Great Work.</term> in Arabic, and Calx <note>original: "calx"; literally "lime" or "ash," referring to the powdery remains of a substance after intense heating.</note> in Latin. Concerning this, the philosopher Datinus says: unless you see your ashes near the end, you will not be certain that you have performed your operation well and perfectly. And know most certainly that when our matter is dissolved and we must coagulate or calcine it, it is then helpful to withdraw it from the heat of the Sun, so that it may be dissolved even better a second time.

And the Philosophers have said: by roasting gently you should perform all decoctions <note>Decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence.</note>, and you shall find knowledge; but if you do otherwise, you will not rejoice in your operation, because sublimation <note>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note> is done with a slow fire, and it is the separation of the subtle parts from the gross parts. Hence we say that metallic bodies are generated from four substances: namely, from a double quicksilver <note>Quicksilver: Mercury.</note> and a double sulfur. First, from a quicksilver that is very clear, pure, clean, and also fixed; second, from a sulfur that is fixed, pure, clean, and clear; and thus perfect bodies are generated.

### John Wittich

*The second is solution, through which the matter is dissolved into water. The third is called putrefaction <note>The process of breaking down or "rotting" the substance to release its inner essence.</note>; for, as the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus in alchemical texts.</note> says, if it has not been putrefied, it cannot be melted or dissolved, and if it has not been dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing. The fourth is washing <note>original: *ablutio*</note>; for it is necessary that the putrefaction be washed away, because washing is the total perfection, since grinding <note>original: *contritio*</note> and washing are one and the same. The fifth is coagulation; because it is beneficial that that water be coagulated together by gently drying it by our Sun <note>Likely referring to the heat of the furnace or the "philosophical sun," rather than direct sunlight.</note>, and be reduced into a stone or into a powder, otherwise it will not be perfected. The sixth is calcination <note>The reduction of a solid to powder by heat.</note>, and calcination is more suitable for dissolving and fixation.*

*First, so that the lunar medicine <note>The alchemical preparation intended for the transmutation of metals into silver.</note> may be known: Take the stone and divide the purest part through the method of separation, and set it aside. This is the first arrangement. Then you should fix that part <note>Fixation refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>. This is the second arrangement. On the contrary, when it has been fixed, dissolve that which was soluble from it. This is the third arrangement. Afterwards, mix all the solutions together and coagulate them. This is the fourth arrangement. Still further, repeat upon that solution until that which is soluble from it is dissolved in every way. Thus this order should be observed by repeating, until the greater quantity of it is dissolved: and this is the fifth arrangement.*

*After this, mix all the solutions together and coagulate, and this is the sixth arrangement. After this, however, observe the aforementioned order of sublimation <note>The process where a substance is heated to a vapor and then condenses back into a solid.</note> until everything is dissolved again, and congeal that which is soluble from it again in a temperate fire. Keep it until that good fire can again be administered for its perfection. You ought, therefore, to repeat these orders of solution four times, and finally calcinate in its own way, not by an external one. And thus you have ruled the stone by its conversion, by sufficiently administering earth to it; and this is the seventh arrangement.*

<note>Vocabulary: solution, putrefaction, washing, coagulation, calcination, lunar medicine, stone, arrangement, fire.</note>

Now we say that all these operations exist in sublimation alone, in a single vessel: And in one sublimation all these seven operations are performed, and as the purification is, so is the perfection. And sublimation is the elevation of the most subtle parts, and the separation or division of substances from the coarse parts; it is likewise the separation of the non-fixed parts from the fixed parts. The non-fixed parts are elevated through smoke, that is, the wind <note>In alchemical theory, "wind" or "smoke" often refers to the gaseous state of a substance as it rises during heating.</note>. Let the fire be guarded, however, lest it cause vitrification <note>The process of turning a substance into glass through excessive heat, which "fixes" the matter prematurely and ruins the work.</note>, and so that the matter which ascends may descend again, and the whole remain below. The more you have repeated this, the more perfection you will find, because our <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; the fluid, volatile principle of matter.</note> is the clearest water, and our <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: *arsenicum*; likely referring to a purified mineral spirit rather than modern poison.</note> is perfect silver, and our <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: *sulphur*; the active, combustible principle.</note> is pure gold, and therefore it has no dross.

Note: when you wish to perform our perfect sublimation, add or subtract nothing from our stone; rather, place the whole substance into the vessel so that it may be dissolved, and close the mouth of the vessel, and seal it with the philosophical seal <note>An airtight, hermetic seal, often made by melting the glass of the vessel shut.</note> until the greater part is turned into black earth, which will occur in 21 days. Then these operations are perfected, and there has been accomplished: sublimation, solution, distillation, descension <note>A process where the essence of a substance is forced downwards by heat.</note>, putrefaction, washing <note>original: *ablutio*</note>, waxing <note>original: *ceratio*; softening the substance to a wax-like state.</note>, coagulation, calcination, and fixation.

Wherefore this <term>philosophers’ stone</term> is called **AZOTH**, **LATON** <note>Azoth is the universal spirit or solvent; Laton refers to the "blackened" stage of the metal before it is whitened into silver.</note>, and foul earth, white earth, red earth, and it is called by many names; and for this reason, it is perfected by one single operation. For it is a gentle remedy, and a friendly way of joining the tinctures <note>The "soul" or color-giving essence of a metal.</note> of all metals, especially of the Sun and Moon <note>The Sun represents gold, and the Moon represents silver.</note>. Quicksilver receives into itself that which was of its own nature, but rejects what is foreign.

Note: If the quicksilver is pure, it will coagulate that white sulfur of ours into perfect silver.

If, however, the sulfur is clear, pure, red, fixed, and perfect, and if there is in it a power of fieriness that likewise does not burn, it will congeal <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; the fluid, volatile principle of matter, often associated with mercury.</note> into the truest <term>Gold</term> <note>original: *Solem*; literally "the Sun," the alchemical name for gold.</note>. And the same applies to other imperfect metallic bodies when treated with our prepared sulfur. And although there is white sulfur in pure silver, and red sulfur in gold, according to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and chemical works were foundational to European science, though he was famously skeptical of some alchemical claims.</note> it is not found elsewhere; nevertheless, it is not contradictory that one has the power to convert it into gold and silver through the art. Therefore, nothing is suited to a thing except that which is closer to it by nature. Note that Avicenna says: "If I had not seen gold and silver, I would say for certain that alchemy was not a true science; but when I see gold and silver, I know most certainly that it is true knowledge."

The modes of governance and the ways of converting the elements into one another are fourfold: namely, to dissolve the coarse into the simple and to make it subtle, to wash the dark into the bright, to reduce the moist into the dry, and to fix the volatile upon its own body; which in this science is nothing other than to dissolve, wash, reduce, and fix. *To dissolve is to divide, to corrupt, and to create the first matter. To wash is to bury <note>original: *inhumare*; likely referring to a "heat of digestion" such as a dung bath or sand bath.</note>, to distill, and to calcine <note>original: *calcinare*; to reduce a metal to a powder through high heat.</note>. To reduce is to treat with wax <note>original: *incerare*; the process of making a substance soft or fusible like wax.</note>, to fatten <note>original: *inpinguare*; adding oily or moist substances to the dry matter.</note>, and to sublime. To fix is to marry <note>original: *desponsare*; the alchemical union of opposites.</note>, to dissolve, and to coagulate.*

Through the first, the nature is changed internally; through the second, externally; through the third, above; through the fourth, below. Now I have shown you, Dearest Son of Alchemy, the entire operation and doctrine: And know that the whole of perfection lies in the solution, where the extraction of water is out of the earth, and the turning of this water from out of the earth back onto the earth, until the earth itself putrefies <note>Putrefaction is the stage where the matter turns black, signaling the "death" of the old form before it is purified and reborn.</note>.

Citron and bluish-gray are born from white and red, for these colors are a proportion of the white and red stages. Sky-blue arises from white and black. Green, violet, and camel-color come from black, white, and red mixed together. Other imperfect colors are perfected by "water," and by this same water they are washed and purified. If the **black color** appears in your work, then you have not labored in vain. If you dissolve the matter through the process of **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage where the matter is allowed to decay or ferment in a gentle heat, usually turning black; this was considered the essential first step of the "Great Work."</note>, you will then see it turn black, then green, then saffron-yellow and reddish, and it will be resolved into many colors during the separation; then you may judge that this mastery is being perfected through a true boiling.

In the third degree, the stone is similarly treated, which constitutes the completion of the preparation through the entire beginning, middle, and end. This is, namely, that we make the already fixed stone volatile <term>volatilization</term> <note>Making a solid substance capable of rising as vapor through heat.</note> by means of sublimation <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where a solid turns into vapor and then solidifies again at the top of a vessel.</note> with the application of fire, and then make the volatile fixed again, until it rests in the intensity of the fire so that nothing is seen to ascend. And this is called the third method. 

Now the fourth administration is that you dissolve the stone, and by means of dissolution make it volatile, and with that which is fixed, let the whole matter be united with its appropriate fire until it rests without any separation; when it has been made so, the matter is most truly joined. 

The fifth administration was found to be that you dissolve the congealed stone, so that you make all fixed things volatile with the administration of fire, and once more make the volatile fixed, until it remains stable in the struggle of the fire <note>original: *pugna ignis*; a poetic description of a substance's ability to remain unchanged despite the "assault" of the flames.</note>; when it is so, keep it until a greater quantity of fire can be applied. And there you have seen the fifth circle.

You shall make it volatile with the greatest skill of fire. And when the whole has been totally fixed, let it rest in the intensity of the fire until nothing is seen to ascend.

# Book of the Philosopher's Stone.

The whole secret <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: *arcanum*; a hidden or specialized mystery of nature known only to initiates.</note> and the entire science consists in the operation of this arrangement. We say to you, son, that you must possess a true natural talent, as well as a true method of operation and intention, so that you may rightly understand the sayings of the Philosophers, and mine likewise; in this way, you shall possess the whole mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>original: *magisterium*; the completion of the Great Work or the substance of the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note>. Now let us pass separately to the solution in the seventh operation. 

We say, therefore, that the seventh operation is: 
1. To dissolve our blessed stone <term>lapis benedictus</term> <note>The "blessed stone" is another name for the Philosopher's Stone in its nascent or developing state.</note> for the first time.
2. To distill it.
3. To sublimate it <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and solidifies again at the top of the vessel, purifying it.</note>.
4. To wax it <term>ceration</term> <note>original: *incerare*; an alchemical process of adding liquid to a hard substance to make it soft and wax-like.</note>.
5. To descend it <term>descension</term> <note>original: *descendere*; a method of distillation where the vapors or liquids are forced to move downward into a receiving vessel.</note>.
6. To calcine it <term>calcination</term> <note>Reducing a substance to a dry powder through prolonged heat.</note>.
7. To fix it <term>fixation</term> <note>Making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand high heat without evaporating.</note>.

Behold the whole mastery, and the whole secret; and everything we say is nothing other than to dissolve, to recongeal, to fix, and to make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved, and the dissolved volatile once again, until it flows and alters in its moon-making <term>lunific</term> <note>original: *lunificum*; the power to transmute base metals into silver (Luna).</note> and sun-making <term>solific</term> <note>original: *solificum*; the power to transmute base metals into gold (Sol).</note> completion. 

From the repetition of the preparation in the medicine, the excellence of the alteration and multiplication <term>multiplication</term> <note>The process of increasing the power or quantity of the Philosopher's Stone so that a small amount can transmute a large mass of metal.</note> results. From the different ways the work is repeated upon the stone through its various degrees, there results a range of excellence in multiplication and a diversity of alteration; thus, some stones may transmute a body into twice its weight, some into sixfold, some a hundredfold, some a thousandfold, and some may transmute a body into an infinite sun-making and moon-making of true perfection. And let these things suffice regarding the stone.

But so that you may better understand the true intention, we wish to show in which hour, on which day, and in which month the beginning of this work ought to take place. We say that whoever acts otherwise will certainly err, but whoever acts according to what we prescribe will certainly see the true art and the use of the mastery.

Although in this matter <note>original: *materia*; referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy or the physical substance being transformed.</note> the Philosophers appear to disagree at a literal level, they are nevertheless in agreement and express the same underlying meaning <note>original: *sententia*; the core intent or "sentence" of the doctrine.</note>. However, they describe their reasoning through different approaches and use various symbols to name the operations of the Stone itself. They have given it diverse names, sometimes calling it male, sometimes female, and sometimes joined together as the **rebis** <term>rebis</term> <note>original: *rebis*; from the Latin *res bina*, meaning "double thing." It is also called by many other various names.

Therefore, from the repetition of that operation—namely, of sublimation and its thickening <note>original: *inspissationis*; the process of a liquid or vapor becoming dense or solid.</note>, which is naturally followed by incineration or the Philosophers' fixation—the excellence of the work results. This is achieved through the skillful preparation of fire, using either one thing alone or with other aids. First, indeed, some Philosophers maintain—and because all the ancient Philosophers in the beginning of their existence stated—that the matter exists as the most subtle substance of mercury, without earthiness <note>original: *sine terrestreitate*; referring to the coarse, solid impurities that do not vaporize.</note> which would hinder its fusion and fixation <note>original: *fusionem & fixionem*; the processes of melting and then becoming a stable, non-volatile solid.</note>.
