# Concordances of the Philosophers

...[we neither] add nor take away, but remove the superfluous. Many sayings of certain Philosophers and numerous authorities placed in the books of the Philosophers move us to hold to this path, which are clear to those who look closely at their books; for now, I intend to insert here some authorities that lean toward this path.

For Senior <note>Senior refers to Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Ibn Umayl, whose *Tabula Chimica* was highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note> says, concerning the truth of the Stone of the Philosophers <note>original: *lapis Philosophorum*; the legendary substance sought by alchemists to achieve transmutation and medicinal perfection.</note> and its single method of working: "Son, consider that whatever is said in our books about waters, sulfur, vinegar, and salts, you should understand as nothing but <margin>one thing</margin> one divine thing, which, according to the variety of signs <note>original: *signorum*; likely referring to the different names, chemical states, or astrological influences assigned to the matter.</note> and preparations, is sometimes called the soul, vinegar, or sulfur."

And he adds: do not focus on many things, even though the Philosophers say that it is made from things, and is a thing composed of things; this is all said by way of analogy <note>original: *similitudinem*; an important warning that alchemical recipes are often allegorical rather than literal.</note>, as will be explained below. And he says the same: "our Stone, which is one thing—if it shared its nature with others, even though they come from it, we would not have called it our Stone, because all men share in other common things." And he says further: "others indeed have added sulfur." Likewise, according to Aristotle <note>The text likely refers to the *Meteorologica* or one of the many "Pseudo-Aristotelian" alchemical works like the *Secretum Secretorum*.</note>, nothing is completed except with a refined ferment <note>original: *fermento*; a substance added to the "matter" to trigger its transformation, analogous to how yeast causes dough to rise.</note>. And such is the refinement, distillation, and fixation <note>original: *fixio*; the process of rendering a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate when heated.</note> of the Philosophers, as well as the waxing <term>inceratio; a process of gradually adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency</term>, because all these things follow one another in nature solely through the governance of fire <note>original: *regimen ignis*; the precise management of heat, which alchemists believed governed the entire natural and laboratory process.</note> according to the requirements of the labor and the degrees of heat it can tolerate, about which I will explain more specifically below.

Likewise, another Philosopher says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," is an ancient and widely cited alchemical text written as a dialogue between famous Greek and Eastern sages.</note>: "Every thing that is bought at a high price is found to be useless in this art; nor..."

It ought not to hinder us, what is said in the *Book of Seven Precepts*, that this thing is in every thing, since the Elder <note>referring to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umayl)</note> explains it thus: that in this thing are all powers, namely whiteness <note>original: *albedo*. ...is the whole matter of the Philosophers, because it has within itself everything that it needs, and it is the mother of gold <note>original: *mater auri*</note>. This likely refers to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose works were translated into Latin and became core texts for European scholars.</note> seems to disagree in his words, and other Philosophers among themselves, as can be seen from the authorities written above. This is the only operation which, following the required degrees of fire, is followed by various other operations—namely fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term>—and the matter itself is given various names, as has been said before.

Now, therefore, it is with good reason that we must approach the "Concordance of the Philosophers." In conclusion, it seems it should be said that all the Philosophers and their authorities agree on this: that the Philosophical Stone is always mercury <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" is not always common quicksilver, but often the "universal spirit" or the feminine principle of matter.</note>. This is clearly evident from their written authorities and can be seen most clearly by those reading their books. However, they seem to be in disagreement regarding "natural mercury" versus "extracted mercury," as has been mentioned. 

First, then, it must be said that the authorities of those who lean toward the path of natural mercury are to be understood and spoken not by way of denial—as if another "extracted" mercury is not or could not be the Stone of the Philosophers. Rather, it is because such Philosophers would find the science—even through the investigation of the method of decoction <term>decoction: the process of prolonged heating or "cooking" to bring a substance to maturity</term>—in natural mercury alone; they did this so that men would not spend money on more precious things when the Stone can also be found just as well in a cheaper substance. This perhaps would have happened least to them if they had labored on the perfection of mercury derived from [perfected] bodies. Therefore, since that which is perfect is more quickly brought to further perfection and is more difficult to destroy, it follows that fewer errors occur, because **nature delights in nature** <note>original: *natura naturam laetatur*—a fundamental alchemical axiom suggesting that substances of a similar "spiritual" nature combine most effectively</note>, and rejoices with it and is befriended by it.

# Of the Concordances of the Philosophers

But then the **mercury of the Philosophers** <term>mercury of the Philosophers: not common quicksilver, but the "soul" or "essential moisture" extracted from metals, believed to be the key ingredient in the Great Work</term> itself, being subtle, should be prepared with skill and fire—which acts as the efficient cause—following the methods and expertise of **Geber** <note>original: *Gebri*; refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath, though here likely referencing the influential Latin alchemical texts attributed to him</note>, who spoke the whole truth of this matter in very few words. One should also follow other Philosophers who agree with him through the diligence of the work. Let this be prepared so that from it the true **Physical tincture** <term>Physical tincture: a concentrated medicinal or transformative liquid capable of curing illness or perfecting metals</term> can be produced. Through this, a response can be given to the authorities cited here from the books of the Philosophers, which are placed here for anyone to examine.

->*Let these brief words concerning the substance and essence of our stone suffice. There follows:*<-

Regarding the second principal point—namely, the specific preparation of our stone and the **governance of fire** <term>governance of fire: the precise control of heat levels, often divided into "degrees," which was considered the most difficult part of alchemy</term>—something must be declared using the authorities of the ancients. In this matter, the first method must be primarily observed. Geber sets this down in his *Summa* <note>original: *summa sua*; likely the "Summa perfectionis magisterii," one of the most famous medieval alchemical manuals</note> in a few true words. It is therefore my view, according to all the Philosophers, that the work must be done thus: take the stone, already well known from the previous descriptions, and prepare it in a single glass vessel without any other, or in a vessel upon which sits another vessel in the style of a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distilling apparatus that holds the substance to be heated</term> and an **alembic** <term>alembic: the cap or "head" of a still where vapors condense</term>. The **preparation** <note>original: *præparatio*</note> consists in **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: *sublimatio*; in alchemy, this is not just turning a solid to gas, but the process of purifying a substance by "lifting" its spirit or essence away from its impure "dross."</term> alone; and through this operation, by the long duration of labor with perseverance and persistence upon this **stone**, and by the **governance of fire** <note>original: *regimine ignis*; the careful control of heat levels over weeks or months</note> according to the intent of the work and the endurance of our **mercury**, our entire **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*; the complete alchemical process or the "Great Work" itself</note> is completed. To better understand this term, "physical fixation," it must be known that one must be extremely careful that the stone, in its endurance of its fire, is not deprived of its **humidity** <note>original: *humiditate*; the "radical moisture" or vital fluid that alchemists believed held the life-force of the metal</note>. If this happens, its humidity could rarely or never be restored to it, and thus the entire work would be destroyed. This has happened to many Philosophers who otherwise knew the stone well. For this reason, they ended up denying the Art, and those among them who denied the Art entered into other erroneous paths. They failed to notice that all the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemical authorities like Hermes Trismegistus, Geber, or Rhazes.</note> cry out that their work is **sublimation**.

But these people merely refined and purified the stone known to them in some small way, and then they aimed for **fixation**, having dismissed sublimation and complete purification. In doing so, they "fixed" the stone again in such a way that they deprived it of its humidity. This should remain in the fire for a good length of time, so that the other labor of the work—namely, **thickening** <term>Thickening: *inspissatio*; the stage where the liquid or "subtle" matter begins to densify and turn back into a solid state.</term>—is not applied to it too hastily. This continues until, through the long duration and the habituation of the fire, you see that part naturally start to thicken through the steady heat of the fire. Then, by continually and slightly increasing such fire until you see some part beginning to **be incinerated** <term>Incineration: *incinerari*; also called calcination, this is the reduction of the matter to a dry powder or ash through heat, preparing it for the next stage of purification.</term>, you must then apply a greater strength of fire. However, one must not depart from the first or second stages of the work through a violent heat. Once a certain part has been incinerated of its own accord and naturally—due to the multiplication of other refined parts—that part is refined again. This proceeds continuously, as was said, through a greater tolerance of the fire until this is done many times: namely, by **sublimating**, incinerating, and so forth.

And you will find that this work is first one of **fixation** <note>original: *fixionis*</note> through a long **decoction** <term>Decoction: *decoctio*; the prolonged heating or "cooking" of the alchemical substance in its vessel to bring it to maturity.</term> of the stone in the fire. Our stone itself will reach such a tolerance of heat that as much fire is required in the second work and labor during the constant application of the stone as was required in the first stage for thickening; and the same follows for incineration and fixation. And this...

...continuing to rule [the fire] in this way, until finally the whole **stone** <note>original: *lapis*; the Philosopher's Stone in its state of development.</note>—following its sufficient preparation, which is a purification achieved by such a method of governing the fire over the stone—provides easy fusion along with its ignition. It then performs true **gold-making** <term>Gold-making: *solificium*; the alchemical process or result of transmuting base metal into gold.</term> and **silver-making** <term>Silver-making: *lunificium*; the process of transmuting base metal into silver.</term> and **transmutes** <note>original: *transmutet*; to change the fundamental nature of one substance into another.</note> metals or **mercury** <note>original: *mercurium*; often referring here to "Quick-silver" or the volatile principle of metals.</note>, withstanding all trials and examinations. This occurs either in its entirety or in part—and I say this notably, "or in part"—because it is of no concern if your entire matter, once put into the vessel, was not prepared to that same high degree. 

On the contrary, it does not harm the work if some part of it remained behind during a stage of governance, namely in **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: *sublimatio*; in alchemy, this refers to purifying a substance by heating it until it rises as vapor and then solidifies again, or more broadly, the "exaltation" of the matter.</term> or **incineration** <note>original: *incineratione*; the process of reducing a substance to ashes through fire.</note>. The reason for this is that such a residue is a sign that the stone was not driven with excessive speed, and this is actually more useful. Indeed, in the highest works, one must take care lest the stone be digested so quickly that it is deprived of some former mode or of the effects of the prior operations. For the "sublimation" of the Philosophers must be continued over the stone for a long time, because it is not merely an elevation upward, but also a remaining below. In this completeness, the entire **Mastery** <term>Mastery: *magisterium*; the finished Great Work or the successful completion of the alchemical process.</term> is thus perfected; then test it by **projection** <term>Projection: *proiectio*; the final stage where a small amount of the Stone is "thrown" onto molten base metal to transform it.</term> upon a body.

If you find the stone itself to have been so **whitened** <note>original: *dealbatum*; referring to the *albedo* or "white stage" of the work, signaling purity and the ability to make silver.</note> and purified that it yields a pure whiteness, and you then see the stone to be so whitened and refined that it penetrates into the nature of the thing to be tinged, then you have succeeded. Once that penetration is achieved—provided the stone is **fixed** <note>original: *fixus*; rendered stable and resistant to the fire.</note> to the degree that the examined metal withstands all judgments and tests—then you have worked enough.

If however it is not so, repeat the first work upon it, and so on consequently, as it is written, until it is accomplished, and it will be so with God's cooperation.

Behold, it can now be confirmed that it is very erroneous to drive the operation of the **stone** <note>original: *lapidis*; the Philosopher's Stone</note> in such a way that one intends to move from one operation to another while the first is abandoned. For if the **mastery** <term>Mastery: *magisterium*; the complete alchemical process or the successful result of the work.</term> is not complete—as happens to many who, having been led to extremes because of this, believe they cannot repeat the first work upon the art itself—then the business would be totally destroyed. But if you do not find the result at first glance, you can nevertheless, through the persistence of the work as I wrote, best reform your defect. Therefore, you may not only complete or reform it, but truly perfect the work by laboring again with the part that is not **fixed** <note>original: *non fixa*; the volatile part of the matter that has not yet reached a stable, fire-resistant state.</note>, just as **Geber** <term>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose works emphasize logic and laboratory practice.</term> says in the last chapter of his *Summa*, that the mastery of the stone can be multiplied to infinity in increase and goodness. Now, however, I will not omit to introduce some authorities regarding the previously mentioned sayings of the ancients concerning the governance of the stone, specifically as to the preparation of its fire, committing this to the diligence of anyone reading the books of the **Philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophorum*; in this context, the "Philosophers" are the ancient and medieval alchemists who sought the secrets of nature.</note>. For the **Elder** <note>original: *senior*; refers to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umayl), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose "Chemical Tables" were highly influential.</note> says first concerning the preparation of the stone and its governance of fire thus: "The preparation of our stone is difficult and most hidden." Likewise, he says in the same place: "The common people, though they have eyes, are asleep."

Also. The Philosophers say of the fire that it is necessary for this fire to be as the **heat of the Sun** <note>original: *caloris Solis*; a metaphor for a moderate, natural warmth</note> when it is in its proper state, and for this reason they called it **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: *putrefactio*; the essential stage of decay or breakdown where the alchemical matter blackens and decomposes before being purified.</term>. Also in the same place: let your fire be that of **baths** <term>Baths: *balneorum*; referring to the *balneum Mariae* or water bath, used to provide a constant, gentle, and indirect heat.</term>. Also in the *Turba* <note>original: *in turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most influential alchemical texts translated from Arabic into Latin.</note>: let your fire be gentle during the **whitening** <term>Whitening: *albedo*; the stage of the work where the "black" decayed matter is purified and turns white.</term> and at that time when the **tincture** <note>original: *tinctura*; the transformative substance that "colors" or transmutes base matter</note> becomes white, a greater tolerance of fire is required. This is because when that matter of the **stone** <note>original: *lapidis*; the Philosopher's Stone</note> begins to be **reddened** <term>Reddening: *rubedo*; the final stage of the Great Work, indicating that the matter has achieved its highest power and perfection.</term> through the sheer persistence of the labor itself—for then, when the stone is worked toward the red stage—so many degrees of fire in the red are required for the first work that perhaps three times the effort of the whitening is required. In this, a man ought to be cautious, that he does not rule the stone before the time of perfect whitening, until the tincture is perfected in the white regime by using degrees of fire that look toward the red; and concerning this the **Rosary** <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical florilegium</note> cries out, saying: "Do not mix the work of the white with the red." <note>original: *non misce opus albi cum rubeo*</note> These things, however, are especially to be entrusted to the practice of those working.

Also in the same place: a **gentle fire** <note>original: *ignis lenis*</note> must be prepared for our stone when it is placed in its vessel for forty days, because through it the corrupting **humidities** <note>original: *humiditates*; superfluous moisture or "volatile" elements that must be driven off</note> are extracted. For he commends the lengthiness of the work, and censures speed and combustion—that is, heat so intense that the stone cannot return to its first work and be perfected in its entirety.

...until the elements are joined to one another and ground down—not by the grinding of hands, as was mentioned above in the *Turba* <note>original: *in turba*; the *Turba Philosophorum*, an assembly of ancient sages in alchemical lore.</note>—but rather, let them be washed with water, which they should then conceive.

Then let them be extracted and nourished, so that the **offspring** <note>original: *genitum*; the product of the alchemical marriage or process.</note> may be produced. He adds: you should know that this preparation takes place in **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: *putrefactio*; the stage of decomposition or "rotting" necessary for rebirth, often associated with the color black.</term> at the bottom of the vessel. This is not the putrefaction of the common sort <note>original: *putredine vulgi*; refers to natural biological rotting, which alchemists distinguished from their controlled laboratory "decay."</note>, but rather through **incineration** <term>Incineration: *incineratio*; the reduction of a substance to ash through fire, used here as a metaphor for deep purification.</term>. For the ancient philosophers nowhere set down anything regarding putrefaction or the distillation of waters, except perhaps allegorically and figuratively. 

The offspring, however, is produced in the "air"—that is, in the upper part of the vessel—if one works with a "vessel upon a vessel" <note>original: *vase supra vas*; likely referring to a reflux apparatus or a double-boiler system where vapors rise and condense.</note>, as **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arab alchemist known in Latin as Senior Zadith.</note> seems to think, which is made clear below. Likewise, it is said in the same place: take the things from their minerals, and **exalt them to the higher places of the mountains** <note>A metaphor for sublimation, where solids are heated to become vapor and then re-solidify in the upper part of the apparatus.</note>, and measure them on the peak of the mountains, and lead them back down upon the root.

And these are clear words, written without any **envy** <note>original: *sine aliqua invidia*; in alchemical texts, "envy" refers to the practice of intentionally obscuring secrets to keep them from the unworthy. To write "without envy" is to claim transparency.</note>. From this authority, some have wanted to derive a particular way of working: they converted purified **mercury** <term>Mercury: *mercurium*; not necessarily the common liquid metal, but the "Mercury of the Philosophers," a specialized substance representing the principle of liquidity and volatility.</term> into water through roasting—either forced together with other things or by itself—and they distilled it through an **alembic** <term>Alembic: *alembicum*; a classic alchemical still used for distillation.</term>. They moistened the "earth" at the bottom with the water, and thus they converted water into earth; they said this should be continued until the perfect **tincture** <term>Tincture: *tinctura*; the final medicine or agent capable of transmuting metals.</term> was completed.

Whatever the case regarding this in the final results or in the past, it does not seem to me that this was the intention of the ancient philosophers, although I do not seem to reject that path entirely, since they also proceed through the mercury...

...prepared by sublimation, through purification and the fixation of its natural moisture. Through this, it is explained what the Philosophers meant when they said: it is necessary to break down our **bronze** <note>original: *æs noſtrum*; in alchemy, this often refers to the "body" or base matter being transformed.</note> and convert it into water and into vapor, and then for it to be thickened again. Likewise, the Philosophers say in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Sages," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> that the beginning of our operation is that the **stone** <term>Stone: *lapis*; the "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the work, though here referring to the material in its early, "dead" state.</term> be worked with a slow fire, so that it might be made as if dead, and then its soul be returned to it; and let this be continued until the soul becomes permanent in the fire.

Third, so that a portion is reduced to ash <term>Incineration: *incineretur*; the process of reducing a substance to ash to reach its pure, essential state.</term> according to the stated mastery.

Likewise, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Alchemist often quoted by later European scholars.</note> commands that when their single thing (to which we add nothing and from which we take nothing) is sufficiently purified—he is speaking here of **mercury** <term>Mercury: *mercurio*; specifically "philosophical mercury," the fluid, transformative principle of matter, rather than common quicksilver.</term>, though naturally purified of earthiness, I should say, of the Philosophers. ### THE SPECIAL DOCTRINE FOLLOWS,
### *which speaks very clearly regarding the preparation*
### *of the stone.*

In this book, which begins "bodies submerged in **mercury** <term>Mercury: often referred to as "argentum vivum" (living silver), the liquid metal considered by alchemists to be the "mother" of all metals.</term> through appropriate **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: a process of decay or fermentation in a sealed vessel, intended to break down the old forms of the matter to allow a new, purified form to emerge.</term> return into the quicksilver that was previously expressed," and afterwards, the metallic types cast into that putrefied matter will be multiplied and grow unchangeably. The method of acting is truly thus, after the manner of nature. Our quicksilver and the power of white and red **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, "Sulfur" and "Mercury" represent the two primary principles of matter: the active/combustible and the passive/fluid.</note> will not be burned when congealed or thickened; first, it is cleansed of every superfluity that can be removed by ingenuity, and that ingenuity is washing or **sublimating** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then collecting the purified solid that forms when the vapor cools.</term>, which is done in this way.

Let one pound of quicksilver be placed [in the vessel] and let all the superfluous **humanity** <note>original: *humanitas*; this is likely a scribe's error or OCR misreading for *humiditas* (moisture), as the text describes removing "watery" and "volatile" accidents.</note> fly off which exists in it accidentally, by which our work would be corrupted—and do not omit this, otherwise you would labor in vain. # Anonymous Treatise of the Concordances [of the Philosophers]

...[it will have] glowed, the fourth sign is most splendidly adorned with abundance and redness <note>original: *rubedo*; the final stage of the Great Work, signifying the attainment of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. If you understand this main principle <note>original: *caput*, literally "head" or "chapter."</note>, then you are able to work in the Art.

The dissolved body <note>original: *corpus solutum*</note>, that is, the mercury, is the soul and the spirit. Understand it thus: dissolve the body into water and mercury, and lead that dissolved substance back into sublimated air, that is, into refined mercury <term>Refined mercury: *mercurius subtiliatus*, a purified, volatile form of the metal used to "spiritualize" the solid body, allowing it to transcend its base physical state.</term>, and thus increase the refined air and afterward coagulate <term>Coagulate: the process of turning a liquid or vapor back into a solid form, signifying the "fixing" of the volatile spirit into a stable substance.</term> it, and you have found [the secret]. Again, place the earth into water, that is, the body into mercury, which is the water of metals; and [turn] that water into air, that is, into refined mercury, and mix it with the dissolved air, and mix the air with fire, and the fire with earth, and afterward coagulate the whole, and it is completed, just as before.

**Note:** when the body is dissolved and refined mercury is amalgamated with it, it rectifies <term>Rectifies: to purify or refine a substance by repeated distillation or processing until it reaches its most potent state.</term> the body. For Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy are attributed.</note> says that every dissolved body will be a perfect body. He says, therefore: Dissolve the bodies and sublimate the spirits, and imbibe the refined spirits with the dissolved bodies; for the dissolved bodies will be coagulated by the refined spirits. Or, as he says: calcine <term>Calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures until it is reduced to a fine powder, or "ash," through oxidation.</term> the bodies, and dissolve the spirits, and grind the calcined bodies with the dissolved spirits. For the bodies will be illuminated by the waters of the spirits, and the Art is easy in its operation.

# THE GARDEN OF LOVE.

Here begins the book on the art of Alchemy, which John Dumbleton <note>original: *Iohannes Dumbeleij*; Dumbleton was a 14th-century scholar at Merton College, Oxford.</note> of England composed based upon the universal opinions of all the Philosophers. ### Concerning the first matter of our tree.

In this way, many things are converted into one thing, which is declared and judged by all the Philosophers to be Quicksilver, the principle of all metals.

### CHAPTER II.

*What the nature of the Principles is, and what the Sulfur of the Philosophers is, and from where it is drawn.*

The <term>Philosophers</term> <note>meaning the ancient alchemical authorities</note> say by common opinion that <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> is the natural principle, the middle, and the end of metals through the mediation of its <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle, while mercury is the passive, metallic, and "feminine" principle.</note>, as <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in medieval alchemy; the text likely refers to the *Summa Perfectionis*.</note> testifies in the chapter on general medicines, saying thus: From these things the Principle of nature is proven to be those things which are most closely joined and which adhere most amicably to them in their deep interior. *And because in the nature of things we perceive nothing besides quicksilver to be more perfectly befriended or mixed with [metallic] natures, we are therefore compelled to say that it is the true <term>medicine</term> <note>original: *medicina*; in alchemy, the "medicine" is the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone that "cures" base metals by transforming them into gold.</note> of alterable things in the total completion of gold or silver by means of its sulfur. For a proper generation does not occur except from things consistent in their genus and nature, because it is known to all who understand the nature of things that nothing is made from a human except a human, from a lion except a lion, from an ass except an ass, and so it is to be understood regarding all other things.* 

But since all the Philosophers say by common opinion that all metals are generated from quicksilver and sulfur according to the purity and impurity of the aforementioned, it must be seen whether that sulfur which is found for sale among the common people <note>original: *apud vulgus venale*; referring to "vulgar sulfur," the common chemical element, which alchemists distinguished from the "Philosophical Sulfur" hidden within metals.</note> is of the essence of the Principles of nature or the generation of metals. And if it does not appear to be that sulfur from which metals are generated, and [it must be seen] where that [true] sulfur is found; I speak following the path according to the order of Geber, Se- <meta>catchword: ri, Se-</meta>

For <term>true sulfur</term>, which is of the essence of the principles of nature, is fixed through a tempered heat without the consumption of its internal moisture.

Wherefore it is sufficiently clear that common sulfur is not what the Philosophers intended regarding the effect of the principles of nature. We must see, therefore, what true sulfur is. The Philosophers say: the principle of sulfur is the <term>fatness</term> <note>original: *pinguedo*; an oily, life-giving essence thought to be the "glue" of the elements.</note> of the most subtle substance of the earth, dissolved in <term>mineral water</term> by a gradual and long-lasting <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of boiling or heating a substance in a fluid to extract its essence.</note>, until the moist [is joined] with the dry, and the dry with the moist

# John Dumbleton of England
<page-num>8</page-num>

...[it] is tempered by moisture and joined in a strong union, and thus that oily fatness <note>original: *pinguedo*; alchemists often described the flammable principle of sulfur as a "fatness" or "oiliness."</note> is converted—through the action of heat and <term>mineral water</term> <note>In alchemy, "mineral water" does not mean spring water; it refers to a mercurial solvent or the "mercury of the philosophers" that can dissolve metals.</note>—into the very essence of nature's principles, which is <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," the standard Latin term for mercury or quicksilver.</note>, just as was stated above. 

But now it remains to see where it may be found, or from what it is extracted—specifically, in what things this mercury exists. Therefore, it is extracted from itself, as <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan. The text cited is likely the "Summa Perfectionis," a highly influential 13th-century alchemical manual attributed to him.</note> testifies in the chapter concerning the coagulation of Mercury; there he says that mercury possesses within itself parts of <term>sulfur</term> <note>Here referring to "philosophical sulfur," the active, dry principle found within the mercury itself, rather than the yellow mineral.</note> that are uniformly and naturally mixed into the very root of its creation. It is not possible to remove or separate these parts through any human artifice, since mercury is itself a homogeneous substance, the perfection of nature's principles, and uniform in its nature.

Immediately following this is the definition of mercury in that same chapter, stating: mercury is a viscous mineral water made of a subtle substance of white sulfurous earth, produced by tempered heat at the root of its mixing in a strong, finite, and homogeneous union, so that the moist is tempered by the dry and the dry by the moist, inseparably. 

But as for what "homogeneous" and "uniformity of substance" mean, as was said above, this is made clear by Geber in the chapter on Iron. He states that mercury does not allow itself to be divided into its composite parts by any means of destruction, because its entire substance either retreats from the fire <note>The author is describing volatility; mercury evaporates as a whole rather than breaking down into separate ingredients.</note> or remains entirely within the fire. 

Regarding this matter, <term>John of the Rose Garden</term> <note>original: *Iohannes de Rosario*; a reference to the author of the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a fundamental text in the alchemical tradition focused on the "mystical marriage" of substances.</note> says the following: "The qualities in our worthy matter, by the command of the Creator, are beyond all other things; they are of such a strong mixture and tempered bond...

### C H A P T E R III.

#### *How all metals are generated, both in general and in particular.*

Now that it has been determined what the natural principle of metals is, it remains to determine the procreation of Metals, both in general and in particular, and how perfect and imperfect bodies are generated in mineral mountains. And how, at the root of their mixing, purity, corruption, and imperfection are produced. First, I shall speak of the generation of all metals in general; thereafter, in particular. The <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: *Philosophi*; in this context, the term refers to ancient and medieval alchemical authorities rather than modern secular philosophers.</note> say that the heat existing at the base of a very firm and solid mountain—whose nature is to ascend through the passages of the earth—meets with <term>viscous water</term> <note>original: *aqua viscosa*; likely a reference to "mercury of the philosophers," a thick, metallic vapor.</note> in the veins of the earth, thins it, and turns it into a subtle spirit. Additionally, the most subtle fatness of the sulfurous earth, liquefied by that same <term>decoction</term> <note>original: *decoctio*; the process of "cooking" or heating a substance in liquid to mature it, mimicking the earth's natural geothermal heat.</note>, runs and flows there; and this is sulfur.

The aforementioned mineral water, having been turned into spirit and finding the fatness and most subtle substance of the sulfurous earth—which has been liquefied by the action of heat—is uniformly joined to it. It becomes sticky through a remote and long decoction, forming a natural and firm union. Furthermore, in that same place, through the heat of the water enduring for a long time, the said united and sticky substances are thickened. This thickening is then refined by the heat and is washed and ground by the mineral water for a very long time, [to be] dissolved- <note>The original catchword *solui-* (from *soluitur*) indicates the text continues with the process of the substance being dissolved or broken down further on the next page.</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

*Whether it might be possible for the **Philosopher’s Stone** to be extracted from pure or impure bodies, or from what things it is drawn.*

Having seen the general and specific procreation of metals, it must further be considered whether bodies diminished from perfection <note>Refers to "base" metals like lead or copper, which alchemists believed were simply "unripe" or "sick" versions of gold.</note> might be brought to the true species of metal by some special thing procreated from the **first matter** <term>materia prima</term> <note>The primitive, formless base of all matter according to Aristotelian and alchemical theory.</note> that is "more-than-perfect." And whether this special substance, from which that special body ought to be procreated, is drawn from one or many things. For nature always operates simply, whether spiritually or physically, in purifying and perfecting bodies, based only on what it has from the first matter without any ingenious cleansing or subtle refinement.

Therefore, it is argued that perfection in them is found to be simple and unmixable, as in **gold** and **silver**. For since they are simply and physically (as said above) perfect according to a greater or lesser degree, impure things mixed with them do not make them perfect, but rather they are made imperfect by their addition. To which it is briefly answered: that which is indeed left diminished by nature for lack of ingenious refinement is aided in this defect by natural ingenuity <note>Here, "ingenuity" refers to the Alchemical Art—the human skill that mimics and accelerates natural processes.</note>. For if, by the most subtle ingenuity of man, who is the servant of nature, [nature] herself...

For in perfect bodies <note>In the alchemical tradition, "perfect bodies" refer to gold and silver, which nature has already "digested" or refined to a state of stability.</note>, there is a gradual and long-lasting union of the most subtle resolved parts, and a very strong digestion without any ingenious cleansing. Even if there were, as stated, a resolution and reduction into first matter, nevertheless because of their strong natural union they cannot be intimately purified <term>mundificari; the process of stripping away "dross" or chemical impurities</term>. Therefore, as is clearly evident, a shining thing can by no means be procreated from them.

Furthermore, this most shining substance is not found in the aforementioned perfect bodies because of the strong union and more difficult resolution they possess. It is also clear from the preceding sections that the separation of the coarser parts <note>The "gross" or earthy parts of a metal that must be removed to reach the spiritual essence.</note> ought to be done from diminished and imperfect bodies. Therefore, it must be seen whether anything for our purpose could be found in diminished bodies.

To this, Geber <note>original: "Geber"; refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century Islamic polymath whose Latinized works were the standard authority for medieval alchemists.</note> responds in the chapter on the management of bodies, saying that bodies diminished from perfection are dark in the depths of their nature, and nothing shining happens to be found in them for procreating the aforementioned **spiritual body** <term>corpus spirituale; a refined, volatile state of matter that can penetrate other metals</term>, since it is not in their root according to nature. Therefore, it is concluded universally by the Philosophers: *one does not find in a thing what is not already in that thing* <note>original: "non invenitur in re, quod in re non est"; a common philosophical axiom used to argue that you cannot extract gold-like qualities from a substance that contains no "seed" of gold.</note>. Therefore, since this substance is most shining, [procreated] from the aforesaid bodies—both perfect...

<summary>The author argues that the alchemical Elixir cannot be derived from gold (because it is too stable to be further purified) nor from base metals (because they lack the inherent "shining" quality in their nature).</summary>

Some Philosophers say that metals are often found where neither sulfur nor quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> can be found. It follows, therefore, from what has just been said, that metals are generated neither from quicksilver nor from sulfur. 

Some also say that gold is found in precious stones, and also in minerals of various kinds and on the shores of waters, where neither quicksilver nor sulfur is found. It follows, therefore, from the aforementioned facts, that the generation of metals does not occur solely by the benefit of quicksilver and sulfur. ### ->Hortus Amoris.<-

...in a natural union. To such a union, other elements arrive according to their proper and natural proportions. They are mixed *per minima* <note>original: "per minima," a scholastic term referring to the mixing of substances at the smallest possible level, similar to a molecular scale.</note> until they form a natural mixture. This mixture, through successive decoction <note>original: "decoctionem," the process of slow, transformative heating within the earth.</note> in the mine, is thickened, condensed, and hardened, until it is converted into metal. These opinions seem to be consistent with reason and close to the truth. However, regarding these opinions, it should be noted that they are not all true, nor are they stated with logical consistency, as I shall demonstrate through probable reasoning.

First, we must turn our pen toward the opinion of **Hermes**, since he is the "Father of Philosophers," who should be believed in all matters as a natural philosopher. He says specifically that metals are not generated from quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note> alone, but from quicksilver and sulfur. Regarding this opinion, I have already cited the testimony of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–813), a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> above. 

However, I do not mean to say that Geber's words should not be supported by reason, given the conclusions that follow. Geber says in the book titled *The Cistern of Alchemy* <note>original: "Cisterna Alchymiæ."</note> that quicksilver, in its uniform nature, is not by itself the principle of the generation of metals; nor is sulfur by itself. Rather, it is both of them, or either one converted into "earth," etc. 

To this opinion, I say that it was not Geber’s intention to speak of common sulfur <note>original: "sulphure vulgi," the ordinary combustible substance, which alchemists distinguished from the "Philosophical Sulfur" needed for the Work.</note>. Rather, the nature of the sulfur he speaks of is well demonstrated in Geber’s *Summa* in the chapter on the procreation of **Mars** <note>original: "procreatione Martis." In alchemical symbolism, Mars represents the metal iron.</note>, where he says: 

*“It happens in the mine, or in the mineral mountain, that quicksilver, through long decoction, is thickened and...”*

### Io. Dumbeleij of England <note>John Dumbleton (c. 1310–1349) was an English scholastic philosopher and mathematician at Merton College, Oxford. This text likely comes from his work on natural philosophy.</note>

That sulfurous earth finds another quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver" or mercury.</note> of the same nature and dissolves it again through a long-lasting decoction <note>A process of slow, transformative heating within the earth.</note> by means of the action of natural heat. 

Once this dissolution is achieved, the said mineral matter is raised by the force and power of a certain air or wind enclosed in the mine itself. This air or wind entered the mine along with the water from which the quicksilver began its existence, and it compels the material thus dissolved to run here and there, until it finds other passages <note>original: "meatus," referring to channels or veins in the rock.</note> through which it can ascend to the surface of the earth. Thus, when coldness comes upon it at the surface of the earth, that ascending matter is thickened and condensed, and is also converted into metal. 

This seems to happen more often near streams of water. The cause, as **Giles** reports in *On Minerals* <note>original: "Aegidius de Mineralibus," likely referring to the scholastic philosopher Giles of Rome.</note>, is because the earthly pores and passages near waters are more open than they are in other places. Reason dictates that where there is greater dryness of the earth, there is greater density; and where there is greater humidity of the earth, there is greater rarity <note>In this context, "raritas" refers to being less dense or more porous.</note>. For this reason, metals are often found near streams of water rather than in other places. 

It seems, therefore, that when the Philosophers said, *"The principle of metals is not in Mercury, but in sulfur and Mercury,"* they were not speaking of common sulfur <note>original: "sulphure vulgari," the yellow brimstone found on the surface.</note>, but of the sulfur which is created by nature from quicksilver within the mine, because quicksilver contains its own "good sulfur." For heat acting upon the moist first creates blackness, and heat acting upon the dry creates whiteness, and in the white, yellowness. ### John Dumbleton of England

...alien and foreign to metals are substances such as **alum**, **arsenic**, **marcasite**, and **orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigmentum." Orpiment is a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral; its name comes from the Latin *auripigmentum* (gold pigment), as it was often mistaken for or used to imitate gold.</note> and similar materials. Many who involve themselves in the art of **Alchemy** are utterly befouled and deceived by these, because they are entirely removed and foreign from the nature of metals. Although they sometimes seem to tint metals either a red or a white color, the metal nevertheless remains exactly what it was before—in weight, in taste, and in every other aspect of its being—except for the temporary hiding of its outward appearance. In such cases, the metal is neither **fixed** <note>In alchemy, to "fix" a substance means to make it stable and resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates or changes state.</note>, nor transformed, nor refined in its essence.

In the symbolic language of alchemy, Sol (the Sun) represents gold, and Luna (the Moon) represents silver.</note>, depending on whether the Elixir was prepared for the "white" or the "red" work. 

By the power of this Elixir, that body is purged of all filth, made bright, illuminated, and fixed; furthermore, it is given its true weight by that elixireal quality, because the pure parts of that metal are segregated and separated from the impure by the Elixir. Therefore, **Elixir** in Greek is called **Power** <note>original: "potentia." The author is linking the transformative power of the stone to the philosophical concept of "potency" or the ability to bring a thing to its full potential.</note> in Latin, because it leads a "sick" metal from one state to another, from one thing to another, from **potentiality to actuality**, from coarseness to refinement, from imperfection to perfection, from darkness to clarity, and from an imperfect state to the most perfect state. It is thus rightly named "power," for it receives its name from its effect. There is no other thing like it in the world that performs such actions, since this substance alone contains within itself the effects and operations of all things...

These are more quickly dissolved in fire than other metals of stronger digestion and better decoction <term>Decoction: The process of "ripening" or purifying a substance through boiling or intense heat.</term>. They are more slowly coagulated again; and even in the fire after their melting, they fly away <note>original: "evolat." The reason for this is as follows: they are not fixed <term>Fixation: The alchemical goal of making a substance "stable" so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</term> nor fully cooked in the mine. By this, it is clearly proven that they drew their origin from quicksilver, since quicksilver flees entirely from the fire before its fixation, but after its fixation, it rejoices and delights in the fire <note>A poetic way of saying that once "fixed," the substance becomes fire-resistant and stable, like gold.</note>, as will appear in the following. ...**sulfur** and **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: known in Latin as *argentum vivum* or mercury; considered the essential liquid principle of all metals</term> are resolved into vapors, and from those vapors—repeatedly condensed, mixed together, and hardened—metals are formed. This is entirely false: for these substances, once brought to their true nature, cannot be resolved into vapors within the bowels of the earth without total destruction. This is especially true of quicksilver, which is of such firm composition and mixture that its parts cannot be separated. This is due to its **homogeneity** <term>homogeneity: the state of being all of one kind; here, it refers to the alchemical belief that mercury is a "simple" substance that cannot be broken down into further components</term>; for if its parts could be divided or separated from one another, it would by no means be homogeneous.

And there is another reason: if the generation of metals were caused by subtle vapors, then no metal would possess a heavy substance with an abundance of earth within itself. The contrary is clearly evident in **iron**, which is earthy, impure, full of dross, and fusible; if it were generated from subtle vapors, resolved and evaporated as previously mentioned, this would in no way be possible. Therefore, it is clearly manifest that such an opinion is false and empty. 

But I believe that **Albert** <note>original: "Albertus." Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the Dominican friar and philosopher whose *De Mineralibus* was a standard text on mineralogy.</note>, when he held that opinion, was young and did not yet perfectly understand the roots of natural things. He seems to contradict himself in the book called *The Plain Way* <note>original: "via plana." An alchemical treatise often attributed to Albertus Magnus during the Middle Ages, though its true authorship is debated.</note>, where he says: those investigating the first principles of natural things affirm that all **liquefiable things** <note>original: "liquabilia." Substances that can be melted or turned to liquid.</note> take their origin from the homogeneity of quicksilver, mediated by its sulfur. Behold, here he affirms that quicksilver is homogeneous in its nature, and that its parts cannot be divided. It is therefore clearly evident from all the aforementioned conclusions that **quicksilver** is the principle of all metals.

...seeing that our most pure Mercury—fixed and yet flowing, entering the work and yet not bringing it to completion—many have been led to believe that the art of Alchemy should be denied. And this method of reduction ought to be performed by means of calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder.</note> in a <term>reverberatory fire</term><note>A furnace design where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof onto the material, preventing direct contact with the flame.</note> cautiously, lest it melt, and with sharp fiery waters. Through this continued operation, it happens that the surface of the Sun is destroyed regarding its moisture, and dryness is generated in its place; therefore, it will be hot and dry.

But because earthly dryness cannot stand alongside fiery heat, the first dryness is destroyed and another is generated, which is more powerful by the degree of the fire. Therefore, that Gold is hot and dry, having acquired the power of fire through calcinations and roastings; and he added, saying: *This operation is immediately completed, for in things that share a common symbol, the transition is easy.* <note>original: "in habentibus symbolum facilis est transitus." This must be understood as the binding of the two birds with the sevenfold regime, which must be repeated seven times and divided by seven times four in respect to the *corsufle*.

And this is the completion of the third regime of our work.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*What the fruits of our Philosophical tree are, and from where they arise.*<-

Senior <note>Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century Arabian alchemist whose works were highly influential in Latin translation.</note> and other highest Philosophers, philosophizing truly upon the exposition of the wise Hermes, have said that the wise man placed ten figures in his description: namely, five on the right and five on the left, leading to the middle. This middle is the half-full Moon and the full Moon on the other side above in the margin of the table, and three figures below, namely two birds and a full moon. These are the five, and this is the half of the whole work; it signifies the distillation and the thinning <note>original: *attenuationem*; the process of refining a substance to make it more subtle or spiritual.</note> of the soul from the body in the spiritual water. 

The half-full Moon signifies the raw mercury <term>mercurium erudum; crude or unprepared mercury, often representing the volatile, "living" principle of the matter</term> infused upon our body in the first composition of our stone <term>lapis; the Philosopher's Stone</term> before the extraction of its soul from the body. 

The full Moon above in the margin of the table signifies the ascent of the spiritual water, in which the soul is lost; and that is the "complete water," which perfects our first work until it reaches the stage of perfect whiteness <term>albedo; the stage of purification where the matter becomes a brilliant white</term>, and for this reason it is likened to the full Moon. 

The other three figures below—namely, the two birds and the full moon—signify the conjunction of the body and soul by means of the aforementioned spiritual water, in which the soul was previously lost. These are said to be five in number and yet they are three: namely, body, soul, and spirit; and it is certain, however, that all those three are one.

The first reason why there are seven roastings is because if the roasting of the body were not repeated seven times, that body would not be perfectly cleansed of its filth. And if the body were not well purified <note>original: *mundificatum*; the process of "mundification" involves removing the "corrupting sulfur" to leave behind a pure metallic base.</note>, it would lack clarity and effectiveness in the end. The second reason why it is necessary to roast our body seven times is because every roasting is like a watering of the earth, or at least a dissolution of that body. For this reason, the Philosophers say: "As often as the body is dissolved, so many times does it gain in its tincture according to the number of the algorithm" <note>original: *secundum numerum algorismi*; likely referring to a mathematical or sequential progression where the potency of the substance increases exponentially with each repeated cycle.</note>. And indeed, this is commonly seen to be true, for the more that arable land is plowed, watered, fertilized, and prepared, the better the grains or seeds sown in it will bear fruit. Whence Senior <note>Zadith Senior, an influential authority in medieval Latin alchemy.</note> says: "Multiple preparation converts our stone..."

# The Garden of Love

...which with God's help we shall complete on the ninth day, and in this lies the greatest secret <term>arcanum: a deep mystery or hidden secret of nature</term>. For Sulfur is mixed with sulfur and from that our fruit arises, because nature recognizes its own nature <note>original: "natura naturam cognoscit," a fundamental alchemical maxim suggesting that substances can only be transformed by things of their own kind</note>. 

Furthermore, Cereus speaks concerning the time of the reduction of the **nine eagles** <note>Sublimations where the substance "takes flight" as vapor nine times</note>, saying that with the first **Brining** <term>salsatura: a treatment involving salts or sharp liquids to break down a substance</term> the stone is dissolved in one day; with the second Brining on another day, the stone is congealed, raising itself from the dung <note>A metaphor for the "prima materia" or the base, impure state of the matter before its transformation</note>. 

And regarding these matters, other philosophers from the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical dialogue</note> have said: do not despise the ash because of its filth and stain, for God will restore to it liquefaction and a soul, and then at last the king shall be crowned with a red diadem by the will of God <note>The "Red King" represents the final successful stage of the work, known as the rubedo</note>. 

The virtue of the *affalia* <note>original: *affaliæ*, likely a technical term derived from Arabic referring to a specific vessel or the power of the "feminine" mercury</note> is nothing other than the power of the female, because her power releases the soul from its bonds and makes it, now glorified, ascend to the higher parts of the chamber—that is, to the **Alembic** <term>alembic: the upper part of a still where vapors condense</term>. This is the substance which is tinted in its ascent and becomes the tinting agent in its return <note>The vapor is colored by the essence of the stone as it rises, and then drips back down to "tinge" or transform the remaining matter</note>. 

And indeed, within this lies the fruit, goodness, perfection, and completion of our most glorious **philosophical tree**, as I shall explain clearly enough below in the summary of the whole, if God wills—whose names be hallowed forever. Now that it has certainly been explained in theory what the **Philosophers' Stone** is, where it originates, and how the tree is planted and composed, I shall proceed, with God's help, to the Practice.

->* * *<-

### CHAPTER IX.

->*Concerning the first regimen: how the root of our Tree arises or is composed, in plain words of practice.*<-

In the name of God, the pious and merciful, let raw **mercury** <term>mercurio crudo: quicksilver in its natural, unrefined state</term> be taken and well washed two, three, or four times with common salt and vinegar as desired. Let it be placed in a round glass vessel with a long neck <note>This vessel is often called a "philosopher's egg" or a matrass, designed to allow vapors to rise and condense.</note> and let the vessel be positioned among hot ashes. Furthermore, let the ashes be underneath and around the vessel to the thickness of two fingers. Let the vessel also be well-sealed with good **lute** <term>luto bono: a paste made of clay, dung, and hair used to protect glass from heat and prevent vapors from escaping</term> at the bottom, so that it might better endure the battle of the fire <note>original: "ignis pugnam sustinere," a common alchemical metaphor for the intense stress heat places on materials and vessels.</note>. 

And let the fire be continued beneath it—as much as the vessel is estimated to be able to withstand—night and day, until the substance is congealed and **fixed** <term>figatur: "fixed" means the substance has become solid and will no longer evaporate when heated</term>. This ought to be tested in this way: when it is considered to be congealed, take a small amount from the vessel and place it upon a glowing metal plate. If it gives off smoke, then it is not yet fixed; if indeed it does not smoke, then it is well. Nevertheless, even if it is fixed, let the fire still be continued under it for forty days or for two months, so that it may acquire for itself the perfect heat of the fire. At that point, it is called the **sulfur** or the **gold of the Philosophers** <note>original: "sulphur vel aurum Philosophorum." This is not common gold, but a perfected, stable state of the matter.</note>, just as was explained extensively above in the theoretical section. 

Then, take one pound from that body so congealed and add to it a tenth part (relative to its weight) of raw mercury prepared with common salt and vinegar. Immediately it absorbs it, just as a **dropsical person** <note>original: "Hydropicus." In medieval medicine, someone suffering from dropsy (edema) was characterized by an unquenchable, pathological thirst.</note> consumes a drink or ash...

### A Recapitulation of the whole, in typical and obscure Philosophical words.

The ancient sages were accustomed, after the composition of their books, to recapitulate the entire intention of the work within a single series of discourse, because the aforementioned method validates the book, and more swiftly and rapidly directs and encourages the mind to remember the book's intention. Therefore, by the grace of almighty God, I shall proceed to recapitulate the whole intention of the work in a single discourse, in the name of God, Amen. 

Let the **half-full Moon** <note>original: "Luna semiplena." This likely refers to silver or the volatile, "feminine" matter at a specific stage of its development.</note> be taken and be placed in a bright, hollowed-out place, whose depth is at least half a foot, and let it be sealed near the **torment of hell** <term>supplicium inferni: a metaphorical term for the intense, constant heat of the alchemical furnace, also called the athanor.</term> for 150 days. By God’s will, the coldness and moisture will be expelled, and the power of fire will be introduced into it, and it will be a **bird without feathers** <note>original: "avis sine plumis." A common alchemical metaphor for a substance that has been "fixed" and can no longer evaporate or "fly" away when heated.</note>. Because of its paleness, it becomes a most wicked poison; this is our **Sulphur** <term>sulphur nostrum: "Our Sulphur" refers to the active, masculine principle of the Stone, which is not common brimstone but a purified, philosophical substance.</term>, which in its action holds the end and all its names. This is hard and dry iron; this is the strong fisherman who has caught every good thing. Through it, the **Light of Secrets** <note>original: "Lux Secretorum."</note> is generated; nor is there any thing performing its action that possesses light, having been made and yet possessing darkness. 

But after it has arrived at perfection, it shall recover from its weaknesses and its thinness, and it possesses the life of a **Roaring Lion** <note>original: "Leonis rugientis." The Lion often symbolizes the "Red Work," specifically the "Red Lion" or the potent, fermented state of the philosopher's stone capable of transmutation.</note>. And then that great "fluxible" thing will appear: this is **gold**, with which our work is to be completed, and we need nothing else. Since truth is without variation, is this not said out of a lack of fairness by the ignorant and the scornful? Thus I would say to the sheep...

# Hortus Amoris
<note>original: "Hortus Amoris." Latin for "The Garden of Love" or "The Garden of Desire," a common allegorical title for alchemical works where the "marriage" of substances takes place.</note>

...gave birth to men, or as if wheat grains produce galbanum resin, or a palm tree produces pomegranates, or winged birds produce fish. They would respond that you have spoken falsely, for things do not beget anything except what is similar to themselves, nor do things bear fruit except for their own fruit. Would not the wicked sheep be turned away from their ignorance, and from the reproach of their deeds, had they themselves first come away from doubt?

Certain **Philosophers** have said: "The father of gold and silver is **our gold**." <note>original: "aurum nostrum." In alchemy, "our gold" refers to "Philosophical Gold," a purified essence or the Living Spirit, rather than the common metal found in coins.</note> From these errors regarding the belief in uncertain things, they remove that which is praiseworthy. By God, if you consider the stars, there is no greater difference between us in this—in what we think of them—and the wise man prepares this matter with a **natural preparation**, <term>præparatio naturalis: the process of mimicking nature’s slow growth within the earth through the controlled heat of the laboratory.</term> and through it our preparation arises, either through bolts or through locks, opening other locks. <note>The author uses "locks" (seraturas) as a metaphor for the chemical or spiritual barriers that must be "unlocked" by specific reagents or "keys" during the work.</note>

By God, if a palm <note>A double meaning: the "palm" of a hand reaching for the secret, or the "palm tree" mentioned earlier.</note> were stretched out toward it, it would not return to him empty; yet in the world, even as it adds sap to the work, men revile its appearance and its designation. O, what a marvelous thing has been done! How blinded are those men who think ill of things in which there is no evil, believing that this work annihilates the person occupied with it. Nor can the common people know what its advancement is, since they have neither the keys nor the locks, nor that which coagulates the **tincture**; <term>tinctura: the transformative essence of the Philosopher's Stone that "stains" or transmutes base metals into gold.</term> nor can anyone reach perfection without **our matter**. And that is it: you have the solution in great numbers, and whatever is fixed from two is from one without another—that is, a part in knowledge without parts—and the whole has become the "eye of the whole." <note>This likely refers to the "All-Seeing" or perfected state of the matter, where the substance is unified and clear.</note> And if you wish to understand these sayings, take your knowledge from the figures: look to the roots with branches separated, doubled by the **conjunction** and **binding** of the two.

# Garden of Love.

This is the reason: because the fiery, hot, and dry body, along with its opposite—namely, the cold and moist water or spirit of nature—is joined to those two extremes with a very strong bond by means of the air, which holds heat on the side of the body and moisture on the side of the water. <note>The author explains the Aristotelian theory of the elements, where "Air" (hot and moist) acts as a bridge between "Fire" (hot and dry) and "Water" (cold and moist).</note> This is therefore what the **Philosophers** call the "new God of nature"; for this is what they say is composed of many things, and yet it is one single thing. From these aforementioned things, it clearly appears that it is a perfect trinity. And this is our stone: made red in its potential, transparent with the clarity of air, easily melted by the benefit of the water, and most heavy in the fire due to the weight of its earthiness.

By grinding <note>original: "contritione"</note> them as finely as possible, until they become a single fine powder. And see to it well that the receiver is well-fitted and joined to the nose of the alembic. # Master Ortelanus <note>Ortelanus was a famous, though somewhat mysterious, 14th-century alchemist known for his influential commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus.</note>

...[gold] <note>original: "rum," likely the end of "aurum" (gold) from the previous page</note> allows itself to be dissolved at the first opportunity with these waters. But (he further says) after the gold has been placed in this water and has stood for two hours among hot ashes <note>The "hot ashes" of a furnace provided a steady, indirect heat for alchemical vessels.</note>, it is then converted into a red or rose-colored powder and is perfectly calcined <term>calcined; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "ash," often to remove impurities</term>. Then that water must be carefully poured off and saved, and other water of the same power and strength must be poured over the said red powder; and let there always be three times as much water by weight as there is of gold filings. Let it stand again among the hot ashes for two hours, and it will be dissolved in part or in whole. If this does not happen, pour that water off and let new water be added again, and the whole will be dissolved by the grace of God, if you follow the order as has been previously stated.

And note that gold would be dissolved much more easily with the help of a small quantity of sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac; ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to make solvents like aqua regia more aggressive</term>. But the Author of this book strictly forbids sal ammoniac from being used in this work, because he says that sal ammoniac infects and consumes all bodies. For it destroys their radical moisture <term>radical moisture; in alchemical theory, the innate, essential fluid within a substance that maintains its internal cohesion and "life"</term> and corrupts it. Therefore, he forbids its use in this work.

Once the preparation of the blackness is complete and the treatment of the earth is finished, as has been said, one must proceed to the preparation of the whiteness of the stone's earth. # TWO LETTERS
## OF THE MOST ACUTE PHILOSOPHER GRATIAN
### CONCERNING THE STONE
->of the Philosophers.<-

### First Letter.

That which was once our intention is now entirely no longer so, and that which never was, is what is yet to be <note>A paradoxical alchemical statement describing the transformation of matter, where the initial "intention" or form of the substance must perish for the final "Stone" to emerge</note>. These two states are distinguished from that which already exists, moving toward that being which it is through both artificial and natural direction—within the earth and upon the earth, and in both a natural and an artificial vessel. Furthermore, **artificial heat** mimics **natural heat** in three degrees: the first is in the **dissolving moisture**, the second in the **aggregating moisture**, and the third in the **incorporating moisture**. 

Therefore, in every **roasting** <term>original: *assatione*; a process of heating matter until dry</term> or **decoction** <term>slow boiling to extract essence</term> by which spirits and bodies are separated and joined together, you must know that the **soul** <note>The volatile principle or vital essence of the metal</note>, though separable from its subject, is not easily separated from the **fixed** <note>The stable, solid part of the matter that resists fire</note> except in the driest conditions; nor is the **living** <note>Likely referring to "Living Mercury," the active spirit</note> easily joined to the **dead** <note>The inert physical body or dregs of the substance</note> except in the moist. 

But in all these things, nature does not allow for sudden changes. **Glass**, **vitriol** <term>Metallic sulfates, usually of iron or copper</term>, **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for Copper</note>, the **Green Lion** <term>A famous alchemical symbol, often representing acidic mineral salts or the raw, "hungry" solvent used to dissolve gold</term>, **poison**, and **mercury** are all from one thing. **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> must be led step-by-step toward **fixation** <term>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>: first, let it and its **windiness** <note>original: *ventositas*; refers to the volatile gases that escape during heating</note> be **calcined** <term>Reduced to a powder through high heat</term> in the first degree of heat. Secondly, let its **rawness** <note>original: *cruditas*</note> [be calcined] in the second degree. Thirdly, its **substantial moisture** in the third degree of heat. And let each calcined thing be dissolved

# GRATIAN THE PHILOSOPHER

...in its own way, so that it may putrefy; and thus at last they come together into one harmony with the living **ferment** <note>A substance, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical mix to "leaven" or trigger the transformation of the base metal</note>. And let them be led again through three degrees of heat, and thus the mercury acts upon itself. When this is completed, let natural alchemy follow—not the "subterranean" kind <note>Mining or raw geological processes</note>, but *animal* alchemy <note>original: "animalis"; here referring to the "anima" or soul-force, implying a more refined, vitalistic process than mere chemistry</note>. 

But regarding the things mentioned above, it must be noted that mercury is not to be placed in any degree of heat unless it is first taken with the extracted mercury—that is, the mercury which is sublimated and **fixed** <term>made resistant to evaporation by fire</term> in the ferment of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note> together in one body. 

In the first degree of heat, metallic vessels are useful; in the second, glass; and in the third, earthenware <note>ceramic or clay vessels capable of withstanding the highest temperatures</note>. Yet, let the shape of all of them be spherical—that is, round. 

Therefore, "passive" mercury receives various names according to the variety of its experiences. Thus, the primary "first" comes from the ferment; the secondary "second" from the same ferment, and so on, until a certain quantity is gradually fixed in the ferment to prepare the **Elixir**. For what nature has joined, art separates; and what art joins, nature separates. Moreover, what art separates, nature alone joins; and what is naturally distant, art joins by imitating nature, though not suddenly. 

And this is the **secret of secrets** of this art: for in all operations, one must take care that the heat is not extinguished, but that the alteration happens gradually so that it is completed in the third "regime" <note>A specific period or stage of the heating process</note>. For unless our **Stone** were cold and airy, it would not be joined to the mercury. 

Furthermore, the "unburnable moisture" <note>A theoretical substance in alchemy that remains liquid but does not evaporate or burn away in the fire</note>, once extinguished, preserves the natural heat, but it is preserved by some protective species until the fire and water are truly joined into one, which happens after a double reduction. Mercury, in every state, becomes **Xir** when fixed in the **lion** <note>The "Lion" often symbolizes the fixed, acidic, or solar principle—usually sulfur or gold</note>; in the ferment, it gradually becomes **exir**, and when "waxed" <note>original: "inceratus"; a process of softening a hard substance to the consistency of wax</note> it becomes **Elixir**. 

Thus the beginning bears witness to its own end, which is: **calcine, dissolve, distill, coagulate** <note>These are the four fundamental stages of the "Great Work": burning to ash, melting/dissolving, purifying through vapor, and finally solidifying into the Stone</note>.
