### SECOND LETTER ON THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

...mercury, and wax it <note>original: "incera"; the process of "inceration" involves adding a liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency</note> with its end; thus the principle of the process is the same regarding the adaptation of mercury. For Mercury becomes *crinonius* <note>original: "crinonius"; likely a technical term derived from the Greek "krinein" meaning to separate or distinguish, referring here to mercury in a state of purification</note> in its adaptation: for first it becomes **Xir**, second **Exir**, and third **Elixir**. 

**Xir** is mercury that is fusible among the metallic medicines prepared in the alchemical manner, and it tinges with a non-fixed tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is the color-changing power of a substance; "non-fixed" means it is volatile and will not survive the heat of a furnace</note>, nor does it endure, nor does it transform. 

**Exir** is mercury prepared and separated, tinging with a fixed tincture according to its own quantity, but it does not transform the metal fully. 

**Elixir** is mercury "waxed," tinging and transforming inseparably to the ultimate degree. 

Likewise, any medicine that binds alchemically prepared mercury upon itself is called **Xir**. Therefore, first extract the oil from the earth, and dissolve in it the binding and coagulating medicine, and again sublimate and **calcine** <term>to reduce a solid to a fine powder through prolonged heating</term>, and it remains, once the calcination is completed; then dissolve, distill, coagulate, and wax it with its own oil, and cast it upon the fermented mercury in the state of Xir, and it will be Exir, fit for making the Elixir. 

Therefore, this saying of his is resumed twice through the names of **nine species** prepared in such a way—either together or individually—with the tenth, namely mercury, in its tenderness; when this state is reached, it will be Xir, from which one extracts Exir, from which the Elixir is made. 

**Ir** <note>A symbolic or coded term used in this specific manuscript to represent the initial state or the "agents" of the work</note> does not produce Xir except by the benefit of long-lasting heat, prevailing equally and continuously for thirty or forty days: because then the mercury diffuses itself into the medicines, just as a mineral diffuses itself into the most diverse stones; and afterward it is separated from them. 

**Ir** is interpreted as "fettered hands": for we cannot work on mercury with our own physical hands, but rather with the nine species, which we call our "hands" in this work. 

**Xir** is interpreted as "fettered" or "captured by the hands." 

**Exir** as "emancipated" or "released from the hands." 

**Elixir** or *elexir* as "emancipating all things." 

Let it be adapted...

### THE PHILOSOPHY OF GRATIAN

...[is turned], therefore, the left hand moves from the species brought forth toward the body, and the right hand from the bodies brought forth toward spirituality. Let mercury be treated toward maturity in these things—salt and saltiness—just as the fingers are said to be full of the most choice myrrh upon the thumbs <note>This is a mystical allusion to the Song of Solomon 5:5, used here to describe a state of ritual purity or the "sweating" of a substance during the heating process.</note>. 

But let it not deceive you when it is said: "let the spirit become body," as if you should understand it to be **fixed** <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable in heat and does not evaporate, unlike "volatile" spirits.</note> at the first glance; and what is written, "let the body become spirit," must be understood in a similar way. Therefore, once the softness of the mercury has been wiped away, let it become accustomed to the fire with **alkibrit** <term>an Arabic alchemical term for sulfur</term>, from which it separates its most red substance, by the benefit of boiling olive oil or the fat of animals taken from the most rich pastures. 

Regarding the fact that the body becomes spirit and the spirit body, understand this to mean that the spirit and body become one; and when the body has been dissolved into saltiness, it **tinges** <note>original: "tingit"; the act of a substance communicating its color and medicinal properties to a base metal</note> and is spiritual. Note that if all things are prepared together, it is considered good among experts. However, there is greater experience for those seeking when each thing is prepared individually and examined one within the other. 

In the water of the **rebis** <term>from the Latin "res bina," meaning the "double-thing"; a symbol of the union of opposites, often depicted as a hermaphrodite</term> you shall dissolve the **rebis**: for the spirits represent themselves one way in the body, alum in another; saltiness <note>original: "sedina," likely referring to the sediment or residue left after evaporation</note> in another, and each of the others in another way. The water of the **rebis** has a further, wider effect after the coagulated mass is purified from that which first received it when it was added. 

The dissolver and the dissolved cannot occupy the same place in a single water proportioned to one; instead, both embrace each other and fall to the bottom, and the original water floats on top, yet it becomes more solvent. In every dissolution, there occurs an incorporation of the dissolved and the dissolver, because there the body can become spirit, and the spirit body. Just as from the simple or most basic letters of the alphabet—namely from vowels and consonants—syllables are made, and from syllables words, and from words sentences; so from the primary sources of all minerals does the process occur...

### Letter II. Concerning the Philosopher's Stone

...[suc]cess in the work. These things are brought back to the first, simplest, and purest essence of this work through the corruption of the corruptible form and the division of parts that are not well-joined; then, they are gradually brought back to composition until the generation of forms and the final cause. The stages of composition are modeled after the stages of division and corruption.

And note that there are also primary sources which are named differently by various elements, such as those born in the earth, in living things, and in minerals. If one thing among all these can be aggregated from the **Athamus** <gloss>that is, the material fruit</gloss> <note>The word "Athamo" here likely refers to the "Athamor" or furnace, but the gloss "pomo materiali" (material apple or fruit) suggests a reference to the spherical mass of the starting matter</note>—meaning it can be transmuted into some species—the aggregator for that same species is present. For that reason, an aggregate <gloss>that is, the result of another species</gloss> has no place there; it is necessary that some third thing be present, namely the **form**, which is the life-giver <gloss>the efficient, containing, and naturalizing force</gloss>.

Also note that the primary sources are the cause of all things that can be generated or corrupted, which are made from various elements. Whoever says that **fetid earth** <note>original: "terra fœtida"; the dark, foul-smelling residue or "lead" that remains after the initial stage of decomposition or "putrefaction"</note> is sulfur, let him understand it as the spirit itself. The **Green Lion** <gloss>that is, raw mercury</gloss> acts upon the **amalgam** <gloss>that is, the amalgam itself is the recipient of the action</gloss>. 

**Fetid earth** stands as the foundation; weigh whatever is mixed with it first, and afterward let the mercury be taken and placed in safe-keeping between the burning and the burnt. # Gratian the Philosopher

It is itself emptied out. And all dryness desires water, yet it desires most that which is of its own nature. This is not the work of the moisture itself, but of the **saltness** <note>original: "salsedinis"; salt was considered the third principle of alchemy, representing stability and the means of joining soul and body</note>, while the moisture remains; in this moisture, the body is joined with the mercury by reason of its **metallic humidity**. This humidity is more friendly to the metallic body, because the soul does not enter except into its own body <note>A fundamental alchemical maxim: a substance can only be transformed by something of its own kind.</note>. 

And because two bodies cannot occupy the same place, they descend to the bottom, and the original water floats on top and is called **secondary water**. In this water, the simple dissolved mercury does not sink. This is a good secret, provided you understand the cause. 

There are four elements and a triple classification of things made from elements:
1.  **Mineral**, which exists in the earth only.
2.  **Vegetable** (or earth-born), which is partly in the earth according to its root and partly above the earth, such as herbs and shrubs.
3.  **Animal**, which moves entirely upon the earth.

In all of these, fire is not hidden, except when they are crushed. Nature is hidden in division <note>referencing the "Seventh Book," likely a specific volume in the alchemical corpus being studied</note>. In all of these, fire is not hidden. Nature in minerals and in other things vanishes. 

The **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy itself.</note> therefore wishes to drive the vessel—the enclosure of the spirit—toward the containment of that spirit; for if the spirit exhales, the entire body is corrupted. Furthermore, the **external fire** excites the **internal fire** <note>The internal fire is the innate energy or "sulfur" within the matter, while the external fire is the heat of the furnace.</note>. The external fire must be equal in its stages until the internal fire completes its work. 

The internal fire requires nourishment, or rather a fuel, by which it may be more vehemently excited within while the heat outside remains weak. This is so that even what is dispersed may be gathered and joined together, and even that which is varied (due to the variety of combustible things formed uniformly under the pole) may be united. To achieve these three benefits, that **liquor** is taken or required which has been cleansed of all earthiness. ### Third Letter concerning the Philosophers' Stone

...is also necessary according to its own nature. Just as the Sun pours into the earth a simple and excellent fire, which the earth pours back into things growing from the earth according to their own nature: for all elements are in the firmament, and from a small spark a very great fire is born. And what you sow in the earth, you shall reap from it, such as a vegetable above the earth, with its root in the earth, and its thickness <note>original: "grossibile"; referring to the physical mass or body of the plant</note> entirely above the earth. 

But the mineral in the earth, according to the nature of its own seed, incorporates into itself the **living water** <term>aqua viva: in alchemy, this is not common water but a potent solvent or the "mercurial" essence of a substance</term>, whose airy nature must be preserved within it, so that air is in water, water in fire, fire in the seed, seed in air, and the whole in the earth. Thus a fourth part will be the **ferment** <term>fermentum: a substance, often compared to yeast, that transforms and "leavens" the base matter into gold or the Stone</term> in its content, a fourth part air in its own, and a fourth part earth in its own. 

Therefore, unless our stone is airy, mercury will not be joined to it. Now I speak of a Mercury which, like water, is not perceived by sight; yet it is sensed by smell, nor does it leave a trace when touched, and it coagulates dissolved mercury into its own likeness. And they say it can do anything, yet it is one single thing, and every corporeal thing is reduced back into it. 

Yet one substance is more effective than others in this act, about which some believe it to be **arsenic** <note>original: "arsenicum"</note>, while others say **myrrh** <unclear>myrrham</unclear>, others glass, others **vitriol** <term>vitriol: metal sulfates, often used to create strong acids for dissolving metals</term>, others **Venus** <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>, others the saltiness of salts, and thus they differ.

And join this dry substance with the ferment, and calcine and dissolve the whole. 

And again coagulate the dissolved mercury with it, and this is what is called "the combustible," and **alkibrit** <term>alkibrit: an Arabic term for sulfur, considered the active, "burning" principle in alchemy</term> is burning. ### Gratian the Philosopher
<meta>catchword: Earth</meta>

*The spirit must be treated within a bodily medicine, so that it might learn from and become accustomed to the body: otherwise, it passes away invisibly or escapes uncontrollably through unsealed pores or cracks in the vessels. The bodies of minerals send nothing above the earth during their production; they are produced within the earth and share a single material principle, but they vary in form and time because of the variety of their specific earths. Furthermore, because of the variation of the air or the fire, they are "cooked"* <note>original: "decoquuntur"; referring to the natural maturation of minerals by the earth's internal heat</note> *in quantity, quality, and dryness. Note that everything born of the earth arises from the earth according to the species that is in the earth, and according to a natural aptitude for being born from the earth, provided the seed remains.*

In a similar way, every metal exists within the "new mercury" <term>mercurius novus: a purified or philosophical form of mercury that acts as the "womb" for the metals</term>; therefore, what you sow in it, you shall also reap from it. For it contains within itself an incorruptible and "fixed" <note>original: "fixum"; referring to a substance that is stable and does not evaporate when heated</note> seed, and it also contains a moisture—that is, a superfluity—which serves as the medium through which the fixed part passes. When we "ferment" this matter, therefore, what more do we seek but the cooking of the sulfurous fire? Therefore, whiten the <term>laton</term> <note>original: "latonem"; an alchemical term for a base metallic body or alloy, often copper or brass, that is in an intermediate state of purification</note>—that is, the copper—with mercury, because *laton* is a yellow-orange body composed of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Once you have whitened it and brought it back to its original yellow color through long cooking, you possess the *laton* once again. In this state, it is malleable and available in whatever quantity you desire; and thus you have the "principle of the art." 

Then, you must calcine, dissolve, distill, coagulate, and "wax" <note>original: "incera"; a process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency so it may be fused or projected</note> the material. Proceed in this manner through the middle stages, and if you make that which has been "resurrected" <note>referring to the matter after it has been reduced to its components and recombined</note> capable of penetrating <note>the ability of the Stone to permeate and transform base metals</note>, then you have reached the end of the work. Fire in the air becomes light; thus, when moisture fails, brilliance also fails. From copper comes "lime" <note>original: "calx"; a powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures</note>; air within the "egg" <note>the *ovum philosophicum*, or the sealed glass vessel used in the Great Work</note> becomes spirit. Hence, if the thin film is cracked, the spirit evaporates. Water in the earth becomes glass; thus, gathered juices always become harder, yet they possess no "fixity" <note>the quality of being permanent and resistant to fire</note> in themselves. Earth in the fire becomes Salt, and from these elemental transformations, various things are subsequently produced.

Second Letter on the Philosophers' Stone
I
<meta>catchword: nature</meta>

Earth is resolved into water, water into air, air into fire, and this is the path by which the body becomes spirit. Fire, through attrition <note>original: "contritionem"; refers to the grinding or wearing down of elements against one another</note>, becomes air; and this is the path by which the spirit becomes the body. The invisible atom, therefore, is our "airy stone," and it coagulates the "virgin's milk" <term>lac virginis: a symbolic name for the mercurial water or the white stage of the work</term>. Let separation be performed in water, on account of salts and alums; in oil, on account of combustible things; in the "belly of the horse" <note>original: "ventre equi"; a technical term for the gentle, moist heat generated by a heap of fermenting horse manure</note> for the sake of coloration; and this separation leads to resuscitation. And even if you find what you need in dung, do not hesitate to take it. For this reason, they have compared the work to an egg, because the shell surrounds everything within it: it contains in itself everything that the operator requires for its preparation. And this is the dragon that devours its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, a classic symbol of the cyclic nature of the alchemical process and the unity of matter.</note>. The dragon is the "divine water," and the tail is its sulfur and the ash that remains within the ash. And from this ash descends a living rain, giving life to the earth; and this ash is the ferment. The water, which Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist known for teaching the secrets of the Stone to the King of Egypt.</note> called ash, is the "coagulum," since it is the substance that coagulates water into earth, etc.

# ->The Philosopher Gratianus<-

...their nature conquers all other natures. Therefore, anyone who tries to fix <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it no longer evaporates.</term> quicksilver without these specially prepared bodies is blind in his practice; for gold and silver bestow their own qualities upon gold and silver, but they provide the color to the mercury. From these bodies, white or red living sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur viuum"</note> <term>Living Sulfur: In alchemy, this represents the active, "combustible" principle of a metal—its internal fire or soul—as opposed to common sulfur.</term> is extracted through sublimation; this is because the purest substance of sulfur is found within them, having been thoroughly purified by the work.

For this reason, Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina, c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and philosophy were central to medieval European alchemy.</note> says: "Unless I saw gold and silver living, I would say the alchemical art did not exist." <note>original: "nisi aurum & argentum viuerem, dicerem, quod ars non esset alchymica"</note>

Thus, the first of all operations and regimens <term>Regimen: A specific stage or period in the alchemical process, often associated with a particular temperature or "governance" of the fire.</term> is the dissolution of the body into its own essence—namely, into mercury—and this is done through mercury itself, because it possesses the power to reduce bodies back to their original nature and matter. The purpose of this dissolution is none other than to extract the purest substance of sulfur and mercury from the bodies and spirits of which the elixir consists. Therefore, first sublimate the mercury; next, join it with a most pure body; finally, grind and cook them until they return to their "prime matter." <term>Prime Matter: The fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made; in alchemy, reducing a metal to this state is necessary for its rebirth and transformation.</term> The sign of this dissolution is a form that is black in color and feels subtle and crumbly to the touch; both of these are signs of perfect cooking <note>original: "decoctionis"</note> and dissolution. Take great care also that you do not mix impure mercurial water with a pure body: for the clarity of the mercurial water determines the purity of the body it washes. The more the body is washed, the whiter it will become; for the preparation of its perfect coloration is achieved through water and fire. Because of this, if the body is not fully white, grind it with the water and then calcine <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in order to reduce it to a powder or "ash," removing volatile impurities.</term> it again. In this way, *Azoth* <term>Azoth: Often called the "universal medicine" or "universal solvent," it is the essential mercurial spirit used to cleanse and transform the metals.</term> <note>original: "azot, id est, aqua mercurialis"</note>—that is, the mercurial water—and the fire will wash away and cleanse the hidden impurities. Do not let yourself grow weary of the long repetitions of grinding, cooking, and roasting.

Do not grow weary of repeating this many times, because the body does not ascend unless it has been incorporated with mercury. It can by no means be incorporated unless it is first dissolved in mercury. We perform these concoctions <term>Concoction: The application of heat to a substance to "ripen" or refine it, much like cooking.</term> for this reason: so that we might refine <note>original: "subtiliemus"</note> and lighten the hardness and tenacity of the bodies. 

Therefore, take the "first water" <note>This likely refers to the mercurial solvent or the "universal solvent" of the alchemists.</note> set apart from all corruption, in which you must cook the "thing named by its own name" <note>A common alchemical trope referring to the "Secret Matter," which the authors often refused to name directly.</note> for forty days in its own vessel, and you will find the body converted into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>. And when, through sublimation, it has been deprived of its blackness <note>The "nigredo" or blackening stage, representing the death of the old form.</note>, it will become a "sublime nature," lacking shadows—that is, free from the gross dregs of the earth and from scorching. 

Therefore, refine the body as much as you can and cook it with clean mercury. When the body has drawn into itself and enclosed a small part of the mercury, refine it quickly with a fire as strong as you can manage, until it ascends in the likeness of a very white powder, like snow, adhering to the joints of the aludel <term>Aludel: A series of pear-shaped pots used as receivers in the sublimation process.</term>. The ash remaining at the bottom, however, is the dregs and slag of the "vituperating" <note>In this context, metals or minerals that are impure or "defile" the work.</note> and rejected bodies, in which nothing of life is held. Then, having cast away the dregs, repeat the sublimation of the very white powder by itself without its dregs; and then you will have the tinging soul <term>Tinging Soul: The transformative essence that can "tinge" or change the color and nature of other metals.</term>, which both coagulates and purifies, and the sulfur and arsenic that do not [burn]...

We perform this sublimation for this reason: to reduce the bodies into a subtle nature, so that they may be like spirits—penetrating and transforming every body into living Sun-making <term>Solificium: The alchemical process of "making gold," as the Sun is the celestial symbol for gold.</term> and Moon-making <term>Lunificium: The alchemical process of "making silver," as the Moon is the celestial symbol for silver.</term> substances. If, however, any useful matter still remains at the bottom, you shall repeat the sublimation by incorporating more mercury into it, until the whole has ascended.

# Gratianus the Philosopher

## Notable Observations on the Weights of the Ferment, Sulfur, and Mercury.

It should be understood that in every fermentation, you must take note of the weight of the substances to be mixed into the elixir. The first of these notable rules is that the total amount of the volatile <term>Volatile: In alchemy, a substance that easily evaporates or escapes when heated, often associated with the "spirit."</term> must not exceed the weight of its cleansed, fixed body. Otherwise, the "bond of the marriage" <note>original: "ligamentum sponsalicii"; a metaphorical term for the chemical union between the volatile spirit and the solid body.</note> would be turned into the flight of the unfixed spirit and the volatile sulfur. As Plato says: if too little sulfur is projected <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process, where the finished Elixir is "thrown" onto a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</term> upon a great quantity of bodies, it will have such power over them that it converts the material into a powder, the color of which will be like the color of the body upon which the spirit of gold or silver is projected. 

But because the sulfurs cannot enter the bodies except by the mediation of "water"—that is, by mercury—this water creates their "marriage," because it is the medium for joining the tinctures <note>Tinctures: The transformative essences that give the metal its new color and properties.</note>, namely the sulfur and the ferment. Therefore, in that arrangement, you should first place the lime <term>Lime (Calx): The powdery residue left after a metal has been "calcined" or burned to ash.</term> of the body or ferment into the Earth; second, you place the Water, which is the spirit; third, you place the Air, which is the soul or the sulfur extracted from the bodies. Here, I am using philosophical eloquence and doctrine. 

If you first mix oil into the earth, the oil will be mortified <term>Mortification: The process of "killing" a substance's outward form to release its inner essence; here, it refers to the oil being absorbed and rendered inactive.</term> in the earth, because the oil would enter the earth and be swallowed by it. If, however, you first place the water and afterwards the oil, the oil will stand upon the water. Or, if you first place the water and afterwards the earth, the water will be heavier than the earth <note>This sequence describes the specific density and layering required to keep the active "sulfur" (the oil) from being lost or "drowned" before it can act.</note>. 

Therefore, fix the substance according to the precept of the Philosophers in this manner: prepare the ferment (that is, the body before fermentation) so that it is dissolved and calcined; for if you have not prepared the ferment, it will be worth nothing. Likewise, prepare the non-burning sulfur from the lime through sublimation <term>Sublimation: Heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the sulfur and make it "living" or active.</term>, so that it may be simple and "living." For if you do not mix this into the elixir, the body upon which the projection of sulfur is made will not be colored. And if you have not cleansed <note>The Latin text ends here mid-sentence; the catchword "ueris" completes the word "mundaueris," meaning "you have cleansed."</note>

It emphasizes that the body must be properly calcined and the sulfur sublimated to ensure the final transformation (projection) is successful.</summary>

...[if you do not cleanse] the body, even if it is mixed into the elixir, the body will not direct the spirit, nor will it retain it. And if you have not sublimated <term>Sublimated: A process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify and "exalt" the material.</term> this kind of sulfur which you wish to put into the elixir, the resulting gold or silver will be very dark. And if you do not cleanse the spirit, it will not withstand the fire: because in its impure state, it will not be joined to the body at the most fundamental level <note>original: "per minima"; literally "through the smallest parts," referring to a perfect, microscopic blending where the substances become one.</note>.

You must also be very cautious to make the elixir a medium between hard and soft: because unless you know this, the tinted gold or silver will not be fit for working—that is, for hammering or casting. For the medicine <note>Medicine: A common alchemical synonym for the Elixir or the Philosopher's Stone in its transformative state.</note> must be of a finer and more liquid substance than the bodies themselves, and possess a greater degree of fixation and retention than quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury.</note> has in its own natural state. 

When you wish to make the composition of the elixir, create a lime <term>Lime (Calx): The powdery residue left after a metal has been "calcined" or burnt to ash; the metal's "body" reduced to its simplest form.</term> from the primary material <term>Primary Material: The "prima materia," the primitive, formless base of all matter which the alchemist seeks to isolate.</term> of which the body consists, and add its own sulfur to it; as I said above, if it is gold, use gold; if silver, use silver. For the "marriage bond" <note>original: "sponsalicium"; a metaphorical term for the chemical union of volatile and fixed principles.</note> is nothing other than joining the ferment with its own body, from which you wish to make the elixir. 

Therefore, when you join the elements—namely, air and water—so that they are fixed in earth; if it is for the white elixir <note>White Elixir: The stage of the Great Work capable of transmuting base metals into silver, as opposed to the "Red Elixir" for gold.</note>, there should always be more earth than any of the other elements. Otherwise, the earth would not fix the spirit; instead, the spirit would fly away with it. And this must be done according to a ratio following the measure of "de-watering" <term>De-watering (Deaquatio): An alchemical term for balancing the moisture of a substance or reducing it to a dry, fixed state.</term>. For example: if there is one and a half weight of air, there should be two weights of water, and three weights of earth. And let the ferment of the earth be as much as the white sulfur; so that if half a part of the other weight was white sulfur, there should be three parts of ferment and two of water, and the elixir will be complete. Therefore, keep this precaution in the composition of the true elixir, and work as has been said, so that you know how much you should add of earth, how much of water, and how much of air for the white elixir,

# Second Letter on the Philosopher’s Stone
->Page 141<-

The **remote primary matter** <term>Materia prima remota: The most basic, underlying substance of all metals, before it takes on a specific form.</term> of metals is an **aqueous humidity**, by which, while they melt, they flow like water. By reason of this single aqueous humidity, these same metals—through the use of **strong waters** <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; these are mineral acids, like nitric acid, used to dissolve metals in laboratory chemistry.</note>—are strongly coagulated into salts, alums, and other mineral intermediates by either natural or artificial heat. They are distilled from these substances and artificially dissolved into a clear and fluid water. 

Since metals, after the action of heat, are naturally coagulated by cold, it is necessary for them to be dissolved back into water by "strong waters" (which have been coagulated and distilled by heat) acting as their opposite; in this process, the **radical moisture** <term>Radical moisture: The fundamental, "living" humidity within a substance that preserves its essence and prevents it from becoming a dry powder.</term> of the metal itself truly remains incorrupt.

This form of solution, however, is improper and **unnatural** for the physical work <note>The "physical work" or "physica opus" refers to the Alchemical Great Work (Magnum Opus).</note>. This is because it relies on the mediation of heterogeneous things <note>Materials that are different in nature or species from the metal itself.</note> and different species; the humidities that dissolve the metals in this way cannot be re-congealed back into a metal alongside them after the action of heat. Instead, they are separated from the metals by fire itself—which separates the heterogeneous and gathers the **homogeneous** <note>Things of the same kind or nature.</note>—leaving the metals behind in their own nature. 

For no "water" truly belongs to these solutions, nor does it resolve the metallic species through reduction, unless it remains with the metals in their congelations <note>The process of turning from a liquid or gas back into a solid.</note> in both matter and form, and unless the dissolved metals can themselves congeal that water back into metal. 

But since these things do not occur when using "strong waters" <note>i.e., acids</note>, the **physical solution** of metals will not happen in that way. Rather, it occurs through the disturbance of the compound—namely, the **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Mercury (argentum vivum). In this context, it refers to the "spirit" or "mercury of the philosophers" required to dissolve the metallic body.</term> of the body that is to be dissolved. Such aqueous humidity of "strong waters" is called here by Lord **Gratian** <note>Gratian is a cited authority in alchemical literature, often associated with the "Turba Philosophorum".</note> "the ancient floating water," salty, manifold, and a multifaceted example of physical solution. 

The **proximate primary matter** <term>Materia prima propinqua: The stage of matter just before it becomes a specific metal, closer to the final form than the "remote" matter.</term> of metals, however, is a **subtle unctuous moisture** <term>Unctuous moisture: A greasy or oily substance, representing the "Sulfur" or soul of the metal that allows it to bind and take form.</term>, which is naturally incorporated with a subtle earth, mixed so strongly that the majority of both is not only

## Second Letter on the Philosopher’s Stone
(Catchword: from more-)

The **remote primary matter** <term>Materia prima remota: The most basic, underlying substance of all things in their most distant, unrefined state, before they take on the specific form of a metal.</term> of metals is a **watery humidity**, through which, while they melt, they flow like water. By reason of this one watery humidity, the metals themselves are powerfully coagulated into **Salts, alums, and other mineral intermediates** by either natural or artificial heat through the use of **strong waters** <term>Aqua fortis: Literally "strong water," referring to corrosive mineral acids (like nitric acid) used by early chemists to dissolve metals.</term>; and they are distilled by these same waters, and artificially dissolved into a clear and flowing liquid. For since metals, after the action of heat, are naturally coagulated by cold, it is necessary that they be dissolved back into water by strong waters (which have been coagulated and distilled by heat) as if by their opposite—while the **radical moisture** <term>Radical moisture: The essential, life-sustaining fluid inherent in a substance that preserves its identity and "soul."</term> of the metal itself remains truly uncorrupted.

However, this type of solution is improper and unnatural for the **physical work** <note>original: "physica opus"; here referring to the Alchemical Great Work or the natural process of transformation, as opposed to "vulgar" or purely chemical experimentation.</note>. This is because it is achieved through **heterogeneous** <note>original: "heterogeneis"; substances that are different in kind or nature and cannot truly "bond" or grow together.</note> materials and different species; their dissolving humidities cannot be congealed back into a metal together with the metals themselves after the action of heat. Instead, by the very power of the fire (which separates different things and gathers together like things), they are separated from the metals, leaving the metals behind in their own nature. For no "water" belongs to these solutions, nor does it resolve the metallic species through reduction, unless it is a water that remains with them in their congealing in both matter and form, and which the dissolved metals themselves can congeal back into a metal.

But since these things do not happen in strong waters, the **physical solution** of metals will not occur in that manner; rather, that way is a disruption of the compound—specifically, of the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti viui"; Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or base of all metals.</note> of the body being dissolved. And such a watery humidity of strong waters is called here by **Lord Gratianus** <note>Gratianus is an authority cited in several alchemical compendiums, such as the *Turba Philosophorum*, known for his theories on the "pristine water."</note> the **pristine water floating on the surface**, salty, multifaceted, and a many-sided example of physical solution.

The **proximate primary matter** <term>Materia prima propinqua: The "near" matter; the stage of a substance just before it becomes a specific metal, often described as a perfect balance of sulfur and mercury.</term> of metals is a subtle **unctuous moisture** <note>An oily or "fatty" substance that alchemists believed allowed metals to be malleable and to bond.</note>, which is naturally incorporated into a subtle earth that is most strongly mixed with it, so much so that the majority of both is not merely...

<vocab>Remote primary matter, metals, watery humidity, strong waters, Salts, alums, congealed, distilled, Physical solution, heterogeneous, homogeneous, Quicksilver, Gratianus, pristine water, unctuous</vocab>

It emphasizes that a true "physical solution" requires a moisture that can re-congeal with the metal as part of its essential form.</summary>

# Gratian the Philosopher

...from the abundance of both, but also within the abundance of both. This **oily moisture**, however, is **mercurial water** or **quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum: Literally "living silver," the common Latin name for mercury.</term>; and it is called by the master Gratian **secondary water**, a friend to the metallic body, and even the **soul of the body** <note>original: "anima corporis"; in alchemy, the "soul" refers to the volatile or oily principle that gives a substance its specific qualities and life-like properties.</note>, being alone of the same nature as the metals themselves. 

This water is necessary for the **physical solution** <note>original: "solutione physica"; a "natural" dissolution where the metal is reduced to its essential liquid state without being destroyed by harsh acids.</note> of that same body. Only through subtle and hidden methods—connected physically by both nature and art, yet known to few—can coldness itself re-congeal this water into a metal, along with the dissolved metals, after the action of heat upon it. An experimenter who understands the outward natures of things and their proportions must, with wise calculation, proportion this water to the bodies themselves at the beginning of the work.

But because a transition from one extreme to another does not happen naturally except through a middle point—for **wise nature does not make a leap** <note>original: "natura sagax non facit saltum"; a fundamental principle of medieval science stating that natural change occurs through gradual, intermediate stages rather than sudden jumps.</note>, but proceeds in all things gradually and successively—she moves forward without error, using as much intelligence as is needed through divine foresight, especially in the kinship of the perfected metals. 

In these metals, nature, moved by their primary matter—namely the **moisture of the water**—begins through the actions of heat and miraculous modes of mixing (which are entirely unknown to us). Deep within the very bowels of the earth, she forms from that same source a **pure, incorruptible seed** possessing a great blessing: namely, a moisture strongly incorporated into an **oily, mercurial substance** mixed with a subtle earthiness. This is called the **proximate primary matter** <term>Materia prima propinqua: The "near" or immediate raw material that is just one step away from becoming a finished metal.</term> and the true "middle" between extremes—truly mediating between the water and the metallic silver. 

After further actions of heat and its own particular processes, nature itself thickens this substance into metals. And because **art is the imitator of nature** in all things where it is able, it follows that since nature does not make a leap from one extreme to another in the generation of metals...

<summary>Gratian describes "mercurial water" as the soul of metals and explains the principle that nature must move through intermediate stages (the "proximate matter" or seed) rather than jumping directly from water to metal.</summary>

### Second Letter on the Philosopher’s Stone

...without the formation of a middle state of things. Why does such great blindness and such deception still dwell in the hearts of craftsmen who wish to imitate nature? For these men set aside the **seed of nature** or the **proximate first matter** <term>Materia prima propinqua: The "near" or "immediate" raw material. In alchemy, this is the substance that has already been partially refined by nature into a "seed" state, making it ready for the alchemist to use.</term> of the metals themselves—which has already been perfectly formed by nature—and instead they wish to work with the extremes. They strive to create the **multiplication of metals** <note>original: "metallorum multiplicationem"; the process of increasing the quantity or the transformative power of the alchemical medicine.</note>, or the increase of their perfection, starting from their very first principles [the raw elements] rather than from their middle state. This is entirely impossible for art to achieve, because art is weaker than nature, being merely the work of human intelligence.

Indeed, it is impossible for art to form the seeds of animals or plants above the earth, or the seeds of metals beneath the earth, from their first principles; this belongs to nature alone, as is self-evident to everyone. Therefore, such foolish craftsmen will never, in all eternity, bring about the multiplication of metals nor the increase of their perfection through such fictional solutions and false recipes.

However, the true craftsman, desiring to truly imitate nature, takes the **proximate first matter** or the seeds of the aforementioned things—namely of minerals, animals, and plants. By the benefit of his art, acting as a servant to nature, he can naturally multiply those same seeds or their species infinitely. He achieves this through proper operations that are fitting to their species and not foreign to them, and in their own proper places and not in foreign ones, just as is visible to the eye and proven by experience even to **simple country folk** <note>original: "rusticis"; literally "rustics" or "peasants." The author suggests that the basic principle of planting a seed in the right soil to get a harvest is a universal truth known even to the uneducated.</note>.

<summary>The author critiques alchemists who try to create metals from scratch, arguing they must instead use the "seed" or "proximate matter" provided by nature. True alchemy is presented as the art of assisting and multiplying nature's existing biological and mineral seeds through proper, natural methods.</summary>

### M. Antonio di Pietra, Philosopher, etc. ###

...living Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium viuum"; in this context, it refers to "Mercury of the Philosophers," a purified essence rather than common quicksilver.</note>, that it possesses within itself a Mercury purer than any natural kind, and also more prepared for philosophical **fixation** <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance (like mercury) stable and resistant to fire so that it no longer evaporates.</term>, and therefore, in this Mercury, all things are accomplished more perfectly and more swiftly than in natural Mercury, according to the sayings of the philosophers, as will be described in the operations hereafter.

Furthermore, it is not unreasonable to assert—as those do who place the **Philosophers' Stone** in the refinement <term>Subtiliation (subtiliatio): The alchemical process of making a substance "subtle" or "thin," often by changing its state from solid to spiritual or vaporous.</term> of the body, whether in waters or otherwise by the body itself, or by perfect bodies—and not in the common sort of sublimation <note>original: "sublimatione vulgi"; the author distinguishes between the common chemical process of vaporizing solids and the deeper alchemical "refinement" of the metal's essence.</note> (that is, to simply raise it upwards), but to refine the body so that it truly "flies" <note>The "flying" of a metal refers to it becoming volatile or spiritualized.</note>. This is done so that it is refined to the point of becoming spiritual, easily melted, penetrating, and coloring [tingeing]. For by such refinement, perfect bodies are changed from nature to nature; they become incorporeal, and then corporeal again, until through roasting <note>original: "affationem"; refers to a controlled, dry heat or digestion process.</note> they can generate their like from themselves—as Gold [the Sun] generates Gold, and Silver [the Moon] generates Silver, and so on unto infinity.

They say this is the perfection of any nature: that it can generate its like. ...bodies, from which it can be drawn out. The reason for this may be that it is somewhat difficult to "resolve" <note>original: "resolvere"; to break a solid metal down into its constituent parts or a liquid state.</note> perfect bodies of the strongest composition in such a way that they might be compared to Mercury in their subtlety and power of penetration.

For before natural Mercury can be prepared to such a degree that it matches the purity and quality of a metal body that has been reduced back into Mercury (as was previously discussed), a long time must pass. And since it requires much digestion and very "hidden" <note>original: "occulta"; referring to the secret or internal chemical changes that are not visible to the eye.</note> work for its perfection, it consequently becomes more accustomed to the fire, and the tincture is generated most perfectly within it. Therefore, he stated that in Mercury, the tincture is both easier to obtain and more perfect.

...many have erred: hence, laboring with common Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio vulgi"; ordinary quicksilver bought in a market, as opposed to the specialized "Mercury of the Philosophers" prepared by the adept.</note>, working for long periods on its preparation—namely, its philosophical fixation <note>original: "fixionem philosophicam"; the process of making a volatile or liquid substance stable and resistant to heat.</note>—they were brought almost to despair. As nature delights in nature, rejoices in it, and is animated by it—as a certain philosopher says: *In things having a common symbol, the transition is easy.* <note>original: "In habentibus symbolum, facilis est transitus"; an Aristotelian principle often cited in alchemy to suggest that substances with shared qualities transform into one another more readily than those with opposite qualities.</note>

And such are those who have toiled, and continue to toil, in the conjunctions of bodies and spirits through amalgams <term>Amalgam: A mixture or alloy of mercury with another metal.</term>, and in waters, etc., or by working bodies with bodies. In this way, they wished to convert a body into a spirit by means of a spirit, and afterwards to fix one body with a spirit together, or one spirit (or several) with one body (or both), when perfected. 

They say that the tincture <term>Tincture: The potent, refined substance capable of transforming base metals or healing the body.</term> cannot be made except by the joining of a marriage—namely, of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"; alchemical code for gold.</note> as the husband, the Moon <note>original: "lunae"; alchemical code for silver.</note> as the wife, and raw Mercury as the means of joining the tincture. Their sayings are supported by many authorities which are perhaps written literally, or even enviously <note>Alchemical authors often claimed to write "enviously" or "jealously," meaning they deliberately obscured the truth to prevent the unworthy from succeeding.</note> or allegorically, such as those concerning distillations, etc. Yet there is but one stone, as all cry out: which has within itself everything that it needs, and which, according to the various signs appearing during its preparation, is also called by various names, as I have previously written to you more diligently in this treatise.

### A Most Useful Treatise ###

In this context, it refers to calcination, or reducing the material to a fine ash or white powder through the action of heat.</note> by means of the aerial fire—as will be said later—that same part, because of the several non-fixed parts remaining, is again subtilized, again fixed, and again sublimated, according to the precise intention of Geber himself. And you should not be troubled by the fact that some have said an external aid would be necessary for this, so that Mercury itself might be thus subtilized, since it is homogeneous and of a very strong composition. This is especially said of the Sun or the Moon <note>In alchemical code, the Sun (Sol) refers to Gold, and the Moon (Luna) refers to Silver.</note>, if Mercury must be extracted from them and so refined into the Mercury of the philosophers, which is very difficult and, consequently, might perhaps lead the worker to the extreme of despair. I say at the outset that although natural mercury, or even the Mercury of the philosophers <note>Alchemists distinguished between "common mercury" (raw quicksilver) and "philosophical mercury," the purified, living essence of the metals.</note>—namely, the Mercury of the perfect bodies—are of a very strong composition, yet through the continuation of the fire, some part is always separated from the other by refinement, in the manner of a vapor. And because this vapor cannot "breathe" <note>original: "respirare." This means the vapor cannot escape because the vessel is hermetically sealed; it must condense and fall back down.</note> in the vessel, it is thickened and descends again. By means of the proper governance of the fire—namely a slow fire, etc., as the intention of the operation requires—it refines another, finer part along with it. This continues until the whole work is thus completed. And this is the primary intention of the philosophers who write the truth in this art, although other ways (some of which I will set down below) are not denied by this, since they nevertheless tend toward the same end as the philosophers in their manner of working, although by other...

### Master Antonius on the Philosopher’s Stone, etc. ###

...other and various ways and skills of working. But concerning the second point, namely the **perfect bodies** <term>perfect bodies: in alchemy, this refers to gold and silver, metals considered "perfect" because they do not rust or perish in fire</term>, etc., as was just touched upon above, I admit that it is exceedingly difficult to digest such bodies by themselves in such a way that they are converted into the nature of Mercury or into a Mercurial state. Perhaps a human life would not last long enough to see such a **subtilization** <term>subtilization: the process of refining a solid substance into a delicate, vaporous, or spiritual state</term> through natural means alone; nevertheless, it is not impossible. This is because anything that can be generated is also capable of being corrupted and altered—indeed, it is so within itself—and consequently through the administration of an artist's fire, specifically the fire of heat and moisture, as in **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: a stage of alchemical decay, often color-coded as black, necessary for the material to be "reborn" in a purified form</term>. No matter how strong their composition may be, they can still be altered, etc., and consequently be well-refined into Mercury.

However, because of the great length of time required, it is not improper to assert that preparations using external things—namely salts and **corrosive substances** <note>original: "rebus acutis," literally "sharp things," referring to acids or reactive minerals that "bite" into the metal</note>, putrefactions and solutions, roastings, **calcinations** <term>calcination: heating a metal until it oxidizes and crumbles into a fine powder</term>, and any others—may well be admitted, so that these same perfect bodies, which are the "bodies of the philosophers," may be refined into Mercury or prepared into the nature of Mercury. Then, such bodies should be cleansed of their impure superfluities. Once prepared to such a degree of Mercurial refinement, it is first called the **Philosopher's Stone**. From then on, using it as a starting principle—just as one would with one Mercury or another—one must proceed entirely according to the sayings of the philosophers, and in only one way. This is the consensus of all the philosophers, as has already been shown many times from their own words. But as to this part...

<summary>Antonius argues that while naturally refining gold and silver into a mercurial state is slow, the process can be accelerated using corrosive salts and heat. This purified result is the true "Philosopher's Stone" and serves as the starting point for further alchemical work.</summary>

->### A Most Useful Treatise.###<-

...the second part, namely concerning the declared method of the **subtilization** <term>subtilization: the alchemical process of refining a solid, "gross" substance into a delicate, spiritualized, or fluid state</term> of **perfect bodies** <term>perfect bodies: gold and silver, so called because they resist corrosion by fire or age</term> into the nature of Mercury—and not into quicksilver <note>original: "vivum Mercurium," literally "living mercury," referring to the common liquid metal</note>. This is because, with such a resolution of the body into quicksilver, there is one way of working just as with common mercury (though prepared, as it were, in the manner of the philosophers, as was said before, etc.).

Some have adopted such a method of working, and stated that this very method was the intention of Plato in his *Quartals* <note>Referring to the *Liber Quartorum* (Book of Fourths), an alchemical text traditionally attributed to Plato</note>, and also in agreement with the intention of Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father of chemistry"</note>, as has been said, and of other philosophers. For he intends that the work should be done in this way:

They take a perfect body, such as **Gold** <note>original: "solem," literally "the Sun," the alchemical symbol for gold</note>, and subtilize it with sharp waters <note>original: "aquis acutis," referring to corrosive mineral acids like nitric acid</note>, and convert it into small stones. These they dissolve in a "solution of dung" <note>original: "solutione fimi," referring to the gentle, steady heat of a horse-dung bath used for digestion</note>, and then by roasting they congeal it. They call this work "subtilization," and they repeat these dissolutions and **coagulations** <term>coagulation: the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid into a solid state</term> so many times until the whole is subtilized into the nature of Mercury, and flows with an easy fusion, and "tinges" <note>original: "etingat," refers to the power of the Stone to project its quality onto and transform other metals</note> upon entry.

They then keep this matter as the **fixed part** and the **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance, like yeast in dough, that "leavens" or transforms the base matter into gold</term>. They then cook it again with four parts of the body reduced into their own fusible Mercury (namely the "small stones"), roasting and dissolving as before, etc., continuing the labor until the matter again tinges, etc. They say that one can and should proceed in this way toward infinite increase and even an increase in quality.

Others, however, subtilize the perfect body in another way: namely through **calcinations** <term>calcination: heating a metal to high temperatures until it oxidizes and crumbles into a fine powder</term>, and then with water of Ammonia <note>original: "aqua Armoniaci," likely a solution of sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride)</note>, etc., or another solution, and then by roasting, and again by repeating the work; they labor in similarly subtilizing such things, etc.

Both methods aim to make the metal fusible and capable of "tinging" or transmuting other substances.</summary>

->### M. Antony of the Stone, Philosopher, etc.###<-

...[they continue the process] until the bodies themselves are totally converted into the nature of **Mercury**, in respect to the **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a potent substance or "elixir" capable of transmuting base metals or healing the body</term>. 

Some, however, intend to perform this **subtilization** <term>subtilization: the process of making a solid substance "subtle" or spiritualized, often through sublimation or dissolution</term> of the body or bodies using spirits—specifically with **sublimated Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio sublimato," likely mercuric chloride</note>, or with wine, or with other spirits of salts. Then, they either sublimate the spirit from these or simply sublimate the entire mixture. 

They say that a certain part of the body is raised up with the spirits; they continue this until they have a substantial part of the body thus converted into spirit. Then, by using a slow fire for separation, they capture the more "subtle" parts by sublimating them upwards. They say another part remains at the bottom, which is the **fixed part** <term>fixed: a substance that is stable in fire and does not evaporate or "fly away"</term>. Again, they cook this fixed part with a certain quantity of the non-fixed part by gentle roasting, until that part is fixed once more and converted into a **fixed earth**. They continue this until they have fixed a good portion of it, and they call this the "sufficiently prepared earth." 

Then they "raise" this earth again with a good quantity of the non-fixed part, repeating the process again and again until the whole substance is raised [volatilized]. Then they fix it once more. They claim that this process, when repeated four times, will become the **tincture**, according to the sayings of **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist</note> and also of **Hermes** in the *Emerald Tablet* <note>original: "thelesmo," a reference to the 'Tabula Smaragdina,' the foundational text of Hermeticism</note>, who says: 

*“You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity.”* <note>original: "Separabis terram ab igne, subtile à spisso, suauiter & cum magno ingenio."</note>

And: *“It ascends into heaven, and again it descends to the earth, until it retains the power of the superiors and the inferiors, etc.”* <note>original: "Ascendit in coelum, iterumque ruit in terram, donec retineat vim superioris & inferioris, &c."</note>

-># A Most Useful Treatise #<-

[...the sufficiency] of the manner of working itself, as was said before, namely to be understood concerning the **Mercury of the philosophers** <term>Mercury of the philosophers: a refined, essential substance believed to be the "seed" of all metals, distinct from common quicksilver</term>. Nevertheless, to satisfy their operation—which does not seem irrational, since it aims entirely toward **subtilization** <term>subtilization: the process of refining a solid substance into a "subtle" or spiritualized state, often through heat or dissolution</term> and **Mercuriality** <note>original: "Mercurialitatem"</note>, etc.—I say that such ways of working are well supported. However, one must take care in the labor that the bodies are not burned during such subtilization, or dried out too much, and thus entirely stripped of their nature. 

This is because, as was said before, in whatever way the bodies or the Mercury are subtilized, and through whatever path—provided that such preparations and **decoctions** <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence</term>, etc., are made according to the way of the philosophers and their intention—matters which have been discussed before and will be treated more particularly later in this treatise. Indeed, there are many ways and modes tending toward the same end, just as was previously determined regarding the "concordances" <note>the points of agreement between different alchemical authors</note> of the philosophers concerning their **Stone** <term>Stone: the Philosophers' Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and prolonging life</term>. 

It is true, however, that by inspecting the sayings of the ancient philosophers and the writings in this my treatise, the philosophers are more inclined toward the path found in **prepared natural Mercury**, or in **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio viuo," typically meaning quicksilver or the essential "quickening" spirit of the metal</note> resolved from a body or bodies, rather than those ways just described. This is because the ancient philosophers paid much more attention to the unity and uniformity of the matter and the labor than to multiplicity. In a single thing, there is greater unity and a stronger **affinity** <note>original: "symbolus," referring to the internal correspondence or shared nature between substances</note> than in many, etc. Consequently, the labor is easier and less prone to error, provided however that the **method of the fire** <term>method of the fire: the precise regulation of heat, often kept secret, which determines the success of the alchemical transformation</term> and the preparations—which all philosophers have greatly hidden—[are observed].

### M. Antonius de Lapide, Philosopher, etc. ###

...it should be worked first, namely the **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of vaporizing a solid and condensing it again to purify the "spirit" from the "body"</term> of the stone, and then, through a slightly greater **tolerance of fire** <note>original: "ignis modico maiorem tolerantiam"</note>, the **thickening** <term>thickening: also called inspissation, the process where a substance becomes dense or solid as moisture is removed</term> of the stone follows. For the whole **regimen of fire** <term>regimen of fire: the controlled application of different stages of heat (often compared to the heat of a brooding hen or the sun)</term>, its degrees, and the preparation of the stone consist in this: as I can consider from the words of the philosophers, our **one stone** <note>original: "lapis noster vnus"</note> should be kept in one vessel, as it is written, in a slow fire, so that its subtler part may be separated. ### Marcus Antonius concerning the Philosopher’s Stone, etc. ###

...sublimation <note>original: "sublimatio"; the process of vaporizing a substance and then condensing it back into a solid to purify it</note> of the spirits must be continued for so long upon the stone, because it is not merely an elevation upwards, but a remaining below, until the entire **mastery** <term>mastery: the "Magisterium," or the completed Great Work of alchemy</term> is in its fulfillment and perfected. You may test its perfection by **projection** <term>projection: the act of casting a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone onto a base metal to transmute it</term> upon a spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; often referring to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur</note> or a body <note>original: "corpus"; referring to a solid metal</note>. If you find the stone itself has been whitened and purified to such an extent that it gives off a pure and perfect **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"; the second major stage of the Great Work, signifying purity</note>, and if you then see that the stone has been made so subtle that it penetrates into the interior of the thing to be tinged <note>original: "rei tingédæ"; the metal intended for transmutation</note>, and if—once this penetration has occurred—the stone is so fixed that the formerly "lifeless" matter can withstand all judgments <term>judgments: chemical tests or the trial of intense fire</term>, then it is sufficient, and it has been perfectly prepared. 

If it is not yet so, repeat the first work upon it, etc., and it will follow as it has been written until it becomes so; and it shall be, with God’s favorable cooperation. Behold, now you can consider that it is a great error to agitate the operation of the stone in such a way that, once one operation is done, one moves on to another and the first is abandoned. For if the mastery were not in its fulfillment—as happens to many who, because of this, are driven to the very edge of failure in this art—the first work could not be repeated upon it, and the work would be totally brought to nothing. 

Otherwise, however, if you have diligently attended to what I have written to you concerning the **government of fire**, and if we have not hurried the work too much, you cannot easily destroy it. But if at first glance you do not find success, you can nonetheless most effectively remedy your defect through the persistence of the work, as I have written. And you may not only remedy it, but even improve it through the reiteration of the work—again with the non-fixed part, just as you labored from the beginning, etc., as **Geber** <note>Abu Musa Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says in his final chapter.

->### A Most Useful Treatise. ###<-

...of its highest **mastery** <term>mastery: the "Magisterium," or the completed Great Work of alchemy</term> of the stone itself, in increase and goodness into infinity.

Now, however, according to my promises, I shall not fail to include several authorities of the ancients concerning what has been said about the governance of the stone, specifically regarding the fire and its proportions; I leave the rest to the intelligence of any reader and to their diligence in studying the books of the philosophers. For **Senior** <note>original: "Senior"; referring to Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arabic alchemist whose "Chemical Tables" were highly influential.</note> says, first regarding the preparation of the stone and the governance of its fire: "The preparation of our stone is difficult and most hidden." Likewise, he says in the same place: "The common people, though they have eyes, are asleep; for even when they possess the thing, they do not know its preparation." Likewise, the philosophers, when speaking of the fire, say: "It is necessary that this fire be like the heat of a fever when it is in its steady state, and for this reason they have called it **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the "nigredo" or blackening stage, where the matter decomposes to be reborn</term>." Likewise in the same place: "Let your fire be the fire of baths <note>original: "ignis balneorum"; a gentle, indirect heat like a "bain-marie" or water bath, used to prevent the vessel from cracking or the contents from burning.</note>." Likewise in the **Turba** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic</note>: "And let your fire be light during the **whitening** <note>original: "dealbando"; the stage of Albedo, where the matter is purified of all darkness</note>; in that time when the **tincture** <term>tincture: the potent substance capable of coloring or transforming base metals into gold or silver</term> is being worked toward the white, less endurance of fire is required than when the matter of the stone begins to be **reddened** <note>original: "rubificari"; the final stage of Rubedo, where the stone reaches its full solar power</note> by the sheer persistence of the labor." For then, when the stone is worked toward the red, it requires as much heat in the first stage of the red work as is perhaps required in the third stage of the whitening work. And in this, a man must be cautious: that he does not apply the degree of fire belonging to the red stage before the time of perfected whitening—that is, until the tincture is perfected in the white governance. Just as the **Rosarius** <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely the *Rosarius Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a seminal 14th-century alchemical text</note> cries out regarding this, saying: "Do not mix the white work with the red; these..."

# M. Antonio de Lapide, Philosopher, etc. #

[...must], however, be mostly entrusted to the practice of the operator, etc. Likewise in the same place: Once our Stone is placed in its vessel, a gentle fire <term>gentle fire: known as "ignis lentus," a steady, low heat often compared to the warmth of a brooding hen</term> must be maintained for forty days, because through it the corrupting humidities <note>original: "humiditates corrumpentes"; refers to superfluous moisture that must be removed for the matter to undergo proper chemical change.</note> are drawn out. For the philosophers commend the long duration of their work, and they condemn haste and "combustion"—that is, heat so intense that the stone cannot return to its primary work or be perfected in its entirety, etc.

Likewise, it is said in the same place: regarding our vinegar <note>original: "aceto noftro"; in alchemy, "vinegar" typically refers to a specialized solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve the matter, rather than common household vinegar.</note>, caution must be taken lest it turn into smoke and perish because of the violence of the fire.

Likewise, it is said in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between various sages.</note>: In our first work, all things are blackened <term>blackened: the stage of "nigredo," signifying the death or decomposition of the old forms</term>; that is, before the matter is first reduced to ash, it is not perfectly white. In the second, all things are whitened; that is, in the second work, the matter is prepared for greater whiteness and transparency. And in the third, it is necessary that the whole composition be reduced to ash, always with perfect whitening, so that it is not totally reduced to ash unless it is perfectly whitened, as was previously stated, etc.

Likewise, it is said in the same place: do not despise this ash, for its own "sweat" or liquefaction—that is, the refinement or solution, which in this context are the same thing—is returned to it through a somewhat greater application of fire. And thus, in the fourth stage, the "crown of things" and the **tincture** <term>tincture: the final, potent substance used to transform base metals or heal the body</term> is produced, etc.

It should be known, however, that sometimes the matter becomes yellow <note>original: "citrina"</note> after the blackness, and sometimes red <note>original: "rubea"</note> before the whiteness; one should not worry about this, provided that such things are not allowed to continue until perfection, as has already been said. Otherwise, the "red work" would be mixed with the "white work," which must not happen.

# A Most Useful Treatise #

[...must], but the degrees of heat should be adjusted with such insight, and mitigated accordingly, so that one does not stray from the intention which I have already most clearly written to you, etc. The work is directed from blackness <term>blackness: known as "nigredo," the initial stage of the work representing the "death" or decomposition of the matter</term> to whiteness <term>whiteness: "albedo," the stage of purification and washing</term>, etc., so that the work may always be able to return to its principles.

Whence Hermes says, and it is also said in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between pre-Socratic sages.</note>: At the beginning of the mixing, let raw and fresh things be taken, and let them be purified and mixed until the elements are joined together; let them be ground, yet not by the grinding of hands (as is said in the *Turba*), and then let them be washed with waters so that they may conceive; then let them be extracted and nourished, that they may become the offspring <note>original: "genitum"; in this context, it refers to the nascent "Philosophical Child" or the early state of the Stone.</note>.

And know that this betrothal <note>original: "desponsatio"; an alchemical metaphor for the chemical union of opposing substances, such as "sulfur" and "mercury."</note> occurs in putrefaction, at the bottom of the vessel—not, however, by the common sort of rotting <note>original: "putredine vulgi"; alchemists distinguished their "philosophical" decay, which preserved the internal life of the matter, from "vulgar" or common biological rotting.</note>, but through incineration <term>incineration: the process of reducing the substance to a white ash or "salt" through controlled heat</term>, since the ancient philosophers nowhere suggest anything regarding common putrefaction without the distillation of waters, except perhaps allegorically or figuratively, etc.

The offspring, however, is created in the "air"—that is, in the upper part of the vessel, or in an upper vessel if one works with one vessel atop another <note>This refers to a "circulatory" or "pelican" vessel where vapors rise and condense back down.</note>, as Senior <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century alchemist whose work focused heavily on the chemical marriage and the "ascent" of spirits.</note> seems to suggest, which will be made clear below.

Likewise, it is said in the same place: Take things from their minerals, and exalt them to higher places, and harvest them from the peaks of mountains, and lead them back down to their roots, etc. These are clear words, written without any envy <note>original: "sine aliqua inuidia"; alchemists often used "envy" to mean the intentional obscuring of secrets to prevent the unworthy from succeeding; the author here claims his sources are being unusually direct.</note>.

From this authority, certain men have wished to derive this method of working: namely, they converted purified Mercury into water through roastings <term>roastings: "assationes," a process of heating a substance in its own moisture until it is dried and fixed</term>, whether with powders, or with other things, or by itself; and they distilled it through an alembic <term>alembic: a classic alchemical still consisting of a vessel and a cooling cap with a tube to collect condensed vapors</term>, and the earth in the bot[tom...]

### M. Anthony of Stone, Philosopher, etc. ###

...at the bottom they moistened it with water, etc. They converted the water into earth, and they said this must be continued until the perfect tincture <term>tincture: a concentrated alchemical substance capable of transforming or "coloring" base metals into gold or silver</term> is achieved. All good things came to me together with the primal wisdom of the south, who preaches outdoors, in the streets; she gives forth her voice, she cries out at the head of the crowds, at the entrance of the city gates she utters her words, saying: Draw near to me and be enlightened, and your works shall not be confounded; all you who desire me, be filled with my riches. Come therefore, children, listen to me; I will teach you the knowledge of the Lord. This, Solomon proposed to have in place of light; and above all beauty and health, he compared no virtue to it in the operation of that precious stone <term>precious stone: The Philosopher's Stone (lapis philosophorum), the ultimate goal of the work, described here using the language of Divine Wisdom.</term>, for all gold is as a little sand, and silver shall be esteemed as clay in its sight.

# Aurora

<note>original: "meaes" — likely a contraction of "Soror mea es," meaning "You are my sister."</note> [You are] my sister, and call providence <note>original: "prouidentiam"; here meaning forethought or divine prudence.</note> your friend; for to think upon her is a most natural and subtle sense, bringing that sense to perfection. Yet I was ignorant that she was the mother of all sciences who went before me; she bestowed upon me wonderful honors, which I learned without fiction and will communicate without envy, not hiding her nobility.
