# Blessed Thomas Aquinas

## Aurora Consurgens
<note>The title translates to "The Rising Dawn." This is a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript, often attributed to Thomas Aquinas, though modern scholars consider it the work of a later "Pseudo-Aquinas."</note>

[One] does not throw it into the dung-heap, for it is a medicine that puts poverty to flight, and after God, man has nothing better. This glorious science of God, this doctrine of secrets and secret of the Philosophers, this medicine of physicians, is despised by fools because they are ignorant of what it is. They desire a blessing, yet it shall be far from them; <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 108:18.</note> nor does such wisdom suit the unskilled, for everyone who is ignorant of it is its enemy. And not without cause did the observer of all things say: "The derision of science is the cause of ignorance." 

Lettuces are not to be given to donkeys when thistles suffice for them, nor is the bread of the children to be cast to the dogs to eat, nor are pearls to be sown among swine. <note>These are traditional biblical warnings (Matthew 7:6 and 15:26) against revealing sacred or esoteric secrets to those who cannot appreciate them.</note> Such mockers shall not participate in this illustrious science; for he who would reveal the ark of this science to the unworthy would be a breaker of the heavenly seal. The spirit of this wisdom shall not enter into a coarse body, <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 1:4: "Wisdom will not enter a deceitful soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin."</note> nor can the foolish grasp it because of the smallness of their reason; for the wise have not spoken to the foolish. Indeed, he who speaks with a fool speaks with one who sleeps.

Morigenes <note>Morienus (or Morigenes) was a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, famously the teacher of Prince Khalid ibn Yazid. He represents the transmission of alchemical secrets from the East to the West.</note> says: "If I wished to unravel all things exactly as they are, there would no longer be any place for prudence, since the fool would be made equal to the wise man." Nor would any mortal beneath the lunar sphere <note><term>lunar sphere</term>: In the medieval cosmos, the region between the Earth and the Moon was the realm of change, decay, and "stepmother poverty," as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> bewail the hardships of their stepmother poverty, because the number of fools in this science is infinite. <note>A play on Ecclesiastes 1:15: "The number of fools is infinite."</note>

***

Now, the title of this volume is baptized *Aurora Consurgens* ("The Rising Dawn"), and this is for four reasons:

**First**, dawn (*aurora*) is so called as if it were a "golden hour" (*aurea hora*); <note>This is a medieval folk etymology, linking the Latin *aurora* to *aurum* (gold) and *hora* (hour).</note> thus this science possesses a golden hour at its end for those who work rightly.

**Second**, because the dawn is the midpoint between day and night, glowing with a double color—namely, red and yellow. In this same way, this science produces yellow and red colors, which are the middle stages between the black and the white. <note>This refers to the alchemical "Great Work" (Magnum Opus), which progresses through color changes: <term>Nigredo</term> (blackness), <term>Albedo</term> (whiteness), <term>Citrinitas</term> (yellowing), and <term>Rubedo</term> (reddening).</note>

**Third**, because at the dawn, those suffering from all nocturnal illnesses are relieved... <note>original: "alleuiantur" — the text ends mid-sentence as indicated by the catchword.</note>

# Aurora

[...are banished] and find rest; so in the dawn of this science, all **terrors** <note>original: "terrores"</note> and evil vapors that infect the laboring mind fail and grow old. This is **Wisdom**, the **Queen of the South**, <note>A reference to the Queen of Sheba, who visited Solomon. Looking from afar, I saw a great cloud darkening the whole earth, which had exhausted my soul...

Thirdly, it softens—that is, it liquefies—the hardness of the earth, and dissolves its dense and highly compacted parts, concerning which it is written: *the rain or the spirit liquefies.* And the Prophet says: *He sends forth his word and shall melt them; his spirit blows and the waters flow.* <note>Psalm 147:18.</note> And in the *Book of the Fifth Essence* <note>original: "libro quintæ essentiæ." A text likely referring to works attributed to Lully or Rupescissa concerning the "Quinta Essentia," the pure celestial element extracted from matter.</note> it is written that air will open the pores of the parts of the earth to receive the power of fire and water. And elsewhere it is written: *The woman dissolves the man, and he fixes her,* which means the **spirit** <note>The volatile or gaseous aspect of the work.</note> dissolves the **body** <note>The solid or fixed aspect of the work.</note> and softens it, and the body hardens the spirit.

Fourthly, it illuminates, because it takes away all darkness from the body, of which it is sung: *Purge the horrid darkness of our mind, kindle light in our senses,* <note>From the hymn "Veni Creator Spiritus."</note> and as the prophet says: *He was a light to them all night long in the illumination of fire,* and then *the night shall be enlightened as the day.* <note>Psalm 78:14 and Psalm 139:12.</note> And **Senior** says: It makes everything black white, and everything white red, because water whitens and fire illuminates. It shines in color like a ruby through the **dyeing soul** <note>original: "animam tingentem." In alchemy, the "soul" is the agent that provides the permanent color or "tincture" to the metal.</note>, which it acquired from the power of fire; therefore fire is called the **dyer** <note>original: "tinctor."</note>, as you see in the *Book of the Fifth Essence*: *a wonderful light in the darkness.*

And in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "libro Turbæ Philosophorum." One of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note> it is written: that if a cloud [covers] the surface...

...surface <note>original: "superficiem." A naturally occurring salt (sodium carbonate) used in antiquity for cleaning and as a flux in glassmaking and alchemy.</note>, that is, with the extracted spirit; it separates the pure from the impure, because it removes the "accidents" of the soul, which are vapors—namely, bad odors. Thus it is said that fire separates heterogeneous things and gathers homogeneous things <note>A classic Aristotelian definition of fire's function: it divides things of different kinds and unites things of the same kind.</note>. For this reason the Prophet says: *You have tested me with fire, and no iniquity was found in me* <note>original: "Igne me examinasti, & non est inuenta in me iniquitas." A reference to Psalm 17:3.</note>. For the spirit itself, which is of the **sevenfold gift** <note>A reference to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, here applied to the "spirit" of the alchemical substance.</note>, separates the purer parts from the impure, so that, the impure parts having been cast aside, the work may be completed with the pure. And Hermes hints at this **fifth virtue** <note>Referring to the fifth effect of the "baptism" mentioned in this sequence.</note> in his secret when he says: *You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the thick, gently, etc.*

Sixthly, it exalts the lowest things, because it leads the deep soul, hidden in the bowels of the earth, to the surface; concerning which the Prophet says: *He who leads out the prisoners in his strength* <note>Psalm 68:6.</note>. Likewise: *You have brought my soul out of the lower hell* <note>Psalm 86:13.</note>. And **Isaiah** says: *The spirit of the Lord lifted me up* <note>Cf. Isaiah 61:1 or Ezekiel 3:12.</note>. And the Philosophers say: *Whoever has made the hidden manifest knows the whole work, and he who knows our **cambar** <note>term: "cambar." A technical term in Arabic-Latin alchemy, often referring to the "vessel" or the "cauldron" where the transformation occurs, or specifically to the "magnesia" of the philosophers.</note>, he is our son.*

Morigenes says: *He who has raised his soul upward shall see its colors.* And Alphidius says: *Where this vapor ascends, you shall have nothing else, for by it, and with it, and in it the whole work is done.*

Seventh and lastly, it **inspires** <note>In the literal sense of "breathing into."</note>, because by its breath it makes the earthly body spiritual, of which it is sung: *By breathing, you grant what is spiritual* <note>original: "Tu aspirando das spiritale." Likely a reference to a liturgical hymn concerning the Holy Spirit.</note>.

...all such men. **Solomon** [says]: *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world*, wherefore also the Prophet [says]: *By the breath of his mouth is all their power* <note>original: "Spiritu oris eius omnis virtus eorum." A reference to Psalm 33:6, here interpreted as the alchemical spirit that gives "virtue" or potency to the elements.</note>, and **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist.</note> in the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumine Luminum," an influential alchemical treatise attributed to Rhazes.</note> [says]: *heavy things cannot be lightened by the company of light things, nor can light things be pulled to the depths by the combination with heavy things.* And the **Turba** <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between pre-Socratic sages.</note> [says]: *Make bodies incorporeal and the fixed volatile*; all these things, however, are performed and fulfilled by our spirit, for it alone is that which made the world conceived from an impure seed. Does not Scripture say: *Wash in it and be clean*? And it was said to **Naaman**: *Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and you shall be cleansed* <note>A reference to 2 Kings 5:10; in alchemy, Naaman's leprosy represents the "sickness" or impurity of base metals, and the seven washings represent the seven distillations required for purification.</note>. For it is the one baptism for the remission of sins, as faith and the Prophet testify. He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the holy spirit of doctrine says to the sons of discipline concerning the spirit of sevenfold virtue, by which all scripture is fulfilled, which the Philosophers suggest in these words: *Distill seven times and you have separated it from the corrupting moisture.*

**Wisdom** has built herself a house; whoever enters it shall be saved and shall find pasture, as the prophet witnesses: *they shall be intoxicated by the abundance of your house*, for *one day in its courts is better than a thousand* [elsewhere]. Oh, how blessed are they who dwell in this house: for in it, he who asks, receives; he who seeks, finds; and to him who knocks, it shall be opened. For Wisdom stands at the door saying: *Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him, and he to me, and I will be satisfied with him, and he with me.* Oh, how great is the multitude of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those entering this house, which *eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man*; to those who throw open this house, there shall be the holiness that is fitting, and truly length of days, because it is founded upon a firm rock.

The tenth is benignity, of which it is said: *Know you not that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?* The judge is kind, rendering to each according to his works. For benignity returns good for evil, the greatest for the least; but goodness returns good for good, the little for the little.

The eleventh is patience, of which it is said: *If you wish to conquer, learn to suffer.* And the Apostle: *Through patience and consolation of the scriptures we have hope,* etc. Morigenes says: *He who has not patience, let him stay his hand from the work.* And Calec the younger <note>original: "Calec minor," referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early figure in the Arabic alchemical tradition known to the West as Calid.</note> says: *Three things are necessary: patience, delay, and the fitness of the instruments.* The Apostle: *Be patient, for the coming of the Lord draws near,* etc. The twelfth is temperance, of which it is written that it nourishes and fosters all things—that is, it preserves them in health. For as long as the elements are in temperance, the soul delights in the body; but when they disagree within it, the soul shrinks from dwelling there. For temperance is the mutual mixing of the elements with one another, so that heat is tempered with cold, and dryness with moisture. The Philosophers prohibited with the greatest zeal that one should exceed the other, saying: *Beware lest the secret <term>arcanum</term> <note>A profound mystery or "inner secret" of nature that the alchemist seeks to unlock.</note> escape. Beware lest the vinegar turn into smoke...*

*...since it [the Earth] is the principle and mother of the other elements, as the Prophet testifies: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth; and the heavens are the works of your hands* <note>original: "Initio tu Domine terram fundasti; & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli," from Psalm 102:25.</note>, *that is, water, air, and fire. For the elements are separated from the earth by dying, and return to it by being brought to life, because from whatever a thing is composed, into that it must be resolved, as holy speech testifies: Man is ash, and unto ash he shall return* <note>original: "Homo cinis est, & in cinerem reuertetur," a variation of Genesis 3:19. In alchemy, "ash" refers to the solid residue left after calcination, which must be reunited with its spirit.</note>. *The Philosophers* <note>The "Philosophers" are the ancestral authorities of alchemy, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber, whose cryptic writings form the basis of the art.</note> *commanded such ash to be mixed with permanent water, which is the ferment of gold; and their gold is the body—that is, the earth—which Aristotle called a **coagulum*** <note>term: "coagulum" — literally "rennet" or a curdling agent. Into this earth Hermes commanded his son to sow gold, and a living rain shall ascend from it, and water warming it, as Senior* <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century Arab alchemist Ibn Umayl, a primary source for this text.</note> *says: "And when they wished to extract this divine water, which is fire, they heat it with their own fire, which is water," which they measured even to the end, and hid because of the foolishness of fools. And concerning this, all the Philosophers swore an oath to go to a certain place, so that these things might not be set down clearly in writing; instead, they leave it to the glorious God, that He may reveal it to whom He wills and withhold it from whom He wills, because in it lies a great **sophism*** <note>term: "sophisma" — an intentional ambiguity or riddle designed to mislead the unworthy while revealing the truth to the initiated.</note> *and the obscurity of the wise.* 

*And when the heat of that fire reaches the earth itself, it is dissolved and becomes a rushing and vaporous water, then returns to its prior earthly form. Therefore, the earth was moved by the water, and the heavens dripped down upon it, and they were made **honey-flowing*** <note>original: "melliflui." This signifies the stage of "sweetness" where the harsh, corrosive qualities of the chemicals have been neutralized into a perfect, nutritive substance.</note> *throughout the whole world, just as its glory proclaims. For this glory is known only to the intelligent person, because the heavens were made from the earth; therefore, the earth remains forever, and the heavens are founded upon it, as the Prophet testifies: Who established the earth upon its stability, it shall not be moved forever and ever; the abyss is its garment* <note>original: "Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam, non inclinabitur in seculum seculi, abyssus vestimentum eius," from Psalm 104:5-6.</note>. *Upon it shall stand air, water, and fire, and also the birds...*

...is contrary to the sound of the letters; for he who receives the sound of the words and does not have the inner understanding, it profits him nothing, since to him is said that which is written: *to read and not to understand is to neglect* <note>original: "legere & non intelligere est negligere." This was a popular medieval proverb emphasizing that true literacy requires comprehension of the author's intent, not just decoding the signs.</note>. What, therefore, does it seem to you who desire this divine science <note>original: "diuinam scientiam." Do you consider whether that which you hope for exists, whether nature imitates it or is deprived of it, or what fruit you will have, at the end of which you will be ashamed? *Not so the impious, not so, but like the dust which the wind blows from the face of the earth* <note>original: "non sic impij non sic, sed tanquam puluis quem proijcit ventus à facie terræ." And just as elsewhere a similitude is placed, when he is called a rock, a sheep, a cornerstone, and other such things. From these, they are called similarities, not properties. <meta>This page continues from the previous page, completing the word "responding" [respondentes] or "providing" [providentes]. It introduces the "fivefold doctrine" of the Aurora Consurgens, a framework for understanding alchemy through the lenses of other sciences (like astronomy), allegorical language, natural philosophy, laboratory practice, and medicine.</meta>

# Aurora

->201<-

...ing, but as the wise and understanding. Note therefore diligently the words of the philosophers, and mark the mysteries, and do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding <note>original: "nolite fieri sicut equus & mulus, in quibus non est intellectus." A reference to Psalm 32:9, commonly used in alchemical texts to warn the reader that literal, "animal-like" reading will lead to failure; one must use the "intellect" to see the hidden meaning.</note>. Loosen truly the bonds of the wise, and revolve their sayings in your mind, until they taste sweet to you <note>original: "vobis in mente sapiant." The author uses a play on words: "sapere" means both to be wise and to taste. This implies that true knowledge is something to be "digested" or experienced internally.</note>. If you loosen one of the smallest points, the greatest secrets will not be hidden from you, because for the sake of the "little ones" <note>Referring to beginners or the humble.</note> a fivefold doctrine is placed in this booklet, bringing something of use to those who inquire with ingenuity. 

First, in which other sciences this science is surrounded; second, what styles of speaking it employs. Third, to what natural things it is naturally likened. Fourth, by what modes of operation it is carried out; and fifth, it is told by the power of its effect, how each person may use it for the medicine of the human body.

It must first be known that this divine science <note>original: "haec scientia diuina." Alchemy was considered divine because it sought to replicate the creative acts of God through the purification of matter.</note> uses the vocabulary of astronomy, namely the course of the planets, and their effects, and the number and power of the twelve signs of the zodiac circle. So Aristotle testifies to Alexander <note>original: "Aristoteles... ad Alexandrum." This refers to the *Secretum Secretorum* (The Secret of Secrets), a widely read medieval book of advice supposedly written by Aristotle for Alexander the Great, which included sections on astrology and alchemy.</note> saying: That Saturn holds the earth, Mercury the water, Jupiter the air, and the Sun the fire. For everything lacking light among the number of vegetables is ruled by Saturn, and is attributed to him; and every luminous vegetable is attributed to Mercury and ruled by him. And whatever vegetable is flowery but not bearing fruit is attributed to Jupiter and ruled by him; and every vegetable that is both flowery and fruitful is attributed to the Sun, and ruled by him. And again he adds: Then compose and join these divisions, and you shall say that every vegetable bearing fruit but not flowering, such as the apple and the palm <note>original: "pomum & palma." In medieval botany, certain trees were categorized by their "fruitfulness" rather than their biological flowering cycle as we understand it today.</note>, is attributed to Saturn and the Sun; and every flowery thing not bearing fruit is attributed to Mercury and Jupiter. We have now [prepared] two waters—namely, the unique gold and the divider; and two ointments—the purple golden gum and the virgin's milk; and the third of these is the vehicle—namely, the desired body. 

Take the desired body and the virgin's milk, and mix into it a fourth part of the divider, and cover it with unique [gold], and place it in the bath for twelve days at a minimum, thirty at the middle, or forty-two at the maximum, and it will be made...

When this fire comes forth, it blackens the vessel itself and burns every metal, because the oil of every hot thing is its fatness, and the oil of every cold thing is its moisture.

It is also the vessel of resolution <note>The process of "resolutio" involves breaking down or dissolving a solid body into its constituent parts.</note>, in which bodies are resolved: for in it, one thing follows another, little by little in its proper order. The resolution of all parts does not happen all at once, but it is resolved and extracted according to the manner of the elixir. As Senior <note>Senior Zadith: The Latinized name of the 10th-century Arabic alchemist Muḥammad ibn Umayl al-Tamīmī.</note> testifies, saying:

> Since their soul does not go forth from this stone all at once but many times, and because of this, this soul is called the "flower of the soul," and "flowers of blood," and "bloods," "fatness," and "fats"; and yet it is one soul and one spirit leading it out. The bodies are two, namely male and female, which are [nevertheless] three; and the water and the three sisters entering upon those principles are the nourishment and the increase of that which is nourished and increased—just as in an egg, in which it is nourished and increased by the yolk and the white, and is covered by the shell. For it has everything within itself that it needs; it operates in the operation, and the first sister entering upon them...

...in the heat of fire, to the liver in the humidity of air, and to the testicles in the dryness of earth. For the seat of the phlegm <term>phlegm: one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids thought to determine health and temperament in medieval medicine</term> is in the brain, the seat of red choler <term>choler: also called yellow bile; associated with a fiery, aggressive temperament</term> is in the heart, the seat of blood is in the liver, and the seat of melancholy <term>melancholy: or black bile; associated with the element of earth and a reflective or somber temperament</term> is located in the testicles. And this aforementioned nature notably exists within a single body, but their positions and functions are diversified.

For in choler, the **appetitive virtue** <note>original: "virtus appetitiua"; the power of attraction or desire</note> is understood, because it provides color. In melancholy, the **retentive virtue** <note>original: "virtus retentiua"; the power to hold or stabilize</note> is understood, because it retains the colors. In blood, the **digestive virtue** <note>original: "virtus digestiua"</note> is understood, which separates out what is superfluous. In phlegm, the **expulsive** or **cleansing virtue** <note>original: "virtus expulsiua siue mundificatiua"</note> is understood, because it gives true and perfect colors. 

However, there is a **Fifth Power** <note>The "Quintessence" or "Aether," the pure celestial element that exists beyond the four earthly elements.</note> which is neither hot nor cold, neither moist nor dry, neither heavy nor light, neither rough nor smooth, neither hard nor soft; rather, it is properly called **Life**. It is this life which joins these four elements into one, and provides them with a perfect and robust path in the form of the planets, the Sun and the Moon, forever.

From this, the work is truly compared to an **egg**; this is known because within it the four are joined together. The visible shell is the earth; the white is the water; the thin membrane between the thick shell and the white is the air. There is also the red part [the yolk], which is the fire; the membrane containing the red is the air separating the water from the fire, and both are one and the same. Indeed, the air separating the earth from the water is thicker than the higher air, while the higher air is hotter and more subtle. For the fire is closer to the higher air than to the lower air. In the egg, therefore, there are the four elements: namely earth, water, air, and fire. 

Beyond these four, in the middle of the red yolk, there is a **fifth thing**, which is the chick. This is not to be understood as the egg of a bird, but rather the egg of which the philosophers speak <note>The "Philosophical Egg" (ovum philosophorum) is the sealed glass vessel—the "Athanor"—in which the alchemical transformation takes place, as well as a symbol for the Matter itself.</note>. Therefore, all philosophers have described the egg in this most excellent art; they have presented it and many other examples in their books so that the "son of the doctrine" <note>A traditional term for an initiated student of alchemy.</note> might gain understanding from them and investigate the Great Work.

After this, the Stone is said to be similar to the **Basilisk** <term>Basilisk: a mythical serpent king said to kill with its gaze; in alchemy, it represents a potent, transformative substance or the "fixed" sulfur.</term> and to our other "worms," by reason of its nourishment, its feeding, or its infection. For just as the Basilisk is said to be nourished and fed...

<meta>This page continues the instructions for the alchemical "work," moving from the preparation of salts and vitriols discussed on the previous page to the central mystery of Mercury—referred to here as Quicksilver—and the specific "sharp vinegar" required to dissolve and transform the material body of the metal into a spiritual state.</meta>

### Blessed Thomas Aquinas <note>While attributed to the famous theologian Thomas Aquinas, this text belongs to the "Pseudo-Aquinas" tradition, a collection of alchemical works written in his name during the 14th and 15th centuries.</note>

...it with the sharpest vinegar and cook it; take care that the vinegar does not turn into smoke, for then the work would perish. In the comparison of **quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the standard Latin term for Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the fundamental spirit of all metals.</term> it must be noted that there are three types: the first is *fire*, because it is the philosophical fire, and it extracts this; the second is called the *vital soul*; the third is called *fire* or even the *soul*, or it is also called the *quintessence*. Concerning this, the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the most cited authorities in medieval alchemy, written as a dialogue between ancient thinkers.</note> writes, saying:

> Quicksilver is a fire that burns bodies.

And again: It is necessary, therefore, for the body to be overtaken by the flame of fire, so that it may be destroyed and made weak; for from this it is necessary to extract fire by connatural fire, as **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel), a 10th-century Arab alchemist whose work "The Shimmering Table" was translated into Latin and became a staple of Western alchemy.</note> says:

> Our fire is water; if you know how to give fire to fire and Mercury to Mercury, it is enough for you.

Concerning the second type, Senior and other wise men say that the soul is extracted through **putrefaction** <term>Putrefactio: the process of breaking down a substance through heat and moisture, often symbolized by blackness (the nigredo stage), intended to release the "spirit" from the "body."</term>, and when nothing of the soul remains in it, then you have washed the body from its filth. Likewise, it is said:

> Take away its soul and restore its soul to it.

Concerning the third type, it is written thus:

> You must extract the quintessence, otherwise you labor in vain.

And for this reason, quicksilver is said to be triple. Because of its life, death is imposed upon it, just as the common proverb sounds:

> He who knows how to kill and mortify quicksilver shall be called a master and a philosopher in this work.

Secondly, quicksilver is a spirit and is called *permanent water*, or *vinegar*, or *menstruum* <term>Menstruum: a solvent or "solvent of the philosophers" used to dissolve solids; the term implies a monthly or cyclical timing for the process.</term>, or *nourishment*, and it is entitled with many other names. The *Assembly of the Philosophers* reports:

> Let it be the sharpest vinegar, through which gold becomes pure spirit, and without which vinegar neither the blackness, nor the whiteness, nor the redness is produced.

For by such quicksilver the second kind is extracted, mortified, killed, extinguished, and **coagulated** <term>Coagulatio: the process of turning a liquid or spirit into a solid, stable form.</term>, as the *Assembly of the Philosophers* testifies, saying:

> Know that the body is not dyed unless it is first dyed. <note>original: "corpus non tingui, nisi tingatur prius." This refers to the alchemical axiom that the material must be "tinged" or transformed internally before it can act as a "tincture" to change other metals.</note>

Therefore, the philosophers called that substance **poison** <term>Venenum: often used for the transformative agent or "mercury" because of its ability to "kill" (dissolve) the metallic body before "resurrecting" it.</term>, and they treated these many names in various and manifold ways, just as the envious ones have said: *It is a stone and not a stone*, but in truth, it is a gum, as found in the *Assembly of the Philosophers*...

### Aurora

...it is written: I make known to you the disposition of the **gum** <term>Gumma: in alchemical literature, this refers to a viscous, resinous stage of the "Great Work," signifying the thickening of the philosophical mercury.</term>, not out of envy, for a great secret exists within it. Know that our gum is stronger than gold, and it is necessary to hold it as more honorable than gold. This gum of ours is, among the philosophers, more precious and sublime than pearls, because from this gum and a little gold, we buy many things. 

And therefore the philosophers, writing cautiously lest their secrets perish <note>original: "ne pereant caventes," implying the risk of the knowledge being lost or the practitioners themselves being endangered if they spoke too plainly.</note>, did not clearly state its disposition in their words, so that the cause would not be recognized by [the unworthy]. For if the foolish knew it, they would not hold it in contempt. Oh, how many gums there are, yet people do not recognize this one of ours at all! Therefore, the philosophers have hidden the nature of this poison <note>Alchemists often used "poison" as a metaphor for the raw, transformative substances that "kill" or dissolve the metals before they can be reborn as gold.</note>, because through it the whole regime is fulfilled, and the entire mortification and killing of the substances consists within it. 

The third **quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum: Mercury, the "living silver" which is the central agent of change in this text.</term>, however, results from the previous two states; it is white in color before the fire comes to it, but when the fire arrives, it becomes red, and this proceeds from the **divine stone** <term>lapis divinus: a stage or form of the Philosopher's Stone.</term>. 

Whence Elbo the Slayer <note>original: "Elbo interfector." This likely refers to an authority or a symbolic figure mentioned in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: "Whiten the **laton** <term>Laton: a crude alloy of copper or brass representing the "impure" body that must be purified and whitened.</term>, and tear up your books, lest your hearts be torn." 

And the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> says: "Place it upon the coins, and it becomes the **elixir**; through it you may use both life and clean water, extracted from many tinctures and things." Its tincture is life to those things in which it is twice immersed, and it is a perfect coloration, as the Assembly of the Philosophers testifies. This is the most precious Tyrian color <note>original: "color tyrius," referring to the rare and expensive purple dye of antiquity, here symbolizing the highest state of the alchemical work.</note>, which was first announced as a color, and then the purple color will approach. For this quicksilver is what brings forth the sweetness of scent, and it is the true, infallible tincture, providing perfection to every body. 

It is also compared to **arsenic** and **orpiment** <term>auripigmentum: literally "gold pigment," a deep yellow-orange mineral consisting of arsenic trisulfide.</term>, by reason of its burning oiliness; for clearly all arsenic and orpiment possess oily and burning humidities, as well as those that evaporate from fire, by which it blackens and dries the bodies. And arsenic is called the **male** by reason of its heat and dryness, while orpiment is the **female**, by reason of its heat and moisture, as the Assembly of the Philosophers says: "I have shown you the female in the orpiment,"

For it is often substituted for fire, for sulfur, and most frequently for the spirit, which, issuing from the body, is the water by which all things are quickened <note>original: "vegetantur," meaning to be animated or brought to life like vegetation.</note> and increased. It is also compared to marcasite, magnesia, and tutia. To marcasite in color, because just as marcasite has silver and golden sparks mixed within the earth, so in the philosophical work similar signs appear. Whence Mogenes <note>Mogenes is a likely corruption of a name like Hermes or Democritus, frequently cited as an authority in medieval alchemical collections.</note> witnesses, saying: "Know that the foul earth quickly receives golden sparks." By its power, it is also said to be of the nature of magnesia, for a similar reason of weightiness and its role in the fracturing of all metals. It is also said to be similar to tutia <term>Tutia: Zinc oxide, typically collected as a crust from the flues of smelting furnaces.</term> by reason of its quenching <note>original: "extinctionis," referring to the alchemical process of heating a substance and then plunging it into a liquid to purify it or alter its properties.</note>. For just as tutia is ordered to be quenched five or nine or ten or twelve times, so that its earthiness is refined and its sulfurous nature is destroyed: so the philosophers command their work <note>likely "opus": the Great Work or the specific process at hand.</note> to be repeated, so that all that is superfluous in the manifest [outward] part is cast away, and that which is absent in the deep or hidden part may be added.*

*It is truly to be noted that there is one leading spirit in the body, and this is to be removed, and it is of a fiery nature, as the Assembly <note>original: "Turba," referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> witnesses, saying: "Know that the body cannot dye <term>Tingere: to tint or dye; in alchemy, this refers to the transformation of a metal's color and internal nature.</term> itself unless the spirit is extracted, which is hidden in its belly, and it becomes water and body." Without the spirit, which is of a spiritual nature from which colors appear—because that which is thick and earthy does not dye—it is truly the subtle part of the nature, which passes from the body, that dyes and colors. The second spirit, however, is outside the body and is of a watery nature, and it is what dyes the body into an elixir <term>Elixir: the supreme agent of transmutation or the "medicine" of metals.</term>, as the Assembly says: "The male truly is the body, and the female is this spirit."*

*From this, it is truly compared to all metals in qualities, in natures, in colors, in softness, and in hardness...*

# Aurora

This substance, in both its manifest and its hidden aspects, is compared to gold and silver by reason of the perfection of its colors which persist in the fire, as well as its weight and ductility. It is compared especially to gold, however, since gold is more noble and perfect than all the other three bodies <note>In this context, the "other three bodies" likely refers to the secondary metals in the alchemical hierarchy (silver, copper, tin, or lead) or the foundational spirits.</note>. There is, however, a "philosophical gold" which is not bought at a high price, as Alphidius <note>Alphidius is an authority frequently cited in medieval alchemical texts, representing an early, likely Arabic, source whose identity remains debated by historians.</note> says: *Know that this stone, which is the subject of this secret, was placed by God so as not to be bought at a high price; for it is found cast out in the way, so that it may be possessed by both the poor and the rich, and so that anyone, by reason and science, might easily arrive at it.* 

And Morigenes <note>Morigenes (or Morienus) was a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have transmitted alchemical secrets from the Byzantine world to the Islamic world.</note> says: *Every thing that is bought at a high price is a lie, for with a small amount of this gum, and a little gold, we buy many things.*

And again: *Mix gold with gold, that is, ash with water; or sow gold in the white foliated earth, which is the third earth, which belongs to gold. And the elixir tinges it, and it tinges the elixir. The white shall come from the black-red and the pure white; the crystalline shall appear from the citron-red.*

Fourthly, it must be noted in what ways and by what paths that celestial operation is fulfilled. And it should be noted that the philosophers assigned various terms to the operation itself. ...performing [the work]: some by coagulating Mercury <note>the metal quicksilver, or the "philosophical mercury" described on the previous page</note>, arsenic, pigment <term>orpiment; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</term>, sulfur, magnesia <note>not modern magnesium, but likely a mineral like pyrolusite or a specific alchemical preparation</note>, and marcasite <note>iron pyrite</note>, by whitening and fixing [them]; others by preparing sharp salts like oils in the tincture <note>original: "tinæ," likely a contraction for "tincturæ"</note>. Therefore, calcination is placed at the beginning of our work, just like a father in the process of generation; hence we must first see what the calcination of the philosophers is. And it should be known that the calcination of the philosophers is twofold: calcination of the body and of the spirit. The first is the beginning of our work, of which it is said that calcination is the removal of cold moisture by the burning of heat <note>original: "combustione mouentis," perhaps referring to the "moving" or active fire</note>, or the incineration of dry earth. 

And the philosophers have illustrated this using wood, in which there are three moistures: the first is watery and cold, and this prevents the wood from burning; the second is oily or unctuous, and this makes the wood catch fire. These two are vaporizable in the fire and combustible. The third, however, is left in the ash; it is very small and essential, fixed and perpetual, not at all flammable, and it is that which gives substance <note>original: "vivificans," literally "vivifying" or "giving life"</note> and corresponds to glassy transparency. And in such a way the calcination of the philosophers is commanded to be done, as it is in the wood. 

And this is done either through "philosophical vinegar" or through "permanent water," and by no other thing. And these things are to be noted. Such moisture, as has been said, which is the principle of liquefaction, must be in the bodies, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "The principle of all meltable things is water." And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works on chemistry were highly influential in Medieval Europe</note> reports: "We have therefore considered in natural principles that the subject of liquefaction is a flowing moisture mixed with parts..."

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of calcination begun on page 226. # Aurora

->P 2<-

...earthly parts, in which it is moved, while fire dissolves them, and we find the moisture of evaporation—not a violent one—mixed within them; indeed, it is raised from them during the dissolution. And we find the cause of the burning <note>original: "adustionis"</note>, so that the cooking is thus performed: it is mixed with dryness, so that the dryness which is mixed with it reaches that same moisture, along with the excessive accidental heat it has acquired. This happens with the fire so that it is fixed for us for a long time, until the manifestation of that same moisture is found. This requires a violent fire capable of powerful conversion, because the second parts of the body are converted to the substance of fire; before evaporation, the fire is separated and its dregs <note>original: "fax," likely referring to the dross or residue</note> remain—the ash which is burnt. Indeed, when it evaporates and has already been transformed and becomes a flame, this is called the **calcination of the philosophers**.

Furthermore, it must be noted that whoever performs the calcination of any body, if the metallic matter remains—that is, the watery humor which possesses its name and its ability to liquefy in fire—he has already erred. For calcination is said to be the extraction of the corrupting moisture, and after this, the introduction of a foreign fiery moisture, through which their essence and life shall be; and this is the first part, namely: *its father is the Sun* <note>A reference to the *Tabula Smaragdina* or Emerald Tablet, where the Sun represents the active, masculine principle or Gold</note>. 

The second calcination is of the ash itself or the remaining lime <term>calx; the powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</term>, which is the separation of the elements; and this is the second part, namely: *its mother is the Moon* <note>In alchemy, the Moon represents the passive, feminine principle or Silver</note>. This is the "solution of the philosophers," or the extraction of the fifth essence <term>quintessence; the purest, most concentrated essence of a substance</term>, or sublimation, or incineration, or imbibition <term>the process of repeatedly adding liquid to a dry substance to nourish it</term>, or the interpretation of all the aforementioned things. 

For this calcination is performed first so that the parts dried by fire and constricted may become spiritual <note>transformed from a solid into a refined, "spirit-like" gas or essence</note>, or may be subtilized and rarefied by the spirit, which is water, dissolving and moistening that burnt earthy matter. This is done so that the impressed heat, which acts as a corrupting force alongside the moisture, may transform it through digestion into an airy resolution <note>a state of being dissolved into air or vapor</note>.

<summary>This page describes the two types of philosophical calcination: the first involves removing "corrupting moisture" (the Sun/masculine stage), and the second involves refining the remaining ash to extract the quintessence (the Moon/feminine stage).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of calcination from page 227. While the previous page established that the "father" of the process is the Sun (Gold), this page details the specific stages of calcination and introduces "inceration" (softening to a waxy state) using a theological analogy of the resurrection of the body.</meta>

# Blessed Thomas Aquinas

For in the first **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to effect change or remove impurities</note>, two humors <note>original: "humores," referring to the internal fluids or moistures of a substance</note> are removed, namely the cold and watery, and the combustible. In that which is the second [calcination], the earthiness and fieriness are removed toward the resolution of our water. For everything that the sun makes and softens, it then disturbs. From here, by cooking the airy resolution through evaporation, comes the "solution of the philosophers," because the earthy parts soften, so that their dryness—which is hardness—is turned into softness, which is called the moistening water of rain, or of another humidity. For it is said: the more dry a thing is, the more it is made soft, since only dryness **tinges** <term>Tingit: The alchemical power to "color" or transform the nature of a metal</term> and nothing else; this is the thinning of the elements. 

It is also called **inceration** <term>Inceratio: "Waxing," the process of adding liquid to a dry powder until it reaches a waxy, pliable consistency</term>. For that reason, since the earth is [dry] by its own nature, it is necessary to incerate it—that is, to provide moisture—so that it may flow and have entry, and truly represent a metallic form, just as the "Assembly of Philosophers" <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical text</note> speaks figuratively. 

Just as a man in a heap of [stones or dust] becomes powder, once the days are completed God restores to him his soul and spirit; with his infirmity taken away, that [body] is purged and amended by a radiance <note>original: "corruscationem," a flashing or glittering light</note>, just as at the general resurrection a man is stronger and younger than he was before in this world. Therefore, **inceration** is the fixing of the matter with humors together with an incerating substance over the fire. 

And this **liquefaction** of bodies belongs to the philosophers, not to the common people. For the common people liquefy by fire, but the philosophers [liquefy] by water; whence it is said: "Liquefy the bodies with a liquefaction not of the common sort, but our own, which is with water." Inceration is an imbibing or a drinking or a liquefaction of the warm [substance], until it is intoxicated <note>original: "inebrietur," meaning the dry matter is completely saturated with the liquid "spirit"</note>. For everything that is thirsty [desires] to drink, as **Aristotle** says: "Thirst is the appetite for the cold and moist"; for this reason, that earthy thing is also called "the thirsty one."

It uses the Christian concept of the resurrection to illustrate how matter is purified, strengthened, and "reborn" in a more perfect form.</summary>

# Aurora

-> P 3 <-

Now this **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify and "elevate" the matter</note> is the second part, for this reason: because that which is in the lower part of the vessel is elevated and exalted to the supreme vessel, which is named the **alembic** <term>Alembicus: The top part of a still, used for distilling liquids</term> or the long **aludel** <term>Alludel: A series of earthenware pots used in the sublimation process to collect the purified vapors</term>; or it is so that the density of the elements might pass, through this elevation, into their variety. Thus the dryness of earth passes into the moisture of water, and the coldness of water into the heat of air, and the moisture of air passes into the dryness of fire. And these transmutations are said to occur through the degrees of fire, ascending even unto heaven—which is the "alembic of the philosophers"—and by God, that is an infinite dyeing agent <note>original: "tinges infinitum"</note>. And in such a way is the sublimation of the philosophers commanded to be performed. Whence it is said: To sublimate is to extract from the elementary dregs—which is earth—the **fifth essence** <term>Quinta essentia: The "quintessence," the most refined and spiritual element that remains after the four physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) are purified</term> or the oily, ascending nature; or put another way: to sublimate is to elevate a thing from the dregs, or to separate the pure substance from the earthy parts. 

For in all perfection, the sign of success is **liquefaction** <note>Melting or becoming liquid</note> and metallic fusion. And it must be noted that sublimation is twofold: one bodily, the other spiritual. Bodily as far as "earthiness" is concerned; spiritual as far as "fieriness" is concerned. Of the first it is said: "Thus make the body spiritual, and the fixed thing volatile." Of the second it is written: in a thing where there is combustion <note>original: "adustio," a scorching or burning</note>, the first thing that is dissolved in it is the fiery power, as mentioned above. And **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist highly respected in Medieval Europe</note> says: "Let the spirit go out from the body, which is fire." 

It is also called **fixation** <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> because of the addition of that which was absent. For that which is absent is of a volatile nature, without which the study of the **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The "Great Work" or the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone</term> would be in vain. For it is the **elixir** <note>A medicinal or transformative substance</note> of whiteness and the **tincture** <note>The power to change the nature and color of a metal</note> of redness, as well as the dyeing spirit and the metallic water pouring itself into the body, thereby bringing it to life. And the body is the receiver of the tincture from the spirit itself, and from no other; whence it is said that the tincture is from the "nature of flying things" <note>A common alchemical metaphor for volatile gases or spirits that escape the flask</note>, and that which strengthens and fixes the spirit itself is fixed, perpetual, and **unburnable** <note>original: "incremabile," a substance that has reached such purity that fire can no longer consume or destroy it</note>.

<summary>This page defines sublimation as a two-fold process—both physical and spiritual—that purifies the elements and extracts the "fifth essence." It explains how a volatile spirit must be united with a physical body to create a permanent, "unburnable" tincture or elixir.</summary>

And <term>Geber</term> in the *Book of Perfection* says:

> That which is not fixed, unless it be enlightened and the coldest substance be elicited from it, with its own ingenious method.

The philosophers, however, wish to nourish their "grain" with their connatural moisture until it is fixed and brings forth fruit of the same kind that the grain has within itself; they wish to quicken that which is "dead" from its metallic form until it achieves a perfect metallic fusion. Such quickening or nourishment some of the philosophers call **entry** <term>Ingressum: The final stage where the transformative medicine "enters" or penetrates the base metal to change it</term>.

In this process, the elements—namely air, water, and fire—are truly separated from the earth. The earth is left there so that the other three elements may take root in it. If these were not elements, they would have no foundation upon which to build the new house of treasures.

Concerning this decoction, **Avicenna** says:* <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy.</note> *If blackness arrives, it will be scorched during the decoction. And **Senior** says:* <note>Senior Zadith (Zadith ben Hamuel) was a 10th-century Arabic alchemist often quoted in Latin texts.</note> *If the blackness remains in it during its proper time, you will die of grief, for you have corrupted whatever you worked on. One must beware of such a regime, but instead cook it as the **Assembly of the Philosophers*** <note>original: "turba philosophorum," one of the most influential Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> *attests, saying: Cook it continually until it is coagulated; for once it is coagulated, the greatest secret is made. Cook that coagulated stone until it becomes like sea-purple.* <note>original: "mugræ marinæ," likely referring to the purple dye extracted from murex snails, signifying the "rubedo" or final red stage of the work.</note> *Then imbue it with permanent water, until its colors appear. In this decoction, the water most closely imitates nature—indeed, it makes something similar to it.*

*But **Albertus** says:* <note>Albertus Magnus, the teacher of Thomas Aquinas, who was widely believed to be an expert in the "art" of alchemy.</note> *That among all arts, alchemy most imitates nature, and this is because of its decoction and its growth, because it is cooked in waters that are metallic, fiery, and red, which have the most of form and the least of matter. For other arts imitate nature through mere resemblance, but alchemy does so by pure virtue. Therefore, alchemy is not weaker than nature; the artisan only ministers to it—it works and is perfected naturally, as is said by **Senior** regarding the divine water:* <note>original: "aqua diuina," often synonymous with the "Philosopher's Stone" in its liquid, transformative state.</note> *That no one has been born, nor will be born in the future, who can complete this science without nature, which is a heat* <note>original: "calus," likely a variant or OCR error for "calor" (heat).</note> *endowed and infused into things. It is also called **roasting*** <term>Assatio: A "dry" heating process (unlike decoction), used to fix volatile spirits into a stable body.</term> *by reason of the offending moisture of the body itself, or by reason of the spirit which descends and is fixed by the steady application of roasting from the body, as **Calid the Younger** says. And by sweet iteration* <note>The repeated process of evaporating and condensing or heating and cooling.</note> *these things are placed before you, so that you may teach the matter to endure the fire. And **Avicenna** says: If we wish for its mixture to be good, then we roast it with an equal fire, and this is so that it may contain...*

# The Dawn of Blessed Thomas Aquinas

"My Master and Lord, to whom I belonged, visits you; I shall declare his Lord and master to you. You shall cause all kinds of metals to be brought, which you shall prepare, and you shall introduce this powder, which I give to you, for all things are turned into true gold <note>original: *aurum verum*</note>. This being done, you shall liquefy crystal in the manner described before, and once the powder is immersed, it will be changed into red <note>likely referring to a ruby or carbuncle</note>. Afterward, you shall liquefy glass, and with the said powder immersed, it shall be rendered malleable <note>original: *malleabile*; a reference to the legendary "malleable glass" that could be hammered like metal without shattering</note>. When all these things have been seen and completed, you shall say: 'This is the dominion or the mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the finished work or secret of the alchemist</note> of my beloved Lord.' Afterward, you shall declare my mastery: you shall give it to the most unclean lepers in a lukewarm drink, and soon after they have gone to bed, let them be covered with a cloth; these will be healed most quickly and completely, so that it seems to them that they do not walk upon the earth, but upon the wings of the winds <note>A poetic allusion to Psalm 104:3, suggesting a feeling of weightlessness or divine vitality</note>. Now, therefore, go in peace, and fulfill my desire."

Then the notary departed, rejoicing and exulting, and he found everything to be true, just as he had heard from his Lord. He demonstrated these things to the aforementioned Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> and the Emperor. And thus the medicine of the philosophers was proven before the Supreme Pontiff and the Emperor reigning in those times, to have the power of curing the infirmities of man, of transmuting metals into perfect ones, stones into precious gems, and rendering glass malleable. This glorious medicine is possessed by Him, which may Almighty God, and the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ—who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as one through infinite ages of ages—deign to bestow upon every faithful and pious person. Amen.

"My mouth shall meditate upon the truth, and my lips shall detest the wicked" <note>original: *Veritatem meditabitur guttur meum, & labia mea detestabuntur inpium*</note>. From the twenty-eighth [chapter] of Wisdom <note>Although the text cites Wisdom 28, this is actually a quote from Proverbs 8:7. For the Philosopher <note>term: *Philosophus*; in this context, the author refers to Aristotle, who was known simply as "The Philosopher" in the Middle Ages.</note> says that he is called wise who orders things rightly and governs them well. It is therefore the duty of the wise man to put things in order; however, the rule of government and order for all things directed toward an end must necessarily be taken from that end itself. For each thing is best disposed toward its end when it is most appropriately ordered toward it. Moreover, the "end" is the good of every individual thing. This title of "wise" is not simply reserved for those alone whose consideration is occupied with the end of the universe, which is the source <note>original: *principium*</note>; wherefore, according to the Philosopher, it is the part of the wise man to consider the highest causes. The first author and mover of the universe is the intellect <note>term: *intellectus*; refers here to the Divine Mind or supreme rational power</note>. It is therefore necessary that the ultimate end of the universe be the good of the intellect; this good, and that which is the subject of its consideration, is truth. ...the ultimate end of the whole universe <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's "ul-timum" (ultimate).</note> is for wisdom to be chiefly occupied with the consideration of that end. The Philosopher <note>term: *Philosophus*; a standard medieval reference to Aristotle</note> determines that First Philosophy <note>term: *Prima Philosophia*; what we now call Metaphysics, the study of the fundamental nature of reality</note> is the science of truth—not just any truth, but that truth which pertains to the first principle of existence for all things; hence, its truth is the principle of all truth. For the arrangement of things in truth is the same as their arrangement in being. 

Furthermore, it belongs to the same person to pursue one thing and to refute its opposite. We see, for example, that medicine, which produces health, also excludes sickness. Therefore, just as it is the duty of the wise to primarily profess the truth regarding the first principle and to discuss it with others, it is also their duty to combat the contrary falsehood. 

Appropriately, then, from the mouth of the wise man, a twofold office of the wise is demonstrated in the words proposed: namely, the meditation of divine truth, which is truth in the highest sense <note>original: *antonice*; likely a scribal abbreviation for *antonice* or *autonomice*, meaning "by excellence" or "par excellence"</note>. This meditation of speech is touched upon when he says: **"My mouth shall meditate upon the truth"** <note>original: *Veritatem meditabitur guttur meum*</note>. And the second duty is to combat the error of those opposed to the truth, as is added: **"And my lips shall detest the wicked"** <note>original: *Et labia mea detestabuntur impium*</note>. Through this, falsehood is marked as being against divine truth, which is contrary to piety; thus, falsehood is contrary to piety, and piety is named a virtue. 

Among all human pursuits, the study of wisdom is the most perfect, sublime, useful, and pleasant. It is more **perfect** because, in so far as a man gives himself to the study of wisdom, to that extent he already possesses some part of true happiness <term>beatitude: the state of supreme blessedness or eternal happiness</term>. Hence it is read: **"Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and who overflows with pru-** <note>The text breaks here; the full word is likely "prudence." This is a reference to Proverbs 3:13.</note>

# Commentary of Saint Thomas Aquinas

-> ### Page 248 <-

According to the Philosopher, <note>original: *philosophum*; referring to Aristotle, the primary authority for medieval scholars.</note> the principle of demonstration is "what a thing is." <note>original: *quod id quidem est*; this refers to the "essence" or definition of a subject, which serves as the starting point for logical proof.</note> For it is necessary that the manner in which the substance of a thing is understood determines the manner of those things which are known about it. For everything that is grasped by the human intellect is grasped through certain principles that are self-evident. <note>original: *per se nota*; truths that require no proof, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note> Hence, if the human intellect comprehends the substance of a thing—that is, its definition—such as that of a stone, a triangle, or a circle, then the intelligible aspects of that thing do not exceed the capacity of human reason.

However, a different situation occurs for us regarding **God**. For the human intellect cannot reach the point of grasping His substance <note>His "essence" or "what He is."</note> by its natural power, since the knowledge of our intellect (according to the state of this present life) begins from the **senses**. And therefore, those things which do not fall under the senses cannot be grasped by the human intellect, except insofar as knowledge of them can be gathered from the senses. 

Physical objects, <note>original: *sensibilia*; things perceptible by the five senses.</note> however, are least of all able to lead our intellect to the point where the divine substance might be seen, or where we might perfectly see "what it is." Even though the world is an effect caused by divine power, the human intellect can only proceed from the senses toward divine knowledge in order to know concerning God **that He exists**, <note>original: *quia est*; Aquinas distinguishes between knowing *that* something exists and knowing *what* its nature is.</note> and other such things which must be attributed to the first principle—namely, to God the most high and glorious, who rules and governs all things.

By a similar analogy, the same is said regarding the **philosopher’s stone** <note>original: *lapide philosophico*; the legendary substance capable of perfecting base metals and human health.</note> by wise men and ancient philosophers in the books they composed about the stone itself. This science is, moreover, no—

# Commentary of the Blessed Thomas Aquinas

[it] is called, from **Al** which is "sublimation" and **Kym** which is "vial" <note>original: *ampulla*; a glass vessel used in laboratory work.</note>: Hence **alchemy** <note>original: *alkymia*</note> is the sublimation of mineral bodies in a vial. 

But I say that **Alchemy** is a <term>ministerial science</term> <note>A "servant" science that assists or completes the work of nature through human art.</note> of natural parts, reducing and perfecting the weak or diminished bodies of metals toward their perfect or natural completion, by purifying them through the required fire, through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The process of breaking down a substance to its base state before it can be "reborn" or transformed.</note> and the power of mineral bodies. 

To clarify this definition, I have said that **alchemy** is a science in regard to its theory, and ministerial—that is, preparative of parts—in its natural or manual operation, taking its principles from nature, as we have named. When we previously said "weak or diminished," we mean to declare their immediate matter and doctrine; for all bodies of metals, by the intention of working nature, ought to have been gold, since nature always intends toward the perfection of any body. 

But through the diminution of natural work, or of formal power, or of both, they [the metals] remained weak, diminished, and incomplete, according to a greater or lesser degree from the substance of gold. They failed to reach its optimal perfection due to the infection of natural vapors, or of the places and caverns of the earth where their substance takes body, arising from vapors cooked and congealed by natural heat. <note>This reflects the medieval belief that all metals are made of the same materials (sulfur and mercury) and that base metals are simply "diseased" or "under-ripe" gold affected by the impurities of the earth.</note> 

Hence the intention of this art is to teach how all minerals, whether stones or [metals], may be led from weakness to health, or from diminution to completion and the most perfect state.

<header>Blessed Thomas Aquinas's Commentary</header>

-> ## Page 252 ## <-

He is nowhere fully encompassed, and in comparison to Him, substance is a mere accident, and an accident is nothing. For **God is love**, and the more of His presence one possesses, the more one pleases God <note>original: *plus habitus... plus placet Deo*</note>; He is the one whom no figure of speech can describe because of His excellence, and whom no minds can fully understand because of the great dissimilarity between sensible things and God. Concerning Him and His power, we can say nothing directly. And therefore, the ancient philosophers, naming Him through negation <note>This refers to "apophatic theology," the practice of describing God only by what He is not (e.g., infinite/not-finite, immortal/not-mortal).</note>, said that He is neither "this" nor "that." But they did say: **God is that than which nothing better can be imagined** <note>This is a famous definition by St. Anselm of Canterbury, used here to bridge the gap between human thought and divine reality.</note>. From this they said: the **First Cause** <note>original: *causa prima*; a philosophical term for God as the ultimate origin of all motion and existence.</note> rules all created things. It is clear that He is mingled with them, yet He exists in all things according to His own disposition, whereas all things do not exist in Him according to a single disposition. For all powers <note>original: *virtutes*; can also mean "virtues" or "efficacies."</note> which have no end are dependent upon the infinite **First**, which is the **Power of powers**; for these powers are not fixed by themselves within the changing things of the world.

Hence **Hermes**, the king of these philosophers <note>Referring to <term>Hermes Trismegistus</term>, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note>, said in the book of the ***Secret of Secrets*** <note>original: *Secretum Secretorum*; one of the most popular medieval texts, framed as Aristotle's secret advice to Alexander the Great, covering everything from politics to alchemy.</note>—which is called the "treatise of truth without any falsehood" and begins in this way:

"I, Hermes, who am exalted above the circles of this world, saw three faces proceeding from or born of one father; a part of these is received in the mountains, a part in the sea, and a part in the trenches. The father joined these three into one, and when they had seen one another, they spoke with a single voice, saying: 'Let us go seek the natures of the **four elements**, which the ants lead out from the belly of the earth.'"

Similarly, our father **Hermogenes** <note>A name often used in alchemical literature as a variation of Hermes; the title "triplex" refers to the "Thrice-Great" (Trismegistus) nature of the author.</note>, who is triple...

...would speak, etc. The sayings of this Eximidius <note>original: *Eximidii*. Likely referring to one of the speakers within the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical dialogue.</note> come first, as Pythagoras—the master of this book of the "Assembly"—speaks concerning the principles and indications of this work, saying: *That the nature of all created things is a certain perpetual and first nature*, etc. 

Because he calls it "perpetual and first," someone might perhaps understand this as referring to the "first essence," namely, the act of creation. But this is not true. Rather, he calls it "perpetual" meaning spiritual, and "first" meaning the most noble of all creatures existing within the elements. To think otherwise would be false, since the rational soul and the angelic nature are far more noble [than material elements]. 

By "cooking all things," he means the digesting and shaping of natural heat, as described in the book *On Minerals* by Brother Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the Dominican scholar and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, who wrote extensively on the "natural heat" required for the formation of metals.</note>, in the chapter beginning "furthermore into the aqueous," and throughout nearly that entire chapter. I teach you that the stars are fiery, for the stars and the higher celestial bodies were created from a more subtle and rare fire—which is why they are called "fiery"—and that the air contains them, etc. This relationship is accidental, because the air acquires heat from its proximity to the Sun and the stars; conversely, the heat of the Sun and stars is tempered by the moisture of the air. This is proven both through the intellect and the senses in the *Summary* of Master Damascene <note>referring to John of Damascus, whose writings on the elements were frequently cited in the Middle Ages</note>, for he says: *since air is hot and moist*, etc. 

The intention of Pythagoras, the master of this book, was to provide a straight path through the most obscure words of the "Great Work" regarding the **Stone** <term>lapis: the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of alchemical transmutation and spiritual perfection</term>, which concerns minerals. He employed these obscure phrases so that the path would be open only to students of the art seeking to complete the work, as Archelaus expressly states: *Although in the previous volume...* And Aristotle in the book...

**Air** is the aforementioned heat, which by reason of temperance is called "air" here; it creates harmony between water and fire, that is, between extrinsic moisture and earthy moisture. # Commentary of the Blessed Thomas Aquinas

...quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*. Known today as mercury.</note>. And therefore, quicksilver is sufficient in this art, since it possesses an aqueous substance from water, an earthy substance from earth, a moist substance from air, and an unctuous and fiery substance from fire. Therefore, this art is compared to an egg, which contains these four elements, with the **point of the Sun** in the center, which is the chick—that is, the **radical** or **formal heat** <note>The "radical heat" was considered the innate, life-sustaining energy within matter that allows it to grow or transform.</note> which exists in metallic matter, and indeed in every elemental body. This is found in the book *Light of Lights* <note>original: *Lumen luminum*. A highly influential alchemical treatise often attributed to the Persian physician Rhazes or occasionally to Aristotle.</note>, in the chapter "Since therefore to this," and above in the first chapter of this book, in the section "In this way."

Furthermore, we have often said that heat—through the heat of fire and the **formative power** <note>original: *virtus formativa*. The internal force believed to guide the development of a substance into its final shape and nature.</note> which is likewise present in matter by the influence of the heavens and the stars—directs matter toward its proper end, form, and species. This is stated just above in the previously cited book *Light of Lights*, from which Aristotle is quoted in the aforementioned book *Light of Lights*.

Since, therefore, for this reason, that heat is the root from which the elements emerge like branches. Hence, this **Pandofilus** <note>Pandolphus is one of the "philosophers" who appears as a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum* (*The Assembly of the Philosophers*).</note> provides the example of the egg for this heat: the **point of the sun**, that is, the germ of the egg which is in the yolk, which germ is moved by the heat of the brooding hen; the chick is brought to life, always operating through the formative power, as has been said.

The Speaker said: The creatures which **Lucas** <note>Another philosopher character from the *Turba*.</note> described are only two, namely body and spirit, both of which are entirely within Mercury. It possesses both a corporeal and a spiritual substance, as seen in the first chapter of this book, "On true quicksilver," etc. Nor is it known or described except through its "piety"—that is, through the effect it produces when it is joined with bodies...

...that virtue written above, which they call **piety** <note>original: *pietatem*. In alchemical literature, "piety" often refers to the purity of the material or the devotion of the practitioner.</note>: Parmenides says: "Know that the envious have treated the waters in many ways," etc. Toward the understanding of this obscure science, that saying of Master Peter of Damascus <note>original: *Petri Damasfana*. Likely referring to a medieval authority or a specific manuscript tradition attributed to a "Damascene" author.</note> seems relevant, who treats most excellently the generation of natural and mineral bodies and spirits; for he says: "That in the generation of every elemental body, the elements are corrupted in the conjunction of that generation, and from that corruption bodies are birthed."

Behold what remains, and what corrupts, and what generates **enmity** and **friendship** <note>In alchemy, "enmity" (inimicitia) represents the reactive, volatile struggle between opposing elements, while "friendship" (amicitia) represents their final stabilization into a new compound.</note>; because the elements are corrupted and dissolved in conjunction—which signifies **enmity** in the generation of the body produced from them—yet they are brought into harmony, which signifies **friendship** between them through the process of generation.

This is because through such heat, all the muddiness of the quicksilver, the superfluous moisture of the sulfur, its thick earthiness, and its combustible, evaporable oiliness—which it possesses from the nature of sulfur—are gradually purged and refined, without disturbing or raising the aforementioned internal oiliness.

# Commentary of the Blessed Thomas Aquinas #

Once purged, the body of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurij*</note> is made incorporeal and becomes, as it were, similar to the aforementioned hidden power; and then the fire is increased slightly, so that the said power might be gathered and joined to its purged body, and thus their **indissoluble marriage** <note>original: *desponsatio*; in alchemy, this refers to the "chemical wedding" or the permanent union of the volatile spirit and the fixed body</note> takes place. 

How our **regimen** <term>regimen|the systematic method of applying heat and managing the alchemical process over time</term> can be recognized is taught below where it says: **Azaragus** <note>A figure mentioned in the *Turba Philosophorum*, often thought to be a corruption of a Greek name like Anaxagoras</note> spoke where it is stated, "stop this up," because in the **first decoction** <term>decoctio|the process of heating or "cooking" a substance to mature or refine it</term> it becomes **black**, and then it is known that the work is well-guided. In the **second decoction** it becomes **white**, and in the **third**, **red**. <note>These colors—*nigredo*, *albedo*, and *rubedo*—are the primary stages of the Alchemical Great Work.</note> And note above, where it is said: "I will repeat this for you in several other places," this can be gathered from those various sections. 

If, however, some cause its **redness** to appear prematurely by rushing the process with greater heat—which can happen to the lazy through excessive burning—the body will not be truly purged, nor reduced into an incorporeal nature. Therefore, the **hidden, fleeing spirit** <note>The volatile part of the substance that tends to evaporate when heated</note> is never mixed with the coarse body without immediately flying away in the fire. The fire did not cease to burn them, etc., because it was from **extrinsic heat** <note>External heat from a furnace or lamp</note>, namely in an artificial fire which had exceeded its limits, pushing itself into the **intrinsic heat** <note>The natural, "vital" heat residing within the matter itself</note>. 

And so, the intrinsic heat was not able to draw the moisture to itself at the root, by which it could defend the substance from the fire; and thus it did not cease to burn the spirits of the intrinsic heat. **Aristotle** treats this excellently in his book *The Meteorologica* <note>original: *Meteororum*</note>, in the chapter "Water in Potentiality," etc.—that is, concerning extrinsic heat. He forbade this—meaning a material fire in this art that is not so tempered that it would not exceed the intrinsic heat—so that the intrinsic heat might retain the moisture, since it naturally draws it with itself; and then many...

**Azaratus** <note>A philosopher cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> said: "He who wishes to attain the truth, etc. Join it to its own water and cook it again, etc." Note that above, **Socrates** <note>In alchemical texts, "Socrates" is a traditional authority figure, often distinct from the historical Greek philosopher</note> named four successive **decoctions** <term>decoctio|a period of "cooking" or heating the matter to mature it</term> to be performed; here it seems to be said that it must afterward be **vivified** <term>viuificari|to "bring to life" or re-energize the chemical matter, usually by adding "mercurial water"</term>.

This, I believe, is the final decoction, in which the body is fixed and turned into spirit.
