Let it be **cooked** <term>decoquatur|the process of "decoction" or applying steady heat to mature the substance</term> again, until all the **sulfurousness** <note>original: *sulphureitas*; in alchemy, this refers to the volatile, impure, or combustible principle that must be purged to reach the "fixed" state</note> is consumed.

And thus they are joined more conveniently—that is, they are prepared for joining, with no impediment existing. Afterward, it is imbued with **permanent water** <term>aqua permanente|a stabilized, incorruptible alchemical liquid that does not evaporate when heated</term>, meaning they are made perpetual and incorruptible to one another, all their impediments and superfluities having been removed. Thus, it will require a stronger fire to be cooked, because they are now as if **fixed** <term>fixae|the state where a substance is stable and no longer flies away or evaporates when exposed to heat</term>. By this last decoction, they are inseparably joined and are stabilized by a perfect **fixation**, and the **tincture** <term>tinctura|the transformative property of the Stone that allows it to "dye" or transmute base metals into gold</term> becomes permanent; and so I believe the work is completed.

Also, when he says: "Join it to its own water," was it not joined to its water before all those decoctions? Since it is certain that the substance itself is watery, and the "watery" is one of the three principal substances—insofar as the substance cannot be separated or plucked away without the destruction of the whole essence of the thing—how then does he command it to be joined to that which could not be disjoined from it?

It must be said, however, that he speaks very well. For its watery part is overabundant in extrinsic moisture, as is the earthy part in **muddiness** <note>original: *lutulentia*; the dregs or physical impurities that cloud the "subtle" or pure essence</note>. And although in the four aforementioned decoctions the watery part is not entirely separated from the earthy part, yet they are altered and, as it were, constricted. And so, by altering and breaking them through continuous and gentle heat, the muddiness is consumed and the overabundant moisture is evaporated. These two impurities were hindering the **subtle earth** and the **radical water** <note>the "radical" or "root" moisture is the essential life-force of the matter, which must be preserved even as external moisture is dried away</note>, so that they could not embrace each other completely. And with these two hindrances removed, there is a place for true mixing, when it is said:

### On the Shorter *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: *in Turbam Philof. breuiorem*; the *Turba Philosophorum* is one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient philosophers.</note>

...[Becau]se <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "um," likely continuing from a word like *quoniam* (because/since) on the previous page.</note> according to the philosopher, quality or substantial form <term>substantial form|In medieval philosophy, this is the essential nature that makes a thing what it is; for example, "heat" is the substantial form of fire.</term> is unchangeable, and therefore it cannot be increased—which is not surprising—it is rightly asked how fire can be "cold." For fire, by its substantial quality, is properly hot, and it cannot be diminished from that quality; therefore, fire cannot be cold. Consequently, fire cannot cause a thing to perish through "coldness," and thus what this philosopher says appears false. Furthermore, making fire **intense** seems easy. But since it can be increased much further in intensity, it is asked at what degree, or by what heat, the philosopher says it is "intense," such that it causes the matter to evaporate.

When it is seen which fire is called "cold," and at what degree or by what heat it is called "intense," the **tempered heat** necessary for this work is easily discovered. Thus it must be known that every hot thing is either in the first degree, or the second, or the third, or the fourth—which is the last—because in the fourth degree it is likened to the heat of simple fire. 

<margin>4th degree of fire</margin>For the fourth degree of heat, at the touch of hands, immediately harms the one touching it, yet it does not entirely destroy them immediately. Likewise, a small simple fire, once lit, immediately harms, but does not entirely destroy at once. Hence, the fire necessary for this work must be hot, but not intense beyond its natural degree, nor "cold"—that is, slackened—below the second degree. 

Therefore, I say that the fire must be tempered regarding the intensity of the heat and regarding the place where the **enclosed old man** <note>original: *senex inclusus*; a famous alchemical metaphor for the base matter (often sulfur or lead) being "rejuvenated" or transformed within the sealed vessel.</note> sits, so that the ashes in which this old man sits are and always remain of such [heat]...

...heat <note>original: *caloris*; this completes the sentence from the previous page discussing degrees of heat.</note>, just as a very small and very gentle natural fire has within itself—not ignited by anything external—such that those ashes do not immediately harm the hand touching them. This heat is applied specifically where the aforementioned **Old Man** sits <note>In alchemy, the "Old Man" (*senex*) is a symbolic name for the base material or the "King" who must be dissolved and rejuvenated into a "Young Boy" or "New King" (the Philosopher's Stone).</note>, and even up to the height of this Old Man, namely to the middle of the belly of the flasks <term>ampullae|Glass flasks or vials used in distillation and digestion.</term>.

And such a fire is called a **bath** <note>original: *balneum*; likely referring to the *Balneum Mariae* or water bath, which provides a gentle, even heat.</note>, in which that Old Man becomes young again, and his veins are softened, and his flesh is made tender and increased. For fire, as was said above, cannot in any way be cold in itself so that it could cause chilling, since its proper nature is to heat. But because of the distance of the place in which the thing to be heated is located, the fire cannot heat it unless they are brought closer together or the fire is increased. Therefore, when it is said that the fire should not be intense, you should say that the fire here is the heat touching the Old Man.

**Mosius** <note>Mosius is a legendary figure and speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical dialogue.</note> says: "Know that the envious <note>The "envious" (*invidi*) are the ancient masters who were said to hide their secrets from the unworthy using metaphors.</note> have hidden the way of forming the **chick**, the lead, etc." He says this is done by three companions, etc. Therefore, it is necessary that there be four, and who those four companions are must be sought; they are indeed the **colors of Mercury**, which are four:

<margin>=</margin>1. The first is a shimmering off-white, common to unprepared Mercury.
<margin>=</margin>2. The second is its **blackness**, which appears in the second decoction <term>decoction|The process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its state.</term>.
<margin>⸗</margin>3. The third is a **bright white**, which appears after the first decoction.
<margin>⸗</margin>4. The fourth is **redness**, which appears in the third decoction.

The first color performs no work. The second **vivifies**—that is, it alters and confirms the matter. The third **cleanses**—that is, it purifies and refines. And the fourth **liquefies** the subtle and meltable parts that are ready for mixing. As according to **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note>...

...the father <note>original: *trem*, completing *Patrem* from the previous page</note> of all philosophers, etc. That which is above is as that which is below. <note>This is the famous opening of the *Emerald Tablet*, the foundational text of Hermeticism, expressing the idea that the macrocosm (the universe) and the microcosm (the individual or the chemical vessel) operate under the same laws.</note> **Pythagoras** intended to show this with the greatest brevity and obscurity: that from **Mercury** alone the right work and the highest, most perfect **elixir** <term>elixir|A medicinal or alchemical substance capable of transmuting metals or prolonging life.</term> is completed, through perpetual fermentation.

Therefore, first note its utility and subtlety when he says: *That which is above is as that which is below, and vice versa.* This refers to the sublime and most noble thing—that is, the **hidden virtue** <note>original: *virtus occulta*</note> that exists within Mercury. Through this virtue, the most worthy of all works is made from a seemingly abject thing—that is, the "body" of Mercury, which is considered worthless in comparison to the end to which it can be led. 

And since within Mercury there exists both that sublime spiritual virtue and a body that has been cleansed ten times—which is also called "abject" in the book of the *Turba*—**Equistes** <note>Equistes is one of the legendary speakers in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an ancient alchemical dialogue.</note> spoke, saying: "The foundation of **quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum|Literally "living silver" or mercury.</term> is stronger and more sublime among philosophers, yet more worthless among the foolish." 

And **Parmenides** says: "Unless the nature of Mercury is turned, it achieves nothing." This means that what appears worthless in it must be refined <note>original: *subtilietur*</note> and transformed into a sublime nature. Likewise, Parmenides praises that nature thus: "O strong nature, conquering and overcoming natures, and making your own natures rejoice!" Because with this nature, Mercury becomes both body and spirit; it is clear that by right governance <note>original: *recto regimine*; refers to the careful control of heat and timing in the alchemical process.</note> the body has been purged and brought back to a sublime nature, which can indeed be achieved, as is stated throughout almost that entire book. 

Therefore, the "worthless" body is likened to that sublime virtue, because both—the worthless and the sublime—[are] in one...

**Its father is the Sun**, that is, the sealing and fixing power <note>original: *virtus sigillativa & firmativa*</note> which it receives from **Sulfur**, which acts as the paternal seed, as is stated in the book of Master **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican scholar to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note> in the chapter "Now order demands," etc.

The "wind" is the entire coarse, oily, and muddy substance of Mercury which undergoes exhalation, attrition, or consumption, and which vanishes like wind. "In its belly" refers to the intrinsic substance of Mercury itself, which is a subtle watery element mixed with a subtle earthy element. The aforementioned Brother Albert treats this watery element in the chapter "The Art, however."

**Its nurse is the Earth**, namely the subtle earthy element in which it holds its radical moisture...

### Blessed Thomas Aquinas’s Brief Commentary on the *Assembly of the Philosophers* ###

...as is found in the book *The Light of Lights* <note>original: *Lumen Luminum*; an influential alchemical text often attributed to the Persian polymath Razi (Rhazes) or to Aristotle</note>, in the chapter beginning "Now, however, concerning our discussion," and in the passages that follow. # A MOST EXCELLENT BOOK ON THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE
## Written by an ANONYMOUS Philosopher.

### THE SUMMARY OF THIS ENTIRE ART.

1. *Resolve the stone into its first matter.* <note>original: *primam materiam*; the formless, fundamental substance from which all metals originate.</note>
2. *Reduce the matter into black earth.* <note>This refers to "Nigredo," the stage of decomposition and blackening.</note>
3. *Convert the raven’s head into the swan’s head.* <note>Alchemical metaphors for the transition from the black stage of decay to the white stage of purification.</note>
4. *Animate the foliated earth with the Soul.* <note>original: *Terram foliatam Anima*; "foliated earth" refers to the purified solid matter which must be reunited with its volatile essence or "soul."</note>
5. *Tinge mercury and all imperfect bodies.* <note>original: *Tinge ☿*; to "tinge" is to transform base metals into gold or silver using the finished Stone.</note>

->In the name of the Lord, Amen.<-

Aristotle says in the 4th book of the *Metaphysics*: <note>This famous quote is actually from the *De Mineralibus*, a text often appended to Aristotle's *Meteorology* in the Middle Ages, though likely written by Avicenna.</note> "Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot be changed." This is true, as he adds, **unless they are reduced to their first matter.** However, the reduction of these metals into their first matter is easy, as will be clearly explained in the following sections. The same philosopher also says that a transition from one contrary to another does not occur except through a **medium.** <note>A middle state or substance that bridges the gap between two opposites.</note>

On one side, the extremes of our philosophical stone are the two **Luminaries** <note>The Sun and Moon, representing Gold and Silver</note>, which are the perfect bodies; but on the other side is the completed **Elixir** or **Tincture** itself. The **medium** is the philosophical **water of life** <note>original: *aqua vitæ*; here referring to a specialized alchemical solvent rather than medicinal alcohol</note>, which must be entirely purified.

# CHAPTER II.

## On the preparation of the first Water of Life.

Take of Roman Vitriol <note>original: *Vitrioli Romani*; a term for iron or copper sulfate crystals</note> and calcined Alum <note>original: *Aluminis calcinati*; alum that has been heated to drive off its water content</note>, one pound of each; and one pound of saltpeter <note>original: *salis nitri*</note>. Let these be crushed together and placed in a suitable, well-luted <note>sealed with airtight clay or paste</note> vial, and let it be placed in the distillation furnace with an alembic <note>original: *Alembico*; the "helmet" or cap of the distilling apparatus</note> placed on top, the joints being well-closed so that the spirits do not evaporate, together with its receiver. Distill the "strong water" <note>original: *aquam fortem*; this recipe produces nitric acid, a corrosive liquid used to dissolve metals</note> according to the proper manner: as you know, first with a slow fire, second with a stronger fire, and finally with the strongest fire, so that every spirit may come out and the alembic becomes white. Then cease the firing.

This water is the simple solvent of Moon <term>Moon: the alchemical name for Silver</term>. Collect 3 or 4 pounds of this water. The signs of this water are: it dissolves Moon, it separates Sun <term>Sun: the alchemical name for Gold</term> from Moon, it calcines <note>reduces to a powder through heat or corrosion</note> raw Mercury, and it stains human skin with a black color that is difficult to remove. This is the first common philosophical water; keep it carefully, because it contains within itself the first degree of perfection.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On the preparation of the third water, qualified through sublimated Mercury.

Take of the second water, for example, 1 pound, and 10 ounces of the aforementioned clear, pure, and heavy sublimated Mercury, well ground. ## CHAPTER VI.

### How all bodies are calcined and reduced into their first matter.

When you wish to convert any body into first matter through the water of life or the sharpest vinegar, then prepare the body itself in this way. Take <note>original: *℞.*, the symbol for *recipe*</note> the body of whichever metal you wish—for example, one mark of Moon <term>Moon: Silver (Luna)</term>. Have it filed, and grind the filings upon a stone with common salt, so that it may be made more subtle and pulverized. Then dissolve the salt away from it using warm water and let the pulverized lime of Moon <note>A "lime" or calx is the powder resulting from the initial breakdown of a metal.</note> settle at the bottom, and cast away the water. Next, dry it, and afterwards soak it three times with oil of tartar <term>Oil of tartar: A concentrated, caustic solution of potassium carbonate</term>, and always let the oil be dried out. 

Afterwards, place the lime into a clean glass vessel and pour oil of tartar over it so that it stands above it to the thickness of two fingers. Then close the glass and place it over a very slow heat of fire. Then, visibly, the lime itself is converted in that water of life into Mercury <term>Mercury: Quicksilver (*Merc.*)</term>. Continue the glass in a temperate heat and in the action of the water itself until the whole lime is converted into corporal Mercury. 

When this is done, carefully pour off the water and take out the corporal Mercury. Place it into an earthen vessel and purify it with water and common salt as you have seen [described previously], and dry it. Then place it in a linen cloth and squeeze it through the cloth drop by drop; if it all passes through, it is well. If, however, any part of the body remains amalgamated and not perfectly dissolved, let that part be dissolved again with the aforementioned new water without any residue remaining in the cloth. Rather, let everything most subtly penetrate the cloth in the manner of quicksilver, which is then corporal Mercury—not the common kind, but philo-

He is suggesting that the "philosophical" versions of the precious metals are actually derived from base metals.</note>

From this alone is said to come all the power of the art of Alchemy, and in its own way the white and red tincture <note>A "tincture" refers to the Elixir's power to change the color and nature of base metals into silver (white) or gold (red).</note> itself. Therefore Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose works emphasized systematic experimentation.</note>, the Master of masters, says: "Our art is not perfected in a multiplicity of things." For it is one thing, one stone, and one medicine, in which consists the whole mastery, to which we add no foreign thing, except that which we separate as superfluous during its preparation. For in it and through it are all things necessary to this art; we add no other foreign thing to it besides gold and silver, which are not foreign to the Stone itself if they are added during its fermentation, because they are the two helpers through which the Alchemical work is completed. 

And another philosopher says: "There is a certain one thing, for the sake of which many have perished." And the philosopher Diomedes <note>Likely a reference to a pseudo-epigraphical alchemical author or a corrupted reference to a classical authority.</note> says: "Work with a venerable nature, because it is not improved except in its own nature; do not introduce anything foreign to it—neither powder, nor any other foreign thing, nor any water—because diverse things do not improve our Stone." 

And thus it is briefly evident to the observer that the tincture of the philosophical stone is not extracted except from the Mercury of the wise, setting aside all other useless things, such as salts, alums, and strong waters <term>Strong waters: Corrosive mineral acids, such as nitric acid (aqua fortis), used to dissolve metals.</term>. This aforementioned Mercury is the philosophical root, a tall tree from which infinite branches multiply, and it is called the "known stone" in the chapters of the philosophers' books. The first operation pertaining to the perfection of this stone, which at other times is called the Elixir, is called sublimation <term>Sublimation: In a common sense, the transition of a substance from solid to gas; in alchemy, it often refers to the purification of a substance by vaporizing it and letting it collect again as a solid.</term>. How the Mercury of the philosophers ought to be made will be revealed in what follows without any concealment. But note that this sublimation is not the common kind, but philosophical, because sublimation...

Our [sublimation] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of chemical operations.</note> is nothing other than subtilization <note>Subtilization refers to the process of making a substance more "subtle"—finer, purer, and more spiritual—through heat.</note>, because in the sublimation of this stone, the superfluities are removed.
Sublimation of the philosophical Mercury is its subtilization, which differs from the sublimation of common mineral Mercury <note>Common or "vulgar" mercury refers to the liquid metal found in nature; philosophical mercury is the purified, spiritualized essence prepared by the alchemist.</note>.
The Mercury of the philosophers is the primary matter of metals, but in this matter there are two substantial parts: sulfur and quicksilver <gloss>argentum vivum</gloss>. Sulfur is fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means a substance can withstand fire without evaporating, while "volatile" means it flies away or turns to smoke when heated.</note>, and quicksilver is volatile; yet quicksilver is also converted into sulfur, which then desires other quicksilver—at that point, multiplication <note>Multiplication is the stage where the power or quantity of the alchemical medicine is increased.</note> occurs. The sublimation of the philosophers, however, is the [elevation] of non-fixed parts and their rising away from the fixed parts, because the subtle non-fixed parts are raised through smoke, while the fixed parts remain below, until finally in the work the non-fixed are also fixed together, so that they are never separated from one another.
And you should know that whoever correctly sublimates our philosophical Mercury—in which the power of our stone resides—attains the whole mastery, as Geber <note>Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) was a foundational authority in alchemy; his "Summa Perfectionis" emphasized that all metal-making operations are essentially forms of sublimation.</note> says. The entire perfection of this art consists solely in sublimation, in the vessel, and in great governance <note>original: "regimine." This refers to the "regimen of fire," or the careful control of the furnace's heat over time.</note>, because in that process all these stages consist: namely sublimation, distillation, ascension, descension, coagulation, putrefaction, calcination, fixation, immersion, the white tincture, and the red <note>The "white tincture" transforms metals into silver; the "red tincture" transforms them into gold.</note>—varied in one vessel—until its final completion and bonding <gloss>glutinationem</gloss>, regarding which the philosophers have handed down many chapters, so that the science might be made obscure to understand, and so that the foolish

# CHAPTER IX.

## On Sublimation.

<margin>Process <note>original: "P.", likely an abbreviation for *Praxis* (Practice) or *Processus* (Process).</note></margin>
*℞. <note>The traditional symbol for "Recipe" or "Take."</note> Take the aforementioned venerable Mercury, the primary water of the philosophers, which is called the first matter of the perfect body, in whatever quantity you wish. Place it into its small vessel <note>original: "alueolum"</note>, which must be clean, clear, bright, and round. Its opening should be well obstructed with the seal of Hermes <note>A "seal of Hermes" or hermetic seal refers to sealing a glass vessel by melting the neck shut, though here the author suggests it should still be able to "breathe" slightly.</note>, as you know, so that it may be able to breathe in some way. Place it into putrefaction <note>Putrefaction is the process of breaking down a substance through gentle heat, often associated with the color black.</note> to be stifled in its well-layered bed, which is tempered and warm, for a philosophical month—that is, in dung <note>original: "fimo". Decomposing horse manure was used as a natural, steady heat source for alchemical incubations.</note>. Keep it there for forty continuous days in a warm state, maintaining it in the sublimation of its own sweat, until it no longer sweats by way of ascent and descent <note>This refers to the internal circulation where vapors rise, condense, and drip back down.</note>. This continues until the matter itself begins to rot from within and coagulate by the power of the sustaining fire, and thus becomes fixed, so that it no longer ascends as a smoky, airy substance. Instead, it remains at the bottom, dry and exhausted of its moisture, putrefied and coagulated, converted into black earth. This is the black raven’s head <note>original: "caput corui nigrum". This is the famous *Nigredo* stage, symbolizing the death of the old form before rebirth.</note>, and it is called the dry and earthy element. When the sublimation of the philosophers is truly completed and dispatched, all the aforementioned modes are prepared—such as sublimation, calcination, distillation, coagulation, putrefaction, and fixation—all within one vessel and one furnace (that is, the horse dung), as has been said. For when our stone is in its vessel and rises as smoke to the head of the vessel, it is called sublimation and ascent; but when, on the contrary, it rushes from the heights to the depths and descends to the bottom, it is then called distillation and descent. But when the stone begins to rot, and through such manifold descent and ascent begins to coagulate, then it is said to be, and is caused by, putrefaction and coagulation,*

...so that it may finally be calcined <note>Calcination is the process of reducing a substance to a dry powder through prolonged heating.</note> and fixed <note>Fixation is the process where a volatile or "spirituous" substance is made stable and resistant to heat, so it no longer evaporates.</note> by the depletion of the moisture of the radical water <note>original: "aquae radicalis." Radical water refers to the essential, fundamental moisture inherent in matter that allows it to live or transform.</note>. Then calcination and fixation are said to be caused in one single act by boiling them together all at once in one vessel and in one furnace, as was said before.

In this sublimation, the separation of the elements is also achieved, as the philosophers say. The operation of our Stone is nothing other than the separation of the elements and their subsequent conjunction. For in our sublimation, the earthy element—which was dry and hot—is made watery, moist, and cold. From this, it is clear that the separation of the four elements in our Stone is not a common separation <note>The author distinguishes between chemical separation (like distilling water) and "philosophical" separation, which is a spiritual and physical transformation of the matter's inner nature.</note>, but a philosophical one. Because in our aforementioned philosophical sublimation, the elements are separated. In our Stone, there are only two formal elements: earth and water. The earth virtually contains fire within itself by reason of its moisture <note>original: "humiditatis." This is a paradoxical statement in alchemical theory; usually, fire is associated with dryness. The author suggests that the transformative heat (fire) is hidden within the essential moisture of the earth.</note>. And here it is clear that in that Stone of ours, there are only two elements formally, although four are present virtually. 

Therefore, the Philosopher says: "The separation of the elements in our Stone is not as the unlearned <note>original: "idiotae," referring to those without philosophical or alchemical training.</note> understand it, but in our Nature there is a certain secret, hidden thing whose work and power are felt, and these are earth and water." The other two elements are air and fire, which are neither touched nor seen, nor do they bestow anything visible, nor is their location seen, nor is their power known, except through the prior elements of earth and water. This is because fire, in the boiling <note>original: "decoctione"</note> of them, changes the colors into white or red.

Now you have the second element in the philosophical stone: the black earth, the raven’s head <note>original: "caput corvi." A standard alchemical term for the *Nigredo* or black stage, signifying the "death" or putrefaction of the matter before it is reborn.</note>, the mother, the heart, and the root. Upon this earth, as upon a foundation-post <note>original: "stipitem"</note>, all other things are established. This dry, earthy element is called by many names in the books of the philosophers. It is called...

...for it is called Laton <note>original: "Laton." A term for impure or unrefined metal, often used to describe the matter of the Stone in its initial state of impurity.</note>, Treasure, black dregs, our brass, and black sulfur. It is called both male and female, and it has an infinite number of other names; yet however much these names may differ, they are always understood to refer to one and the same thing. Thus, through the deprivation of moisture caused during the philosophers' sublimation, the volatile is made fixed, the soft becomes hard, and the watery becomes earthy. According to Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century scholar and "Father of Chemistry."</note>, this is a "change from nature into nature," such as the nature of water into fire, and air into earth, as the philosophers say in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba." Likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note>. Likewise, a change of "complexions" has occurred—from cold and moist into hot and dry—according to the Physicians. Furthermore, the spiritual has become corporeal, according to Aristotle. Likewise, the liquid has become thick, according to Alphidius <note>Alphidius was a semi-legendary Arab alchemist frequently cited in medieval texts.</note>. Furthermore, the manifest has become occult <note>In alchemy, "manifest" refers to the outward, physical appearance, while "occult" refers to the hidden, inner spiritual essence or power.</note>, according to Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note>. And thus the meaning of the philosophers' words is clear when they say: "The operation of our Stone is nothing other than the change of natures and the rotation of the elements." For through this incorporation of moisture, we make the moist dry, the volatile fixed, the watery fiery, and the airy earthy; and here we truly change natures and rotate all four elements.

# CHAPTER XI.
## On the fermentation of the white foliated earth.

Next, one must proceed to the fermentation of the whitened earth <note>original: "terrae," referring here to the purified solid matter remaining after distillation</note>, so that the dead body may be animated and live again, and its power may be multiplied even unto infinity, and the Elixir itself or the tincture may be perfected, and the desired white substance may be produced, dyeing Mercury and every other body into the truest Silver <note>original: "Lunam" — literally "the Moon," the alchemical name for silver.</note>. 

But note: The ferment cannot enter the dead body except by the mediation of the "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ" — in this context, a specialized alchemical solvent or distilled spirit, not necessarily alcohol</note>, which brings about the marriage and coupling between the ferment and the white earth. Likewise, in all our fermenting, the weight of each ingredient must be carefully observed.

# CHAPTER XII.
## On the fermentation of the foliated earth.

If, therefore, you wish to ferment the white foliated earth <note>original: "terram foliatam" — a term for the purified, flaky, or layered substance achieved through repeated sublimations</note> into the white Elixir, so that it may reach the completion of the tincture for bodies diminished from perfection <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper were considered "diminished" or "sick" versions of the perfect metals (gold and silver).</note>: 

Then take <note>original: "℞" — the recipe symbol for *recipe*</note> three ounces <note>original: "℥" — the symbol for *uncia*</note> of the whitened foliated earth or "dead body," and of the reserved water of life take two parts to one and a half parts of the ferment.

Furthermore, prepare the ferment so that it is a very subtle white powder <term>calx: the crumbly, ash-like substance left after a metal or mineral has been burned or "calcined" to remove its moisture</term> if the work proceeds toward the white stage. If indeed it proceeds toward the red stage, then let it be the most yellow-colored powder <note>original: "citrinissima" — an intense lemon-yellow color indicating the transition from the white stage to the final red stage of the Great Work.</note> of prepared gold; for there shall be no other ferment for silver than silver, and no other for gold than gold. 

The reason for this is that these two bodies are luminous by nature. Those two perfect bodies have within them a "good sulfur" in which reside splendid, dyeing rays that act upon other bodies with a natural redness and whiteness.

# CHAPTER XI.

## On the fermentation of the white foliated earth.

Next, one must proceed to the fermentation of the whitened earth, so that the dead body <note>In alchemy, the "dead body" or "corps mortuum" refers to the solid, inert remains of the matter after its "soul" or volatile components have been removed through heating.</note> may be animated and live again, and its power might be multiplied even unto infinity, and the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Elixir" or "Tincture" is the perfected substance capable of transmuting base metals into noble ones.</note> or tincture itself may be perfected, as well as the desired white substance which tinges <term>Mercury</term> and every body into the truest <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunam" — the alchemical name for silver.</note>. But note: the ferment cannot enter the dead body except through the mediation of the water of life, which brings about the marriage and coupling between the ferment and the white earth. Likewise, in all our fermentation, the weight of each part must be strictly observed.

# CHAPTER XII.

## On the fermentation of the foliated earth.

If, therefore, you wish to ferment the white foliated earth into the white <term>Elixir</term> so that it achieves the fullness of a tincture for "bodies diminished from perfection" <note>A common alchemical phrase for base metals like lead or tin, which were viewed as "diseased" or incomplete versions of gold and silver.</note>: Then take three parts of the whitened foliated earth (or the dead body) and two parts of the reserved water of life to one part of the medium ferment.

Prepare the ferment, moreover, so that it is a very subtle white lime <note>original: "calx" — a powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures until it oxidizes or crumbles.</note>, if you are proceeding to the white work. If, however, you are proceeding to the red work, then use the most lemon-yellow lime of prepared gold; for there shall be no other ferment for silver than silver, and no other for gold than gold. The reason is that these two bodies are by nature luminous. Those two perfected bodies contain within themselves a good <term>sulfur</term> <note>In this context, "sulfur" refers to the active, masculine, and coloring principle within a metal, not the common chemical element.</note> in which are splendid rays that tinge other bodies with natural redness or whiteness.

Accordingly, all philosophers say: our stone is composed of three things, namely of a **body**, a **spirit**, and a **soul** which provides the path by means of the **water of life**, which is called the spirit.

The draft of water it has drunk will be dried up in its bowels. Repeat this time after time, many times over, until through these steps you have prepared the most excellent **white stone**. *...turns of solution and coagulation, of grinding and roasting; and by this exuberance of coagulation, the goodness of the medicine is multiplied more and more.* <note>The "Medicine" is a common alchemical term for the Philosopher's Stone, viewed as a substance that "heals" base metals into gold.</note>

*For example, if one part of that medicine first converts one hundred of any body into the **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam" — silver</note>; in the second reiteration it turns 1,000 parts; in the third, 10,000; in the fourth, 100,000; in the fifth, 1,000,000; and so on unto infinity.*
*Wherefore the Philosopher says that the wise praise the multiple reiteration of the work; because the more it is multiplied, the more it grows in quantity and power, and indeed with each turn it is improved by a tenfold power.*
*And this is the very thing that the cohort of philosophers so greatly wished to emphasize regarding the work of multiplication—namely in form and matter—which both always tend to walk with equal pace in our mastery, until they increase unto infinity, tinting and transforming every metallic body into the true **Sun-making** <note>original: "Solificum" — gold-making</note> and **Moon-making** <note>original: "Lunificum" — silver-making</note> substance, without any deceit or falsehood. ### Of the Philosophers’ Stone

...and you place it thus into its furnace of digestion, let it be converted into a most deep-red stone, which among the philosophers is called "blood," "purple gold," "the red," "coral," and "red sulfur." When this color is seen, let it shine forth as a red so bright that it appears like dry, burnt saffron <note>original: "croceus" - This refers to the vivid orange-red of the highest quality saffron, a common comparison for the final state of the Stone.</note>; then take out that "king" with joy, and diligently keep him aside. 

And if you wish it to become the tincture of the highest Elixir of redness—transforming, fixing, and tinting **Mercury**, **the Moon** <note>original: "Luna" — silver</note>, and every metallic body—then ferment three parts of it with one and a half parts of the purest prepared gold. Solis" — the spiritual or liquid essence extracted from gold</note> extracted artificially.

Place it back under the vessel with a suitable fire so that it may be digested until the final completion, and so that the stone may shine forth as a most deep-red bloodstone. 

You shall increase it again with its own "Sun-making" part—that is, the Mercury extracted from the Sun—which was set aside, so that you may proceed step by step in the manner of a stronger digestion in the increase of its perfection. You may increase its quality to a higher level by repeating the work and adding from its own part unto infinity. And thus you possess the treasure of the entire universe, sought indeed by many, but discovered by very few. 

This stone of ours in its first generation is watery; afterwards it is coagulated and becomes most black <note>The "Nigredo" or black stage, representing the death of the old form.</note>; then white <note>The "Albedo" or white stage, representing purification.</note>; and finally red. For heat acting upon the moist first produces blackness, but acting upon the dry, it produces whiteness, and finally redness. For white is nothing other than the washing away of black, and from much white collected and digested by a stronger fire, a yellow-gold color <term>citrinitas|The "yellowing" stage that bridges the gap between the white and red works.</term> is generated.

# THE VISION OF JOHN
## D A S T I N

SINCE the generation and growth of all things existing in nature is a certain effect, we take the necessary indication of the Planets from their very root. Therefore, seeking the origin of the Sun <term>Sol|In alchemy, the Sun represents gold, the most perfect metal.</term> and the Moon <term>Luna|The Moon represents silver.</term> with great desire, we saw such a vision. We thought ourselves snatched before the sight of the Ancient of Days <note>original: "antiqui dierum" — a biblical reference to God from the Book of Daniel, here representing the primordial source of all things.</note>. And behold, seven Planets coming forward, with Nature herself prevailing, they appointed their firstborn brother as king, and marked him with the diadem of the kingdom. It was as if, while adoring him, they were revealing their defects to him; for almost all of them were infected with either leprosy or mange <note>In alchemical allegory, "leprosy" and "mange" represent the impurities and corruptions found in base metals like lead or copper, which prevent them from being gold.</note>.

The King, however, wishing to comfort his brothers, said: "It is certainly expedient that one of us die without blemish for the people, so that the whole nation does not perish <note>original: "Expedit certe vt vnus ex nobis sine macula moriatur pro populo..." — Dastin here adapts the words of Caiaphas from the Gospel of John 11:50, framing the alchemical process as a redemptive sacrifice.</note>, so that anointed with his fresh blood, you may obtain health." For, as Plato says, forms are given according to the merit of the matter. 

But the other Planets, hearing their king, said: "And which of us lacks blemish? For we were conceived in iniquity, and in sins did our mother bear us <note>original: "in iniquitate concepti sumus..." — a quote from Psalm 51:5, emphasizing the inherent "imperfection" of base metals compared to gold.</note>. Who, therefore, can make a clean thing from a seed conceived as unclean? For that which is not in a thing cannot be found in it."

### Vision

...[lest he] should possess her once she was exhausted, it appeared by what means she might revive the dead man. And since she had learned diligently from <term>natural science</term> <note>original: "scientia naturali" — the study of the laws governing the elements and their transformations.</note> that nothing could be revived without many alterations, first, lest the dead body infect the air, she burned it to ash. Having magnificently celebrated the royal funeral rites, she gladly buried the burnt ash within herself.

But the jealousy of the ancient serpent, envying such love, vomited out poison little by little; never ceasing from his haste, he labored to destroy and betray the woman's work. This, however, happened at the first light of *October*. 

The woman, in a motherly fashion, diligently gathered her husband back into her innermost womb <note>original: "visceribus" — literally 'entrails' or 'innards,' here signifying the internal vessel or the "matrix" where the chemical reaction occurs.</note> so that he would not be harmed further, wishing to repel the poison. And the more the offspring was infested by the serpent's toxin, the more he was hidden away, admitted into the motherly womb, lest he suffer a miscarriage from excessive heat. But the woman, exhausted by the labor, the conflict, and the weight, became most foul; her face was blackened <note>This "blackened face" refers to the *Nigredo* stage, the first official phase of the Great Work, characterized by putrefaction and the darkness of the "materia prima."</note>, and her whole body was prostrated upon the earth; she could neither lift her eyes nor stretch out her hands because of her weakness. # John Dastin

...nor did he find it: returning therefore to the little nest from which he had departed, and finding no rest which he sought, again and again many times with wings spread he flew upward, but since the exit was barred <note>This "barred exit" refers to the sealed alchemical vessel (the Hermetic seal), which prevents the volatile spirits from escaping during distillation.</note>, he was forced to turn back. And while he strove to fly in this manner, our begotten son <note>term: "our begotten son" <gloss>the nascent Philosophers' Stone or the evolving metallic matter.</gloss></note> devoured three virgins, so that with their wings plucked, they were entirely deprived of flight along with him. Seeing this more cautiously, the six other virgins were greatly afraid, seeking the air with a moderate course. He himself, drying himself in the sun, was turned from a black to a white color. These things were done on the day before the <term>Calends of March</term> <note>February 28th or 29th. Alchemical texts often use specific dates to align with astrological timing or symbolic seasonal cycles of rebirth.</note>. 

Therefore, when the Serpent <note>The Serpent often represents the corrosive "acid" or the "raw mercury" that must be tamed, or the impurities being purged by fire.</note> had learned of these things, filled with excessive fury, he incinerated the King with a stronger heat. But he [the King], drinking more and more water from the <term>fountains of the savior</term> <note>original: "fontibus saluatoris" — a biblical allusion used here to describe the life-giving mercurial solvent used to "wash" the charred matter.</note>, devoured the six virgins one after another, always coagulating himself with them at the fire as he had done with the others; within the space of another 40 days <note>The period of "40 days" is a common alchemical trope mirroring the biblical duration of the Great Flood or Lent, signifying a complete cycle of purification.</note>, he was entirely turned into earth, and then after another 40 days, persisting continually in an equal heat, he finally put on a most white garment. 

However, he changed his faces many times, sending forth an appearance sometimes black and dark, sometimes red and saffron, sometimes lemon-yellow and white, so that I might say with Horace:

->>With what knot shall I hold Proteus as he changes his faces?<- 
<note>original: "Quo teneam nodo mutantem Prothea vultus?" — Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.90. Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape, a perfect metaphor for the unstable states of matter in the crucible.</note>
->What he sought has perished; he seeks again what he recently let go,<-
->He pulls down, he builds up, he changes square things for round.<-
<note>original: "Quod petijt perijt, repetit quod nuper omisit, Diruit, ædificat, mutat quadrata rotundis." — Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.98-100.</note>

Because the thing whose head is red, whose feet are white, and whose eyes are black, is the entirety of the <term>mastery</term> <gloss>original: "magisterium" — the completion of the alchemical Great Work or the Philosophers' Stone itself.</gloss> <note>These colors—red, white, and black—correspond to the three primary stages of alchemy: Rubedo (redness), Albedo (whiteness), and Nigredo (blackness).</note> Since, therefore, it persisted in pure whiteness, we knew that it required marriage to its sister, the <term>Moon</term> <gloss>Luna, representing the metallic principle of silver or the "feminine" cooling aspect of the work.</gloss>; marrying him with her, therefore, we made a <term>projection</term> <gloss>the act of casting a small amount of the Philosophers' Stone onto base metals to transmute them.</gloss> upon other bodies, and behold, one part of it turned a thousand thousand <note>original: "mille millia" — literally a million; a common alchemical way of describing the infinite transmutative power of the Stone.</note> "fathers" of other <term>Planets</term> <gloss>In alchemy, the seven "planets" refer to the seven metals: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Mercury (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</gloss> into the truest silver. 

Therefore, when the <term>Serpent</term> <gloss>often representing the volatile, corrosive, or "poisonous" raw materials that must be tamed.</gloss> perceived that it was being crushed, touched by an internal heartache with all its might, it labored to destroy the King clothed in white, so that he who had previously been neglected might, even if late, at last provide for himself. But the King, strengthened in his bones and resisting bravely, trampled the serpent more and more. And at last, after some time, with the serpent killed, he feared no one’s poison from then on. 

In truth, from the anger, the movement, and the duel, having been heated excessively, he was turned from a white to a blood-red color. And thus, resuming his empire, he triumphed over all, and left no fault unpunished. Therefore, when we projected the royal purple-clad <term>Sun</term> <gloss>Sol, representing the "Red Stone" or the "masculine" principle of Gold.</gloss>, coupling him with the Sun upon other bodies, behold: one part of it changed a thousand thousand others into the truest gold. # THE BOOK OF THE MOST
## WISE KING SOLOMON
### CONCERNING THE MINERAL STONE, WHICH
#### they call the Stone of the Philosophers.

->In the name of the Lord, Amen.<-

*John Damascene <note>A famous Syrian monk and scholar, here credited—likely pseudepigraphically—with translating the text. Medieval alchemists often attributed their works to great historical or religious figures to lend them authority.</note>, an Athenian Theologian, investigating the natures of things like another Solomon, considering more deeply from the highest hinge of heaven down to the center of the earth, translated this treatise of Solomon from Arabic into Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldæum"; likely referring to Aramaic or Syriac</note>, and later into the Greek language. He first performed what he taught, declaring that he found the truth and immense benefits; follow him with a studious mind. Later, this treatise was translated from Greek into Latin by Giles, Archdeacon of the Magnificent Pontiff, who directed it to the Lord Pope Gregory IX <note>Pope from 1227 to 1241; his mention suggests the text claims a 13th-century origin in the West.</note>, by whose Chamberlain it was delivered in confidence to Theodoric the German, his nephew.*

*And because the lesser stone <note>The "lesser stone" often refers to a preliminary or specific mineral stage of the Great Work, as opposed to the final "Greater Stone" or Elixir.</note> has many branches and leaves, the wise man treats the stone in various ways, showing that it can do much in nature. He teaches how to make the stone from minerals, both body and spirit, because—as Solomon himself agreed—all natural metallic bodies consist of Mercury and Sulfur <note>The "Mercury-Sulfur theory" was the standard medieval explanation for the composition of metals: Mercury provided the metallic, fluid nature, while Sulfur provided the color, hardness, and combustibility.</note>; and he says that the Mercury and Sulfur of those bodies which are fixed <note>original: "fixa" — meaning substances that do not evaporate or change when exposed to high heat.</note> are more suitable for the work and more secure, because they fix others that are not fixed.*

### On the Mineral Stone.

...it commands others, rules over all, finds no equal, frees the body from want and the soul from impiety, and opens the excellent door of happiness. Therefore, do not hesitate, my son, to approach the peaks of our art like certain delirious poets <note>The author uses "poets" here as a derogatory term for those who speak without practical knowledge or experimental proof.</note> who doubt the experiments of nature and the natures of things, saying that the forms of things cannot be produced by art, and that locations and times are the sole principles of generation; and that it is not possible for the species of things to be altered one into another.

My son, these ideas are veiled in the mind by a dizziness of fantasies; because the mind of a prudent man acquiesces more to experiments than to the aforementioned fantasies. Does Art labor in vain? Does it not produce that which is possible? Again, what Art performs, reason does not diminish, but nature is only the intellect of reason <note>This suggests that human reason and "Art" (alchemy) are the tools through which nature's inherent logic is understood and applied.</note>. Again, glass and cultivated shrubs are produced by Art, and from a duck, a frog is created by Art <note>This refers to the medieval belief in "spontaneous generation" or "equivocal generation," where one life form was thought to arise from the decay or transformation of another.</note>. Is not the egg of a hen transformed under the hen, and similarly, is not a chick generated under warm dung? <note>Alchemists frequently used the heat of decomposing horse dung (*venter equinus*) to provide a steady, gentle warmth for their experiments, mimicking the incubation of an egg.</note> Again, the seed of the silk moth, carried under a woman's breasts for the space of twenty days, is converted into a worm; but Art performs this in a short time. Likewise, seeds cast upon heated dung and watered with certain waters germinate and bloom in the space of one hour—something nature would not do in two months. Art assists nature very much, as no one doubts.

Likewise, we do not say in our Art that the essences of forms, which reach the final degree of nature's perfection, are mixed into one another <note>The author is clarifying that they are not creating entirely new, unnatural species, but rather working within the potential of nature.</note>; but we propose only to help the defect of nature, and to relieve what has been produced by the ministry of medicine. Since that in which nature errs, Art corrects and amends.

### On the Mineral Stone.

It commands others, rules over all, and finds no equal; it delivers the body from poverty and the soul from impiety, and it opens an excellent gateway to happiness. Therefore, my son, do not hesitate to approach the summits of our art, unlike certain half-mad poets who doubt the experiments of nature and the very natures of things. They claim that the forms of things cannot be produced by art, that specific places and times are the only principles of generation, and that it is impossible for the species of things to be changed into one another.

My son, these ideas are merely veiled in a whirlwind of fantasies within the soul; for the mind of a prudent man rests more upon experiments than upon the aforementioned fantasies. Does art labor in vain? Does it not produce what is possible? Likewise, we do not say in our art that the essences of forms which reach the final degree of nature’s perfection are mingled into one another, but we only propose to assist nature’s defects and to restore what has been produced through the ministry of medicine. <note>The author is clarifying that alchemy does not "break" the laws of nature by mixing incompatible essences, but rather acts as a "physician" to matter, curing its "diseases" (impurities) to help it reach its perfect state (gold).</note> For that in which nature errs, art corrects and amends;

### On the Mineral Stone.

It commands others, rules over all, and finds no equal; it frees the body from poverty, the soul from impiety, and opens an extraordinary door to happiness. Therefore, my son, do not hesitate to reach the heights of our art <note>The "Art" (Ars) is the standard term for alchemy, the practice of transforming and perfecting matter.</note>, unlike certain delirious poets who doubt the experiments of nature and the very natures of things. They claim that the forms of things cannot be produced by art, that specific places and times are the only principles of generation <note>original: "generationis principia"; the fundamental rules by which life or substances are born.</note>, and that it is impossible for the species of things to be altered into one another.

Son, these ideas are veiled in the mind by a whirlwind of phantoms; for the mind of a wise person rests more on experiments than on the aforementioned phantoms. Does Art work in vain? Does it not produce what is possible? Furthermore, reason does not diminish what Art achieves, but rather nature is the very intellect of reason. Consider this: glass and shrubs are produced by art, and even a frog can be created from a duck by art <note>The author likely refers to the historical belief in "spontaneous generation," where one species was thought to arise from the decay or transformation of another under specific conditions.</note>. Does not a hen’s egg transform under a hen, and is not a chick similarly generated under warm dung? <note>Alchemists frequently used "horse dung" (fimus) in their laboratories as a source of gentle, consistent heat for incubation, mimicking the warmth of a nesting bird.</note> Again, if the seed of the silk-butterfly <term>silk-butterfly: a silkworm (Bombyx mori)</term> is carried beneath a woman’s breasts, it is converted into a worm in the space of twenty days; yet Art can achieve these things in a short time. Likewise, seeds cast upon heated dung and watered with certain waters will germinate and flower in the span of a single hour—something nature could not do in two months. It is beyond doubt to anyone that Art assists nature immensely.

Likewise, we do not claim in our art that the essences of forms which have already reached nature’s highest degree of perfection are mixed into one another. Instead, we propose only to aid nature where she is lacking, and to restore what has been produced through the service of medicine <note>original: "medicinae ministerio"; alchemists often described their work as "curing" base metals of their "sickness" (impurities) to reach the "health" of gold.</note>. For that in which nature errs, Art corrects and mends;

# The Book of King Solomon

*And where nature fails, art assists and helps. For nature always intends perfection, and yet, when external aid ceases, it rests and proceeds no further; therefore, it produces what is imperfect. Art regards this weakness and removes it through its own ingenuity. Do not metallic mineral bodies have a composition of a single essence? Therefore, the property of nature—producing like from like—prohibits them from being altered or changed into one another. Art always imitates nature and follows in its footsteps. Is not clay made from moisture and earth, and are not diverse vessels prepared by the potter’s art? What prevents one thing from being made into another from the first, if the prior forms are destroyed? For when Gold or Silver <note>original: "Sol vel Luna"; literally "the Sun or the Moon," the standard alchemical symbols for gold and silver.</note> is produced by our art, no new essence is generated; nature gives the being of the former, but art reveals the light hidden within them. It has deleted and taken away what weakness brought, and revealed the buried light, making it known as it shines with brilliance. Therefore, let the talkative sophist cease his speech, and let the delirious poet be silent, those who deny with a blind phantom what experiments demonstrate. Do not, however, think—as some have wrongly believed—that our blessed stone <note>The "Blessed Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> in its production holds the pattern of the nature of the generation of the macrocosm <note>original: "magni orbis"; the "Great World" or the entire universe.</note>; it is otherwise. For that was a miracle, while this art is a mystery; that was to create, but this is to act through the altering arrangements of time in all its preparation. There, the whole was made from nothing; here, indeed, nothing is produced anew, but the principle already produced is altered by art. Therefore, you should follow its footsteps. But in all things present yourself so that you follow the pattern of the generation of the microcosm <note>original: "minoris orbis"; the "Lesser World," referring to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>, namely man: since in him are all things, and in him is the whole, made in the image of the brightness of God. Hence, just as he is produced by the union of male and female, so it is permitted to work from these two works in our stone, and not otherwise.*

## Subsequently, he touches upon and shows the conditions of the woman and her properties.

*This woman, the mother of the stone, is menstruating <note>original: "menstruata"; in alchemy, this refers to the "menstrual blood" or the raw, corrosive "mercurial" state of the initial matter that must be purified.</note>, having within herself softness, whiteness, blackness, and redness; and when you lift her womb, you will see these four things. ### Here he teaches the method of incineration.

# The Book of King Solomon

But because every perfect natural alteration <term>alteratio naturalis</term> <note>The process by which one substance is transformed into another by changing its essential qualities.</note> must be done through the smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; this refers to the alchemical theory that reactions only occur when substances are broken down into their most minute, atomic-like components.</note> so that it may penetrate to the innermost core, Son, observe the means by which you join moisture to moisture. For then a mixing of the parts will occur, which certainly would not happen in a solid mass because of the coarseness and imperfection (or rather, the lack of dispersion) of the parts. Therefore, it is beneficial for subtle things to be mixed with subtle things and to be warmed and nurtured together for some time, just as Lady Nature—who is the model of our art—does herself. 

Therefore, join the water to the wine: then let them stand together for fifteen days and nights in a water bath <term>B.</term> <note>original: "B."; an abbreviation for "Balneum Mariae" or Mary’s Bath, a vessel of warm water used to provide gentle, even heat.</note>, since in the tincture, they are strengthened when they are united by an unbreakable bond of love. Again, let them be placed in the vessel <note>original: "L."; likely referring to a *lagena* (flask) or *lebes* (cauldron).</note> and let it be warmed in the water bath for six days; pass it through a linen cloth three times, and let it be separated once more. Afterward, let it be purged through the linen; and thus the male seed <term>semen masculi</term> will be prepared for generating, being strong and powerful enough to impregnate the female. 

For just as the female and the male, if they remain by themselves, cannot produce fruit, it is for this reason that it is necessary for the masculine and feminine to be mixed in carnal union <term>carnali copula</term> <note>The author uses the metaphor of sexual reproduction to describe the chemical bonding of active (male) and passive (female) substances.</note>; otherwise, you are merely "plowing the shore" <note>original: "littus aras"; a classical idiom meaning to engage in a continuous but utterly fruitness labor.</note> in this art. Therefore, you shall join the seminal humors and allow them to range together in the water bath for the space of forty days. For there you will see embraces, there you will see kisses, there the playful games of the natures, because nature rejoices in nature <note>A famous alchemical axiom: "Nature rejoices in nature, nature conquers nature, nature rules over nature."</note> and feels the comforts of delight. Just as during that span of time a hen's egg is nurtured by the heat of the mother before it attains the effect of a perfect birth. 

Finally, you shall purify it with linens; after this, using an alembic set over a slow fire, dissolve the "mother" <note>The "mother" refers to the base matter or the "female" principle that has been exhausted or transformed.</note> with what was lost. ### On the Mineral Stone

Here he touches upon four virtues which Saturn <note>In alchemy, Saturn is the traditional name for Lead.</note> receives against the four vices <note>In this context, "vices" refers to chemical defects or impurities in the base metal.</note> which it previously held, when he says: "Because there, beauty and appearance will be acquired," which follow:

*Because Saturn is the "menses" of nature, for the reason that gold ought to be made from it. Truly, because the mixed seeds are converted in the womb <term>matrix</term> <note>The alchemical vessel is often called a "womb" or "matrix" because the Stone is "born" inside it.</note>, they are coagulated into flesh and blood and reach the final degree of their perfection there, by the meeting of a triple heat. You shall hide the vessels in spherical chambers having two compartments, with the middle mouth stopped up so that it cannot breathe, nor can the heat be raised too high. For there, appearance and beauty are acquired, the body is organized, a colored substance is produced, and it is perfectly fixed <term>fixatur</term> <note>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable in fire.</note>, and the superfluous is dried away.*

### The Work upon the Moon follows.

# On the Mineral Stone #

Following this, he makes mention of Jupiter <note>In the alchemical tradition, Jupiter is the planetary name for the metal Tin.</note>, whom he calls the "leprous man" <note>original: "virum leprosum." Tin was often described as "leprous" because of its dull surface and the "cry" or crackling sound it makes when bent, which alchemists interpreted as a sign of internal impurity or "sickness" compared to the "healthy" metal, Silver.</note>.

Five horns are the five things from which Jupiter consists, made from himself; one is of himself, and this is the proper horn; the others are four parts for the spirits sublimated and twice congealed. When these are joined, if copper <note>original: "cuprum"; the metal associated with the planet Venus.</note> is submerged in them, it will not lack silver. It is necessary, however, that the waters be fixed <note>A "fixed" substance is one that can withstand the heat of the fire without evaporating or escaping as vapor.</note>, otherwise they would not bring the work to perfection.

My son, do not despise the leprous man in your operations, because he is close to perfection <note>Alchemists believed tin was "near" to silver in its composition, requiring only the removal of its "leprosy" (impurities) to be transformed.</note>. For he himself has five horns: one proper to himself, and the others by accident—considering them as two and two, above and below—from which, if waters are made two by two, they contribute much to the perfections of the body. This body, being near to perfection, if it be submerged in them, it will not lack silver, just as its father does not lack it. Therefore, keep this secret for yourself. And again, its moisture mixed with the red servant <term>seruo</term> <note>original: "seruo"; the "servant" in alchemy often refers to a base metal or a specific reagent, such as sulfur or iron, that assists in the transformation.</note>, converts everything into the Moon <note>original: "Lunam"; the alchemical name for Silver.</note>. And when you wish to moisten and dry it often, it will retain the servant perfectly. Moses made gold from it. For it suffers from a hoarseness of voice <note>original: "vocis raucedinem"; a reference to the "cry of tin," the distinctive snapping sound heard when bending a bar of the metal.</note> along with a heap, and it possesses the misery of woodiness <note>original: "lignationis miseria"; likely referring to the brittle, fibrous texture tin can develop, or its tendency to "rot" into a gray powder.</note>, being of such rare decoction; wherefore it requires medicines. Yet it is itself a medicine when prepared with the servant and the foot of a million <term>pede milionis</term> <note>This may be a corruption of "pedem leonis" (Lion's Foot), a common name for the herb Alchemilla or a specific chemical weight.</note>, concerning whatever is suitable for it. When two conversions have been performed, it converts purified Venus <note>original: "venerem"; the metal Copper.</note>. Retain and preserve this, guard it and work it. Project one part over sixteen <note>This refers to "Projection," the final act of throwing a small amount of the alchemical Stone or powder into a molten base metal to transform the whole mass.</note>, and it will not lack the light of the Moon.

This medicine prevails in a similar manner. This has been proven in the equal weight of all its parts.

## *Another allegory of the wise.*

A certain King, wishing to surpass all other powers, prepared himself for war; and when he wished to mount his horse, he commanded one of the soldiers to give him to drink of the philosophical water, which he loved. The soldier said: "Lord, what is that philosophical water which you love?" And he replied: "That is the philosophical water which loves me above all others" <note>This "water" is often a metaphor for the universal solvent or "mercury" that dissolves the solid "king" or sulfur.</note>. The soldier indeed understood immediately, and brought it to him. The King, however, drank and drank again, until all his limbs were filled, and all his veins, and he then became greatly discolored. 

This being done, the soldiers said: "Lord, behold, mount the horse." He said: "I cannot." "Why can you not?" "Because I feel myself heavily weighed down, and my head aches, and all my limbs seem to be falling away from me, so it seems to me." "Furthermore, I wish for you to place me in my bright chamber, and place it in a warm, dry, and temperate location continuously through day and night; and thus I shall sweat, so that the philosophical water which I drank may be dried up within me, and I shall be delivered." Which was done, as he commanded. Open— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "Aperientes" (Opening); the catchword "rientes" at the top of the page indicates the continuation on the following leaf.</note>

The King's kin then hurried to the Egyptian and Alexandrian physicians, who were to be honored above all others. They all replied, "Yes."

"Which of you will be the masters of this work?"

The Alexandrians replied, "We shall, if it pleases you."

But the others <note>Presumably the Egyptians.</note> responded, "We do not wish it so. On the contrary, we wish to lead this deed, for we are more ancient than you, even though we appear younger."

The Alexandrians said, "So be it."

Then these masters took the King and tore him into tiny pieces <note>original: "membra minuta." They placed him, thus prepared, back into his bright chamber in a moderately warm place, just as before, and in the same manner for a day and a night.

Afterward, they brought him out looking like a dead man, though he still possessed a small spark of life. At this, all the King’s kin cried out: "Alas, the King is dead!"

But the physicians said: "He is not dead, but sleeps, and has now reached his limit."

They took him up again and washed him with warm, fresh water until the taste of the medicine was gone. Then they mixed him with an equal amount of a similar, new medicine <term>medicina noua: a fresh application of the chemical reagent or solvent to continue the purification</term>, and followed the same procedure in every detail. 

Then they brought him out and found him utterly dead. His kin then cried: "Why have you killed the King, you who were supposed to be such great masters?"

...they became obedient. Hearing this, they immediately came and said: "Lord, command us whatever you wish, and we will do it at once." Then, from that hour, all the kings and powerful men feared him more than any other in this world. And because of this, all who search for this stone go astray. The operation of this stone is described by the philosophers in many ways. For some rectify the materials individually, and afterward they compose and perfect them. That method of operation is varied in many ways; however, it is laborious, difficult, and subtle, and many fail in it, because many foreign things are required to support this operation. 

However, the true method of this art is a single linear path, and it is perfected in only one vessel. Yet its fire is not uniform throughout the entire action. And so that this treatise may be of benefit to students, I say that the fire necessary for this work is like the heat of the sun in the greater world <note>original: "mundo maiori." This refers to the macrocosm—the universe—as opposed to the microcosm of the alchemist's vessel.</note>. For in the springtime, the sun is moderate and gentle in its heat; otherwise the plants, which are tender, would be dried up and would never reach their fruit. This heat nourishes the plants until they grow little by little, and the more they grow, the more the heat of the sun gradually occurs, ascends, or increases, until the crops are whitened <note>original: "dealbentur." In alchemy, the "whitening" or albedo is a crucial stage where the matter is purified before reaching the final red state.</note>. When spring itself is finished, summer begins; then the heat is strong, and then strongest until the end of Leo <note>The zodiac sign of Leo, which corresponds to the height of summer (late July to August).</note>, until all things receive their due perfection and form.

Blessed be God, who by His wisdom has so wonderfully ordained it.

# HERE BEGINS THE LILY
## OF ALCHEMY; WHICH
### THE ROSARY COMPOSED: AND
-> it can be called <-
## THE LESSER ROSARY.

**N**ature is occupied with the Sun and Moon <note>original: "Solem & Lunam." In alchemical theory, these represent Gold and Silver, the "perfect" metals.</note> and the other Planets, and with a certain medicine <note>term: "medicina." In alchemy, the 'medicine' or 'elixir' is the substance that 'cures' base metals, transforming them into gold or silver.</note> for those intending to exalt them. Indeed, in this perfect teaching, which reveals many things that are hidden, symbolic, or figurative in those same subjects, and points out the deviations in the scriptures, all fruitless and vain expenses—as well as the labors of the persons involved—may be avoided. In this work, nothing is set down without mastery; you will find nothing else but what has been plucked from the sayings of the Philosophers. These sayings may please individuals, yet at the same time they are often found to be contradictory or foreign <note>original: "alieni." This refers to the "Decknamen" or secret names and metaphors used by alchemists to hide their meanings from the uninitiated.</note> to one another, so that if by chance something was omitted in what preceded, or was imperfectly proven, they may find it more fully joined in what follows. 

The title of this little book is deservedly called *THE LILY*, as if it were plucked from thorns <note>original: "de ſpinis euulſum." This suggests the text provides clarity and beauty by extracting the truth from the "thorny" and difficult writings of earlier alchemists.</note>. And lest it be left in doubt in anyone's mind who wishes to inquire about the order of the things to be treated—why the worthier things, such as the medicine and the Sun, do not come first? Instead, first the Moon, second the Sun and the planets with certain other extraordinary things, as will be seen below; and thirdly the matter <note>The "matter" refers to the raw material or *prima materia* used to begin the Great Work.</note> is placed, so that the doubter may be satisfied in this way: because the end is worthier than the beginning, or otherwise and better, or less. Since...

For the substances that whiten and those that redden are the same, nor can the red be made unless the white precedes it, as Amphoreus <note>A figure mentioned in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical assembly text.</note> the Philosopher says: "Know that unless you whiten this stone, you cannot make the red through which the dyeing is accomplished." Concerning this, hear the Philosopher saying: "When all investigators of the art see that whiteness appearing and emerging over everything in the vessel, be certain that the redness is hidden within that whiteness. And this is not without reason. Thirdly and finally, let the preceding manner be understood as a gradual perfection: just as it is said of the Father, from whom proceeds the Son, and from both the Holy Spirit.

Now therefore, he who has ears to hear, let him hear and understand Eximeneus <note>Another philosophical figure from the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> speaking in the Assembly of the Philosophers: "Know, all you who persevere, that no true tincture <note>term: "tinctura." And know that one element burns another, and one destroys another; and one strengthens another, and teaches it to fight against the fire. For the elements, when diligently cooked by the fire, rejoice and are turned into alien natures; thus, that which was liquefied is captured, the moist indeed becomes thick and dry, the body becomes spirit, and the spirit becomes a staining agent <note>original: "spiritus tingens"</note>, fighting strongly against the fire. 

Therefore the Philosopher says: *Convert the elements, and you shall find what you seek.* To "convert the elements" is to make the moist dry, and the volatile <note>original: "fugiens," literally "fleeing." Nor is the stone ever diminished by it, since they have been nourished by that very fire. Will a mother kill the son whom she has nourished? Certainly not.

Let no one wonder that through the various sayings of the Philosophers, you will find the names of the aforementioned three—namely, soul, body, and spirit—to be varied. For sometimes they are called "uterine brothers" <note>original: "fratres uterini," meaning brothers born of the same mother/womb.</note>, and rightly so, because they proceed from the same womb. Likewise they are called companions, and truly without envy as partners; for never is one truly separated from the other, although to the sight they may seem superficially segregated; indeed, one cannot exist without the other. For their spirits are tempered through the way of perfect nature; thus they are not separated from one another, as Geber, King of the Persians <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in both Arabic and Western alchemy.</note>, says in the *Book of Roots*. 

Understand this, however, according to the saying of Bonellus <note>Another frequent authority cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note>: namely, that without tempered heat and moisture nothing is ever generated; and a bath <note>original: "balneum." Refers to the *Balneum Mariae* or water bath, used to provide gentle, even heat.</note> with intense heat causes the work to perish; if indeed it is cold, the compound is put to flight, but through tempered heat, it becomes a sweet and suitable body. Sometimes all three are called "spirits," and not without cause: for even their earthiness or thickness, which is called "earth," becomes spiritual air and subtle, all of which consist in the same thing or in our "air"; which is as a body, or made from bodies.
