Likewise, Esistes says: *Take the stone of gold, and mix it with the moisture which is permanent water, and place it in its vessel over a gentle heat, so that it may liquefy, because it, standing, receives the <term>tincture</term>* <note>The "tincture" is the transformative power or color-essence that allows the alchemist to transmute metals.</note> *namely from the spirit lying hidden within it.* Concerning which Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founding father of alchemy.</note> says: *Behold the hidden spirit, and do not despise it; for in it remains the great secret <insert>worthy</insert> to have a greater union with its brothers, that is, the soul and the spirit.* 

This, however, happens so that it may receive the tincture after the companions are truly joined—namely, after the <term>whitening</term> <note>original: "dealbatio." Also known as the *albedo* stage, where the matter is purified of its blackness.</note>. For by that whitening, the spouses are truly associated and united; and that which the female did first <note>In alchemical allegory, the "female" often represents the volatile, cold, or moist principle (mercury), while the "male" represents the fixed, hot, or dry principle (sulfur).</note>, she then <insert>begins</insert> to suffer from the male, or from the quicksilver. ### The Lesser Rosary

...and the female is called the primary power of our honorable stone, and it is called the sharpest vinegar, according to that saying: grind it with vinegar, namely the sharpest, and cook it until it thickens, and beware lest the vinegar turns into smoke and perishes <note>original: "ne acetum in fumum vertatur." The male indeed receives from the female the dyeing spirit, as Socrates <note>Here referring to a legendary alchemical authority, not necessarily the historical Greek philosopher.</note> says: and know that unless you whiten this stone, you cannot make it red. This water, however, is called vinegar; whence "grind it with the sharpest vinegar."

### The Lily of Alchemy, or

...it is. However, it does not possess motion of itself, unless it is perfected by art and operation. Therefore, it was said by the philosopher: "Son, extract the shadow from its ray," as *Mundus*, *Theophilus*, and *Hermes* say. Therefore, our operation is necessary, just as we see in the case of an infant who, as far as its creation is concerned, is born perfect, but is imperfect regarding its function, unless the infant is first nourished with a little milk, then more, then finally stronger food. 

And so it is in our operation: first with a little fire, then more—specifically after the whitening <note>original: "dealbationem." This refers to the *albedo* stage, where the matter becomes white and pure.</note> until the reduction to ash <note>original: "cinerationem." A process of calcination or burning to a powdery state.</note>; and finally, that is, after the reduction to ash until the stronger redness <note>original: "rubedinem." The final *rubedo* stage, representing the completion of the Great Work.</note>. For without fire, nothing is ever generated, as *Bonellus* says: for the death and life of the elements are brought about by fire, as *Hortolfus* and *Pythagoras* say; that matter requires fire. 

Therefore, we must see to the operation of our stone, according to the sayings of *Geber*, as he says in the *Book of Roots*. Furthermore, the operation is performed so that its tincture <term>tincture|The spiritual or medicinal essence capable of "dyeing" or transforming the inner nature of a substance.</term> may be improved beyond what is in its natural state, and also so that it may become an elixir within the allegory of the wise—composed from the species of the stone—a seasoning, an antidote, a medicine, and a cleanser of all bodies that are to be purged, cured, and transformed into true silver-making <note>original: "Lunificum," from *Luna* (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver.</note> and gold-making <note>original: "Solificum," from *Sol* (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold.</note> properties. 

What is *Alchemy* but an administering or ministerial art containing the essence of the seven metals, showing how their forms may be led from a state of deficiency to the natural completion of their natures? Or otherwise, as a second philosopher says: *Alchemy is a certain hidden governance, which is performed by the hand of sons generated for that purpose, toward that which grows young again through the sons.* Or otherwise and better: *Alchemy is a corporeal substance composed of one and through one, joining more precious things to one another through congeneration and effect, and the same na...*

### Lesser Rosary.

...by a natural commixture of a better disposition, converting the natures. For why is the stone that corporeal substance, composed from one and through one, which contains two very thin moistures—namely, the soul and the spirit—so that within it is the spirit we seek? By this spirit, we may tint <note>original: "tingamus." In alchemy, to 'tint' or 'tincture' is to fundamentally transform the inner nature and color of a metal.</note> anything within a body and lead any of them from their state of diminution toward the natural completion of their natures. 

For it is called spirit—that is, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum." Mercury, the fluid principle of matter.</note>—the carrier of the virtues of the soul—that is, of sulfur <note>original: "sulphuris." In the sulfur-mercury theory, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle.</note>—through the body and the bronze <note>original: "æs." This refers to 'aes hermeticum' or the 'philosopher's brass,' a stage of the metallic matter.</note>, which is called spiritual gold. This was hidden in the body of magnesia <term>magnesia|A cryptic name for the primary matter of the stone, not to be confused with modern magnesium; it was often described as the 'mother' of the stone.</term> according to what is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the most influential early Latin alchemical texts, written as a record of a debate among ancient sages.</note>: "Son, extract from the ray its shadow," that is, from the sun its earthiness. 

Magnesia is indeed so named because within it lies a great secret <note>original: "magnum arcanum." The author suggests an etymological link between "Magnesia" and "Magnum."</note>, as Phieras says. But before you come to the operation of our stone, let anyone seeking this science take heed, lest they fall into wandering and error; for the Philosophers have named this stone of ours in such diverse ways. They call it sometimes by the name of stones, sometimes animals, sometimes vegetable things, sometimes salts, sometimes alums, sometimes spirit, sometimes body, sometimes an egg, or by the name of any other thing. 

This is because in its operation, all colors that can be imagined in the world today appear. And so, according to the various colors appearing in the work, its names are diversified by the philosophers. There is also another reason: that this stone is perfected from all four elements; therefore, they call it by the name of any elemental thing. And there is a third reason—namely, so that the foolish might not recognize this stone; for if they knew it, they would not sell it at such a cheap price as they do.

### Lily of Alchemy, or

For even if they sometimes call this thing by its proper name, they always add something fictional to the name for this reason: so that the Stone itself does not become known. And Mundus <note>original: "Mundus." A philosopher cited frequently in the *Turba Philosophorum*, often associated with the cosmological foundations of alchemy.</note> gives this final reason: let him who wishes to work know, before he proceeds to the operation, what it is he works upon. It requires a gentle fire and appears like a corpse for many days, like a man in his tomb. And afterward, God returns its soul and spirit to it, and with its infirmity removed, it is created. 

And even after its creation—that is, after the whiteness <note>original: "albedinem." The *albedo* is the second major stage of the alchemical Great Work, signifying purification and the achievement of a silver-like state.</note>—it is refined until it becomes a more perfect ash through a more intense fire. And know that when the fire is present, you have mixed it most perfectly because that ash receives the spirit; and you must moisten it again with moisture under a more intense fire until it assumes the colors of dry saffron, or burnt blood, or pomegranate syrup <note>These colors indicate the *rubedo* or "reddening," the final stage of the work which represents the perfection of the Stone.</note>. Does it not seem that "sperm" is not produced from blood unless it is cooked quite diligently during the process until it possesses intense heat? Yet nothing new is added to that sperm. Similarly, let our spiritual "sperm" <term>sperm|In alchemical theory, "sperm" refers to the concentrated "seed" or essential mineral vapor of a substance, rather than a biological fluid.</term> be in a state of putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactione." The *nigredo* or black stage, where the matter decomposes to be reborn.</note>, as Pythagoras and Bonellus <note>Two of the legendary sages featured in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> say. 

Although I have said above that this Stone is vile <note>original: "vilem." Often translated as "cheap" or "common," referring to the alchemical paradox that the most precious substance is made from something everyone overlooks.</note>, there is nonetheless something precious within it: namely, the hidden and concealed "tinting spirit," which is invisible, just like the soul in the human body. For the precious is not made without the vile, nor the vile without the precious. This Stone is ground with its own "water" until it drinks all that moisture, and from this, it receives the "battle of fire" which is imminent at the furnace. And then it is called "rust" <note>original: "rubigo." Likely referring to a deep reddish-brown state of the oxidized matter.</note> and it putrefies diligently until it becomes a spiritual powder, which the fire—having been overcome by the help of the "flying wind"—has introduced and colored with an unchangeable color.

Therefore, kings searching for this Stone have not found it, except those to whom God has granted it, as Barsen <note>An alchemist often identified with the figure Baibar or related to early Arabic sources.</note> says. However, this Stone which we seek is sold openly for a very small price,

# The Lily of Alchemy, or

...it, namely nature, as is said below in the same book. And since nature does not correct nature, therefore in its own nature it intends another thing to proceed, according to Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundation of alchemy is attributed.</note> and his followers. And then let him walk by the straight path; he shall work only around our Stone. She who says she does not know herself is wandering; but if she says she knows herself, ask what the nature of the Stone itself is. Concerning which, hear Parmenides <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher often cited in the "Turba Philosophorum" as an alchemical authority.</note> saying:

> O nature of that celestial truth, for they multiply by the will of God; O nature, the very strong water <note>original: "aqua fortis." While this later referred to nitric acid, in this context it signifies the "mercurial water" or universal solvent of the alchemists.</note>, by which she has conquered and overcome natures, and makes her own natures rejoice and be glad.

This, therefore, is specifically what its Lord is, and to whom He grants after Himself that which fire cannot do. And therefore we magnify and honor her, because nothing is more precious than the true <term>tincture|The "active ingredient" or medicine of the Stone, capable of "staining" or transmuting base metals into gold</term>, since its like or equal is not found at all: for she herself is liquefied truth, which, with her bodies, performs the highest work of works. Know, therefore, that the tinting agent overcomes all things and those which are mixed with it, and turns them into its own color: and just as in the case of sight it conquers the surface and overcomes the innermost parts for itself: and if one part is fleeing <note>original: "fugiens." Meaning volatile, or likely to evaporate when heated.</note>, but the other is enduring the fire <note>original: "ignem patiens." Meaning fixed, or stable and non-volatile under heat.</note>, both joined together endure the fire. And if a cloud has whitened the surface of the altars <note>original: "aris." In alchemical symbolism, "whitening the altar" often refers to the *albedo* (whitening) stage of the process, where the matter is purified.</note>, without doubt the innermost parts will be whitened. 

Likewise, ask what the soul of the Stone itself is, and what the spirit, and what the body, and about other superimposed circumstances of the same Stone. And if he says he wishes to work around our <term>stone|The Philosopher's Stone</term> and to know it, ask whether there are any best aids or supports for the operation of our stone? And if he says yes, you are deviating from the truth by far: but if he says no, it is well indeed. For the soul, body, and tinting spirit are together one thing, having all things in itself, to which nothing is added, and to which nothing foreign is introduced, as Sinon <note>Likely referring to a speaker in the "Turba Philosophorum."</note> says.

## The Lesser Rosary.

And the same is said by Rosinus, Ascanus, and Orfoltus, and many other Philosophers in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers) was a highly influential alchemical text, written as a record of a fictional debate between ancient Greek and Arabic sages.</note>: there is one thing, one power, one disposition, one work, one way; the whole <term>mastery|magisterium; the completed process of the Great Work</term> is completed by this. From this one thing, as if from a root, everything else is taken—the powers and the <term>tincture|the active agent of the Stone capable of transmuting metals</term> which is contained within it. For their <term>regimen|the method of governing the chemical process</term> is one, as Bacsen says, and there is one action: namely, to cook patiently and continuously. Concerning this, hear Bacsen <note>Bacsen (or Barsen) is a name often appearing in the "Turba Philosophorum," representing an early alchemical authority.</note> saying:

> O seekers of this art, you cannot arrive at its benefit unless you possess a patient spirit and maintain a continuous regimen.

Therefore, let him who willingly enjoys patience enter into this preparation. But he who desires to arrive too quickly should not look at our books, for they cause great harm before they are understood by higher minds, having been read only once, twice, or thrice. And therefore the Master says: he who bends his back in reading our books, and devotes himself to them, and is not entangled in vain thoughts, and prays to God—you shall reign without fail until death.

Woe to you! You seek the greatest treasure of God, and yet you do not understand the reward. People of this world give themselves to death to achieve even the smallest worldly purpose; what then should they do for this most excellent art or offering? In its power, its governance is almost greater than can be perceived by reason, except through divine inspiration.

Woe to you, sons of doctrine! For any of you who grafts a tree does not hope to have fruit except after a time. And he who sows seeds does not hope to reap except after the coming harvests. How then do you wish to have the result after reading a book once, or after trying the regimen only once? For truth is not discerned except through error.

Understand, therefore, lest you wander from the words, how he has divided the work. Also, cook it; repeat the process, and let it not weary you. For he divided the work into these parts: to mix, to cook, to sublimate, to roast, to heat, to whiten, to grind, to water, and to make <term>Ethelia|An alchemical term for a vaporous or volatile spirit, often associated with the 'soul' of mercury</term> into rust <note>original: "rubiginem"; in alchemy, the "rust" or "redness" often refers to the final stage of the work where the substance turns red (the Rubedo).</note>.

### The Lily of Alchemy, or

*...and to <term>tinge|tingere; to dye or transmute base metal into gold or silver</term>. But if someone knew the whole <term>mastery|magisterium; the complete alchemical process</term> and did not work, even if he were more subtle than all other men, what would his standing be among those who are wise, or those who know? And if he should say that he fears kings and men, perhaps he does; God gave him the knowledge and took away its utility by sending fear into his mind. Therefore...*

### The Lesser Rosary

...should ask God that, after receiving knowledge, He might grant him great understanding concerning the operation; such a person fears neither king nor men. This is also to avoid the diversification and multitude of vessels which the <term>Alchemists|Alchymici</term> use in their various operations.

It must be known that among the Philosophers, they attribute only a single vessel to this operation of ours, concerning which hear Theophilus saying: "I notify you that the <term>dragon|draco; a common metaphor for mercury or the raw, volatile matter of the Great Work</term> never dies; yet the philosophers, by killing their wives—his consorts—gave them over to death: for his belly is full of poison." <note>This allegory describes the chemical stabilization of a volatile substance through union with a "fixed" one.</note> Let a tomb also be dug for the dragon, and let the woman be buried there with the dead man, who is strongly joined to that woman: and the more he is turned, and the more he revolves around her, the more his body is cut into pieces; and having been mixed with the limbs of the woman, he is surely made dead, and the whole is turned into blood. And Bonellus <note>Bonellus is one of the many sages cited in the "Turba Philosophorum," a famous early Latin alchemical assembly text.</note> says, "place it in its own vessel"; and Eximeneus says, "let it be extracted while in the vessel"; and Exister says similarly, as does Mirisindus: "in a narrower vessel"; and Mireris says, "it is necessary to sift it with its own sieve." Many others speaking of the operation always speak of the vessel in the singular. This vessel ought to be of stone and pottery or millstone-clay, fearing neither the fire nor the subtlety of the compound—that is, <term>our water|aqua nostra; the specialized solvent or mercurial liquid used in alchemy</term>. For few vessels, or almost none of those used by glassmakers, endure, because they are corroded in the work and split apart; its hollow space should have a capacity of two pounds.

Fit the bronze of our body into thin plates or draw it out into sheets—as Theophilus and Aristeus say—pure, clean, raw, pleasant, <term>crab-like|cancri; possibly referring to the sign of Cancer or a specific crust-like state of the metal</term>, and straight, as Pandolfus and Orsoltus remark, whose body's fourth part is diminished among its <term>cookers|decoctores; those who refine substances through heat</term>, as Ascanius says. # The Lily of Alchemy, or

*...to treat through a plurality of compositions, nor by those things which the Philosophers have set down in their books; for our Truth is one, which changes that which is natural, because that natural secret* <note>original: "arcanum"</note> *is hidden in its belly; it is neither seen nor known except by a wise person. <meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the chemical transformation of the "stone," shifting from the general theory of colors to the specific use of the "sharpest vinegar" and the management of heat. It builds on the previous page's discussion of the "whitening water" by detailing how to transition from the black stage (nigredo) to the white stage (albedo).</meta>

### The Lily of Alchemy, or

The first power of our stone is called the **sharpest vinegar** <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; in alchemy, this is not household vinegar but a potent, "philosophical" solvent used to break down metals.</note>. Concerning this, it is said that vinegar is the water that introduces any color into a metal, and even into stones that do not easily melt. So that one may know how to tint metals, let them inquire what this vinegar is; however, let them not use common vinegar when intending to create precious stones. Regarding this vinegar, one must also be careful in our work that it is not turned into fire through excessive heat.

Likewise, the vessel must be strongly covered from the heat of the furnace, and its mouth must be strongly covered from above. This cover should have a hole through it crosswise, so that the **flower** <note>original: "flos"; refers to the volatile spirit or the finest substance that rises during heating</note> does not escape, but rather keeps its companion with it and allows its whiteness to be observed. As Lucas says: *for through gentle boiling* <note>original: "decoctionem"</note> *the male receives the tinting spirit from the female.*

Regarding the second part of the water, this is what Efistes says: *I command you, however, not to pour the water all at once, lest the elixir* <note>original: "ixir"</note> *becomes too black.* But when you have divided the water during the process, hear what Therum says: *Cook the male, that is, **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term>, together with the vapor until both are coagulated and become the stone; for then you will have divided the water.*

Therefore, the tinting spirit is life-giving; let it enter after the corrupting moisture has departed, for it is a living thing <note>original: "animal"</note> once it has reached the state of **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"</note>. And this is what Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy.</note> says in his catalog of humors: *For heat in a moist body first produces **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem"</note>, then strips it of that blackness when it has entirely finished off its moisture; and when heat overflows within it, it makes the body white, as can be seen in the lime* <note>original: "calce"</note> *made by common people.*

Thirdly, through an increase in the intensity of the fire, the compound must be incinerated into earth—that is, reduced to ash. And this is the ash of which Morigenes <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit and alchemical teacher.</note> speaks, saying: *Do not despise the ash,* etc.

# The Minor Rosary

And it is said there, that when nature is returned to the ash itself as a sweat or liquefaction—specifically through a greater intensity of fire—the king is then crowned in the fourth and final stage by the second part of the water. And this is the king of whom Diamedes <note>An alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a Greek name like Diomedes or a pseudonym for a later medieval author.</note> says: *venerate the king and his wife, and do not burn them, nor drive them away by burning them with excessive fire, for you do not know when you will have need of those who refine the king and his wife.* Cook them until they become black, then white, then red, and finally let it become a tinting poison <note>original: "venenum"; in alchemical literature, "poison" often refers to a substance of such extreme potency and "penetrating" power that it can transform the very nature of a metal.</note>.

And it should be noted that the bodies are said to be "punished"—that is, whitened—by combustion <note>The process of heating a substance until it changes state, but here specifically without it melting into a liquid.</note>, which is to say, by moisture without liquefaction. Through this process, mortification <note>original: "mortificationem"; the alchemical "death" or breakdown of the base material, usually marked by a change to a black color.</note> is said to follow; this appears in the blackness, as I said before, which shows itself and is called both the "blackness" and the "cloud." 

Concerning this, Lucas says: *Take the cloud which your predecessors commanded you to take, and cook it with its own body, because that smoke is white and whitens all things.* By this smoke, as many things as are commanded to be whitened are indeed whitened. Therefore, mix that smoke with its own dregs <note>original: "faeci"; the solid residue or "lees" left after heating or distillation.</note> until it is coagulated and becomes exceedingly white. 

Then parch this <note>original: "exassate"; to dry or roast thoroughly through heat.</note> until it causes itself to sprout, since **magnesia** <term>magnesia; in medieval alchemy, this was not the modern element magnesium, but a generic term for the "mother" substance or the mineral base being transformed</term>, while it is being whitened, does not allow the spirits to flee, nor the shadow of copper <note>original: "aeris"; here referring to the dark impurities or the "base" metallic nature that must be purged.</note> to appear. This is because "nature contains nature" <note>original: "natura naturam continet"; a famous alchemical axiom suggesting that substances of a similar origin or "spirit" naturally bind together.</note> due to their closeness to one another: for natures, when they encounter their own natures, rejoice. 

And one single thing performs what many things work at. Indeed, you do not need many things, but only one thing, and that one thing is turned into another nature in each and every grade of our works. In this blackness or "mortification," the souls are punished, and the colors of the soul do not appear until the body has finally been punished. Then the spirit is returned to both; this spirit, as far as the sight is concerned, appears to be separated from them, though it was with them substantially. For the spirit never dies, because it is nothing—

And thus is that saying <gloss>saying</gloss> of the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or an early authority like Pseudo-Democritus</note> to be understood: For nature rejoices, namely in the meeting of its own: nature conquers nature <note>original: "natura naturam vincit"</note> by mortifying, and vivifying the body, because it was from it, and into it it is converted, and is augmented and multiplied, and God extracts many from one similar thing. Similarly our bronze <term>æs: while literally "bronze" or "copper," in this context it refers to the base metallic matter at the start of the work</term>, when it is first cooked, becomes water; and the more it is cooked, the more it is improved, until it becomes a stone, which the envious <note>original: "invidi"; a common alchemical term for those who wish to keep the secret of the Stone hidden from the unworthy</note> then call the stone looming over every metal.

And upon this very root all things are founded; but because this foundation of the work has little root, and since the virtue of this root does not abound equally—just as the brightness of the sun is not equal among the planets—patience and delay are necessary. Wherefore Sinon <note>Another figure from the alchemical tradition, often associated with the *Turba* or the *Septem Tractatus*.</note> said: if anyone introduced to this art knew its nature, he would endure the lengthiness of cooking until the goal was extracted by the will of God. # The Minor Rosary. 363

within, so that the external corrects the internal, and the internal corrects the external, until the red is turned into white <note>original: "rubeum vertatur in album"; referring to the major alchemical stages of Albedo (whitening) and Rubedo (reddening)</note>, that is, that which was red hidden within the body is turned into an appearing white in the first part of the work; and that white is turned into an appearing red in the final part of the work, so that they might correct each other in turn. And this is what Bonellus <note>An alchemical authority often cited in early medieval texts like the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: "Unless that which corrects it is within that very thing, what you seek will not come to pass." And it must be noted that the body then receives the tincture <term>tincture: a potent liquid or substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</term> and is said to have greater power when joined with its brothers, namely, the soul and the spirit, as was said before. For it overcomes all things that are mixed with it, and turns them into its own color and spirit, as I have stated above. The spirit is the carrier of the virtues of the soul through the body and the opening; thus the son is said to correct the father, first by mortifying him <note>original: "mortificando"; in alchemy, 'mortification' refers to the symbolic death or breakdown of a substance so it can be reborn in a higher form</note>. And this spirit is properly called the liquefaction, or the soaking, or the moistening, or the infusion of water, as I have previously said according to the allegory of all the wise men. Dry fire is the tinting agent; air is that which truly confirms and binds; water is the whitening agent that expels blackness <note>The *nigredo* stage, or the "blackness" that must be cleansed</note> from the body; and earth is the stable foundation that receives the tincture. 

But why did the Philosophers not agree on the duration of this combustion or roasting? Perhaps it was due to the difference in locations—the moist and dewy versus the dry—because in a moist environment this work congeals more quickly, and in a dry one more slowly, as Ascanius says, agreeing with Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>. And let it be continually repeated until it becomes visible to the sight: for the very change of the work shall teach you. Or you may hold at your pleasure with those who speak of a longer space of time; for each perhaps wrote according to his own experience. 1. By the humidity of winter—that is, the application of moisture—which is the first humor and fruit. 
2. Then by the heat of the air and the coming forth of the flower, which is likened to spring in its gentle heat. 
3. # The Lily of Alchemy, or

<meta>catchword: body,</meta>

the work turns yellow <note>Latin: *citrinatur*</note> and becomes red; yet it is not a true red color, and it is dried and liquefied many times. One should not be concerned with these sorts of colors—specifically those that appear before the "cooking of the whiteness" <note>The *albedo* stage, where the matter reaches a state of silver-like purity</note>—because they are not the true colors. Then, in the union of soul, body, and spirit, all colors will appear, and then they are fixed, and they all converge into one color, namely whiteness. From then on, as has been said, the work turns yellow and finally the work becomes red ----- From that point, this becomes the spirit <note>The volatile essence that has been "fixed" or made stable</note> with which we may dye <note>Latin: *tingamus*, referring to the alchemical "tincture" that changes the nature of a substance</note> any body, and naturally lead any of them from a state of deficiency to its natural perfection. We may also make malleable glass, and even create a carbuncle <note>A legendary deep-red gemstone said to glow in the dark, often identified with the Philosopher's Stone itself</note> from crystal. A small quantity of our Elixir <note>Latin: *Ixir*</note>, when mixed in a small amount during the operation of the planets <note>Alchemical work was often timed to astrological cycles</note>, can transmute a thousand parts, and each of those thousand into another thousand, until the number is complete.

It now remains to look at the final and more worthy part of our treatise, namely medicine. For since man is the most noble creature—for whose sake all things were invented and to whom they are subject, and whose body is beyond price, as all divine and human law bears witness—it is rightly the case that we must seek with the greatest diligence, above all other things, that which may preserve him in health and long life by driving away all ill humors and weaknesses. Our Elixir <note>Latin: *Ixir*</note> performs this better than all the medicines, potions, or various concoctions of Galen, Hippocrates, Avicenna <note>The three primary authorities of medieval medicine: the Greeks Galen and Hippocrates, and the Persian polymath Avicenna</note>, and other philosophers. For it drives away all weaknesses and even leprosy, and keeps one unharmed from future illness so that it does not arise. Let everyone observe through probable and necessary reason how these things come to pass: for as it was said above, this is the spirit we seek, so that with it we may dye any body in

<summary>This page describes the final color transitions of the alchemical Great Work and introduces the "Elixir" as a universal medicine superior to traditional remedies. The author emphasizes that the Elixir's primary purpose is to preserve human health, the most valuable of all earthly concerns.</summary>

### Minor Rosary

body, and thus it becomes an antidote and medicine for curing and purging all bodies. Through this, the spirit is said to be the carrier of the virtues of the soul through the body and the copper <term>copper: the Latin *as* usually refers to copper or bronze, but in alchemy, "our copper" refers to the base metallic body undergoing transformation</term>. For our copper is like a human being, because it possesses a body and a spirit—as Bonellus <note>An authority frequently cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an early alchemical assembly text</note> says—and also a soul, as was stated above. And this is achieved by the nourishing material fire, just as in the bodies of metals, which have no movement of their own except that which comes from our Elixir <note>original: *Ixiri*</note>. Therefore, it acts much more strongly upon human bodies, which naturally possess an innate heat and readiness for movement; it repels every illness and provides both comfort and nourishment as it drives out superfluities.

This medicine, when added to medicinal compounds <note>Latin: *confectis*, referring to prepared medical syrups or pastes</note>, protects the patient so that no future disease may take hold of them. This is true for each of its humors. It is common knowledge among men that great lords, when they seek to preserve their health and youth, have gold added to their medicinal compounds—and in no other way. But if that gold is added in its raw state, it can only perform the aforementioned tasks [weakly], because gold cannot be perfectly digested <term>digested: the Latin *concoqui* refers to the alchemical process of "cooking" or maturing a substance until it reaches perfection</term> within those preparations. Therefore, how much more strongly must it perform these tasks when it has been turned into our Elixir or most perfectly refined by heat? For every medicine is made more penetrative and more effective at producing its results the more it has been refined <note>Latin: *subtilis*, meaning made "subtle" or less dense</note> by fire, as can be seen daily in the actual practice of medicine, etc.

->Here ends the Lily of the Rosary of Alchemy.<-
